about: Facts about trails from resort and club pages, beyond OpenStreetMap. hikes: the same for hiking trails (hike.js; level is the operator's difficulty). Descriptions are short summaries in our own words, each linked to its source. n: names (OpenStreetMap spellings first), matched within r metres of c. no: number on the official map, kind: the source's trail type, where: part of the mountain, km: the source's length. photos: bike parks' own photos of a trail, only where the park's page labels the photo with the trail's name; img/th stay on the park's site (linked, never copied), page is where it appears, by is the credit, cap is our own caption. hikePhotos: hand-picked Wikimedia Commons files (open licences, credited in the app, shown from Commons, never copied) for a hike with one of the names n within r metres of c; hike.js also finds more live by name.

Easy adaptive trail, about 5 km one way from the Montane trailhead (Montane Parkway: parking, map kiosk, outhouse) to Montane Hut. Tourism Fernie says its grade stays under 5% and it is shared with hikers year-round. Private land (Parastone), managed by the Coal Creek Heritage Society (donations).

Giveout zone (the upper face of Morning Mountain, south of Nelson): longer, old-school technical descents, with newer work adding flow and speed. The Nelson Cycling Club names it among the zone's trails to ride.

Giveout zone (the upper face of Morning Mountain, south of Nelson): longer, old-school technical descents, with newer work adding flow and speed. The Nelson Cycling Club names it among the zone's trails to ride.
One of the Ballers (Highballer and Lowballer) in the Giveout zone on the upper face of Morning Mountain: old-school technical descending, with newer work adding flow and speed.
A new, fast descent in the Smallwood trails, a Recreation Sites and Trails BC area built for cross-country and all-mountain riding. Sweet and Salty is the network's new climb trail.

Svoboda zone, inside West Arm Provincial Park: a long climb, then steep, bony trails with rock slabs and views of Kootenay Lake. The club says BC Parks permits riding in this zone, and asks riders to avoid it when the weather is very dry or very wet, and not to build new trails.

A point-to-point singletrack traverse of the Rossland Range, finished by the Kootenay Columbia Trails Society in 2004. IMBA Epic; Bike magazine's 2007 Trail of the Year. The riding area is the main trail, optional sections and the Dewdney Trail at the end.

At about 430 m in Trail, with sandy soil and a south aspect, it is usually one of the first trails to melt out in spring. Two-way, shared by riders and hikers. The Kootenay Columbia Trails Society describes the loop counter-clockwise from Gyro Park, with views of Trail, the Columbia River and the Rossland Range from the flagpole.

The climb into the Malde Creek trails, once a shuttle zone. The Kootenay Columbia Trails Society describes a 2 to 3 hour ride from the Centennial trailhead, out to Upper Drakes by the town trails and up Tamarack.
Neptune Creek area, about 12 km north of Rossland on Highway 3B by the Neptune Creek FSR. Kootenay Columbia Trails Society trail.
KC and Monte Christo trails on the north edge of Rossland, with several loop options; the top of KC Ridge looks over town. Parking at the Centennial trailhead (end of Washington Street).

An 18.6 km purpose-built cross-country trail through subalpine forest to alpine meadows, with a 5.7 km extension past a small lake (Frisby Vistas). Closed every year until July 15 to protect wildlife habitat, mainly grizzly bears. Prone to erosion when very wet. Remote, little water. The club lists Class 1 e-bikes as permitted since 2024. Advanced riders can descend to the valley by UFC and Ultimate Frisby. Trailhead about 9 km up the Sledhalla FSR (4x4 and radios suggested).
The 5.7 km extension of Frisby Ridge, past a small lake to the next high point. Closed every year until July 15 to protect wildlife habitat, mainly grizzly bears.
The Revelstoke Cycling Association's crew worked on it in May 2026; it can be reached from 6K on the Sledhalla FSR. With UFC, the long way down from Frisby Ridge to the valley.

Purpose-built climb trail of the Sunnyside network, on the southwest flank of Mount Mackenzie. One way, uphill. Hikers and runners may use it. The club lists Class 1 e-bikes as permitted. Southwest facing, so it tends to melt out earlier. Trailhead on Airport Way, 9.4 km south of the Illecillewaet River bridge; limited parking.
Sunnyside's rollercoaster-style descent. One way, downhill, for bikes only: no hikers or runners. The club lists Class 1 e-bikes as permitted. The club's crew groomed it in October 2026.

Managed by Recreation Sites and Trails BC, not the club. The first 2.5 km to the lookout melt out early in spring; beyond it is a long, hard push to the summit about 2,000 m above the valley, then a 15 km descent. Shared with hikers climbing it.

An expert descent of about 9 km and 1,580 m from alpine meadows to the valley, with steeps, big rocks, roots and sidehills. Managed by Recreation Sites and Trails BC. Low and mid-elevation access points; 4x4 needed on the Sale FSR (about 15 km to the top). Shared with hikers climbing it.
Adaptive bridge project finished October 2026: about 150 m of bridges and boardwalks on Flowdown and Stimulus rebuilt 120 cm wide, so adaptive mountain bikes (such as trikes) can ride them.
Adaptive bridge project finished October 2026: about 150 m of bridges and boardwalks on Flowdown and Stimulus rebuilt 120 cm wide, so adaptive mountain bikes (such as trikes) can ride them.
Phase 1 of a rebuild finished in September 2026: a new, more sustainable line bypasses the rutted chute, built by volunteers with the Revelstoke Cycling Association.
In fall 2026 the Revelstoke Cycling Association rebuilt the connector to it from the bottom of Snakes & Ladders, which skips a short road climb (October 2026 trail report).
The middle section was fully reworked in June 2026: berms refreshed, brake bumps smoothed and new jumps added.
Part of the 9 km figure-8 course of the club's Iron Horse XC race (2026), with Stimulus, Black Forest, Break-a-Leg, Root Canal and TNT on Mount Macpherson.

Part of Mount Macpherson's 40 km of singletrack linked by logging roads, provincial recreation trails run by the Revelstoke Cycling Association with Recreation Sites and Trails BC. Trails for first-timers to experts, some suited to adaptive riders. The club lists Class 1 e-bikes as permitted. Main trailheads off Highway 23 south.

Boulder Mountain, Revelstoke's main downhill area: fast and flowy to steep and technical, with wooden structures, jumps and drops on some trails. Provincial recreation trails maintained by the Revelstoke Cycling Association. Reached by the Jordan FSR, an active logging road (radios needed when shuttling, 4x4 suggested).

A designated blue, two-way trail climbing from Golden to the summit of Mount 7: 15.3 km and 1,625 m of climbing (Golden Cycling Club figures). Finished in 2018; the first semi-flow trail on upper Mount 7. Can also be ridden down.

Part of the old Psychosis race line, which the Golden Cycling Club lists among its sanctioned Mount 7 trails (three options, rated blue to double black). The club's 2023 trail plan survey measured about 315 m, typically around 55% steep, with notable erosion.
Golden Cycling Club rates it double black, one of the club's sanctioned Mount 7 trails. The club's 2023 trail plan survey measured about 3.1 km, typically around 50% steep, with notable erosion.
Golden Cycling Club rates it double black, one of the club's sanctioned Mount 7 trails. The club's 2023 trail plan survey measured about 1 km, typically around 40% steep with a steep start.

Part of the old Psychosis race line, which the Golden Cycling Club lists among its sanctioned Mount 7 trails (three options, rated blue to double black). The club's 2023 trail plan survey measured about 1.2 km, typically around 35% steep.
Golden Cycling Club rates it blue, one of the club's sanctioned Mount 7 trails and part of the old Psychosis race course.
Part of the old Psychosis race line, which the Golden Cycling Club lists among its sanctioned Mount 7 trails (three options, rated blue to double black).
Golden Cycling Club rates it black, one of the club's sanctioned Mount 7 trails. The club's 2023 trail plan survey measured about 780 m, typically around 45% steep, with notable erosion.
Golden Cycling Club rates it blue, one of the club's sanctioned Mount 7 trails, linking the Schacher to the 5 km trail.
Moonraker network: the Golden Cycling Club names it for fast, cornering descents. The network is mostly smooth and flowing, with four lakes and the Canyon Creek gorge.

Moonraker network's steeper technical terrain (Golden Cycling Club). Canyon Creek climbs and descends along the rim of a gorge more than 200 m deep: not for anyone uneasy with heights (Tourism Golden).

About a 10-minute pedal from Spirit Square in Golden: the first trail of the CBT network (2010), named for the Columbia Basin Trust grant that paid for it, and the way into the Moonraker trails. Signed post at every junction. Two machine-built jump trails in the network.
Connector between Kicking Horse Mountain Resort and the CBT and Moonraker networks, so riders can ride from the resort back toward town.
Double-track road; part of the multi-use network.
Wide fire road with gentle grades through cedar forest and good views. Made for riders who are new to riding off pavement.
Gravel road back to the base, much like Boom Trail.
Fire road used to get to the Provincial Park.
Starts as a wide gravel fire road and turns into wide trail with small berms, rollers and gentle grades through the trees.
One of Fernie's first downhill trails: fast, fall-line and technical through the forest. Racers love it.
Like Will Power, with more rock and loose soil.
Technical corners, several line choices and a few drops and jumps.
Steep pitches into supported corners, with off-camber roots.
Gentle and smooth, with twists, rollers and bridges through cedar forest. Good for families and kids.
Fast, steep and loose. Committing; experts only.
Fire road through Cedar Bowl to the Provincial Park. Expect long climbs to get back to the base.
Hand-built, winding trail through cedar forest beside Mr. Berms. Good for green riders practising berms and carrying speed.
Singletrack with some wooden features; a harder version of Hollow Tree.
Cross-country trail across the lower mountain through shady forest, with bridges over creeks.
Small berms and easy traverses up top. Halfway down you can go to Deer Trail, or carry on to the lower part with bigger berms, which leads to Honey Bee and Eville.
New in 2026: a blue jump trail for progressing, through shady forest and over a creek, ending at Holo Bike and Eville.
Black flow trail with big berms and advanced features. You need to be able to jump.
Short, playful jump trail into the base.
Classic steep singletrack down a cedar ravine, with steeps and drops and a flowy finish.
Medium difficulty, with natural roots, rocks and rollers.
Next to Phat Larry's, but with easier grades.
Home to the resort's biggest built wooden features.
Singletrack side route running alongside Cedar Trail.

Technical corners, off-camber roots and rocky sections, with valley views halfway down. A short top section (from Trespass Trail to Diamond Back) is double black for its must-do drops and rooty corners; the rest is black.
Technical but flowy descent with plenty of natural features.
Old-school downhill trail with rock rolls, tight corners and forest sections. Below Rock Landing the lower part adds technical features and jumps.
Fresh hand-built line in the forest, reached from Lower Rumplestumpskin.
Fire road across the mountain's bowls with big views and a lot of pedalling. Rated black.
Drops in from Diamond Back corner and takes a fast, direct line through steep old-growth cedars.
A favourite: fast, flowy berms and jumps. Every feature can be rolled, so it suits mixed-ability groups or riders stepping up.
Machine-built, fast way to get to Top Gun.
Warm-up trail across a ski run with berms and rollers. A good first blue trail.
Like Eville but bigger: fast, flowy berms and jumps.
Green flow trail through open forest back to the Holo Bike connector, with small jumps and berms to build confidence.
Tight trail through the forest with low ladders and bridges that test balance.
Technically demanding trail through shady forest, with some natural drops and roots.
A rebuild of the lowest part of TNT: machine-built jumps and rollers for progressing on flow and jump trails.
Short technical section that ends on a long wooden ramp down to the parking lot.
On the Kodiak run and as steep and technical as Kodiak Karnage: long steep, rooty chutes.
Flowy jump trail through big cedars near the base. Good for ending the day and working on jumps and berms.
Mellow, obstacle-free beginner trail with small berms, for learning to corner and getting used to gravity riding.
A downhill pump track: machine-built berms, rollers and table tops, rideable fast or slow, and good for learning to get air.
Carries on from Dirt Wave: pump the rollers to keep your speed.
High-speed flow trail with table tops and mogul-like rollers.
Intermediate jumps: a place to learn to jump or go bigger.
Park favourite with rollers, gaps and berms all the way down, plus options for bigger features.
Hand-built downhill track: a fast chute in, then a rough, rocky descent with loam and roots.
Steeper, faster flow trail with tight berms top to bottom.
The park's classic loam trail: several hand-built lines through natural features.
A faster, bigger Hot Lap on sandy dirt, with natural doubles and rollers.
Steep, fast loam trail with optional doubles, step-downs and a rock roll.
Hand-built, rooty singletrack with moderate drops and doubles.
Advanced jump trail with rollable table tops, gaps and optional side hits.
Relaxed jump trail that starts with a drop and ramp, then small gaps and steep berms: a step up for jumps and drops.
Starts with a wooden drop, optional doubles all the way, and a wooden gap at the end. Drops and gaps are mandatory.
Very fast, very big gap jumps (40 to 50 ft). Every feature is mandatory.
Jump trail with large gaps, built by the Coastal Crew. Every feature is mandatory.
Uphill only. One of two trails where riding up is allowed in the bike park.
The resort's starting trail: take the gondola to mid-station and ride it back to the village until you're comfortable.
Riding up is also allowed here (Big Easy Climb).
A beginner learning area with a small pump track, rocks and wooden features to build confidence before the park's trails.
Machine-built beginner flow trail with wide sweeping turns, small rollers, berms and wooden bridges; the next step after Lemon Squeezy. Named after Tim Peck, who worked at Grouse for 39 years.
Machine-built intermediate flow trail after Tim's Trim: gentle berms and rollers, with rock drops, wood drops and bridges, through forest and open meadows.
The park's main jump trail, aimed at intermediates but fun for experts: tabletops and tombstone-shaped jumps, tight berms and big fast berms.
Easy 3 km family trail from the summit with big views over the St. Lawrence River.

Flat gravel path along the river (5.7 km one way), busy with walkers. Parks Canada lists it for pedal-assist e-bikes. The part south of the soft-sided campground is closed May 15 to October 15. Starts at the campground or across from the train station on Sentinel Road.

The old highway, closed to cars (9.8 km one way): rough pavement from Lake Louise Drive over the Great Divide into Yoho. Parks Canada lists it for pedal-assist e-bikes. Its own parking lot is closed: start from the Lake Louise Lakeshore lot (paid).

Rooty, rocky singletrack (9.3 km one way, 485 m up) onto Mount Temple's shoulder, then down to Moraine Lake. No e-bikes. The upper part closes to everyone when the buffalo berries ripen (grizzlies): check the trail report. Starts 2.5 km up Moraine Lake Road, where parking is very limited.

n: Sobo No Michi - Climbing Trail - Upper
trails.text: UROC's climbing trail (ascent only), opened in 2020: just under 5 km with about 90 switchbacks, from the bottom of Broadway across Perseverance Creek to about 491 m, so riders and walkers can reach the upper network without using resource roads. UROC calls it a wide blue square trail. Its official name means Grandmother's Path.

n: Sobo No Michi - Climbing Trail - Upper
trails.text: UROC: the network's main climbing trail, often just called Sobo, and the start of the EPIC 979 route (2026), which climbs to the network's high point at 995 m.

UROC: continues the climb from Sobo No Michi, mostly on an old roadbed and then singletrack, up toward the Switchback access road. Part of the EPIC 979 route (2026), which climbs to the network's high point at 995 m.
UROC calls it a gruelling climb toward the Beaufort Range; the newer Okey Dokey climb on the EPIC 979 route (2026) bypasses it.
Part of UROC's EPIC 979 Ultimatum ending (black diamond, 2026): Upper and Lower Ultimatum, then Bear Buns, Sykes Bridge and Off Broadway back to the bottom of the climbing trail.
The last section of UROC's EPIC 979 Ultimatum ending (black diamond, 2026), which finishes at the bottom of the climbing trail (Sobo No Michi).
One of UROC's EPIC 979 endings (2026), rated double black diamond: a long descent from Upper Ultimatum that joins Prohibition and then China Creek Trail.
UROC calls it a double black diamond trail. In May 2025 its crew doubled the rock roll with a longer run-out and rebuilt the step-up.
Part of UROC's EPIC 979 Chunder ending (2026), rated double black diamond, between Chunder and China Creek Trail.
Part of UROC's EPIC 979 freeride-style ending (2026), Grub, Stub and Pity the Fool, rated double black diamond: gap jumps, drops, roll-downs and very steep terrain.
Part of UROC's EPIC 979 freeride-style ending (2026), Grub, Stub and Pity the Fool, rated double black diamond: gap jumps, drops, roll-downs and very steep terrain.
Part of UROC's EPIC 979 freeride-style ending (2026), Grub, Stub and Pity the Fool, rated double black diamond: gap jumps, drops, roll-downs and very steep terrain.
UROC: the climb to the start of Queso Grande and to the Grub, Stub and Pity the Fool descents (EPIC 979 route, 2026).
UROC's longest EPIC 979 ending (2026), rated double black diamond: about 7 km of technical descent with short climbs along the way.
UROC's EPIC 979 Chunder ending (2026) finishes on this trail, with an exit to Cumberland near the Coal Creek disc golf course.
In February 2026 UROC reported that flooding washed out significant sections of trail in the China Creek floodplain.
In February 2026 UROC reported major erosion around the wooden Perseverance Creek bridge near the end of Hai Gai and DCDH after a log jam, with the bridge's access points washed away.
The Village of Cumberland lists Hai Gai and the Hai Gai access trail with the Perseverance Creek bridge as closed since the January 30, 2026 flood (checked November 2026).

The Village of Cumberland signs it as a Gravity Trail: hikers yield to mountain bikers. The Village lists the Perseverance Creek bridge link from Chinatown toward this trail as closed since the January 30, 2026 flood (checked November 2026).

The Village of Cumberland signs it as a Gravity Trail: hikers yield to mountain bikers. The Village lists the Perseverance Creek bridge link from Chinatown toward this trail as closed since the January 30, 2026 flood (checked November 2026).
Village of Cumberland sign: Advanced, Gravity Trail (hikers yield to mountain bikers). In the Cumberland Community Forest Park.
Village of Cumberland sign: Intermediate, Gravity Trail (hikers yield to mountain bikers). It crosses from Village land onto private forest land, so it is managed by both the Village and UROC.
The Village of Cumberland signs it as a Gravity Trail: hikers yield to mountain bikers. In the Cumberland Community Forest Park.
Village of Cumberland sign: Intermediate, Nature Trail (best enjoyed on foot; the Village says mountain biking is not recommended). In the Cumberland Community Forest Park.
Village of Cumberland sign: Intermediate, Nature Trail (best enjoyed on foot; the Village says mountain biking is not recommended). In the Cumberland Community Forest Park.
The Village of Cumberland signs it as a Nature Trail (best enjoyed on foot; the Village says mountain biking is not recommended). In the Cumberland Community Forest Park.

Managed by the Village of Cumberland (Cumberland Community Forest Park). Since 2018 the Village has removed its old wooden features (ladders and skinnies) and does not plan to rebuild them, the Village said.
The Village of Cumberland signs it as a Nature Trail (best enjoyed on foot; the Village says mountain biking is not recommended).
Village of Cumberland sign: Intermediate, Multi-use Trail (all users prepare to yield).

The Village of Cumberland closed the northern part of this trail indefinitely because of the old bridge crossing there. The Village says the southeast part, with a new bridge built in 2022, is kept up and was not part of that closure.

Runs through the Space Nugget lands, bought in 2016 with funds from the Cumberland Community Forest Society and now part of the Village's Cumberland Community Forest Park, protected by a conservation covenant. A multi-use trail.

Village of Cumberland: an old coal railway grade along the south side of the village, from the foot of Sixth Street to Second Street, leading to the Community Forest trails, the mountain bike network and Coal Creek Historic Park.

On Middle Earth, a 261-acre forest of private timber land the Cumberland Community Forest Society set out to buy in 2025 to protect it; the society reports the purchase was completed on October 1, 2026. The society names this trail among the multi-use trails there.

Opened in 2023: a blue square cross-country trail built to the same gentle grade (about 5%) as Spaghetti Factory and Meatballs. With them and Buck Rub it makes a downhill-trending loop around the south side of Nikkei Mountain, toward the network's Eastern block. North Cowichan and the Cowichan Trail Stewardship Society rate it moderate (blue): 1.3 km built by Cowichan Tribes youth through a totem gateway, leading to the Xylem climb.

North Cowichan and the Cowichan Trail Stewardship Society: Race Trail, once called $1.87, is a 1.7 km descent rated most difficult (double black diamond on their map) on wide off-camber terrain. Mount Prevost's trails are for downhill riding.
North Cowichan and the Cowichan Trail Stewardship Society rate Mr. T most difficult (double black diamond on their map): a 1.4 km fast race-training descent with tight turns and steep pitches.

North Cowichan and the Cowichan Trail Stewardship Society rate Patchworks most difficult (double black diamond on their map): one of Mount Prevost's steepest trails, 1.8 km with technical corners and gap jumps.

Mostly downhill singletrack from the China Ridge trails to the Snowpatch Road near the km 2 sign. Starts about 350 m up the Ridge Trail from the Longhouse, at the L'ill Loop. Smooth with some banked turns, no drops or exposure; a few steep pitches in the middle make it intermediate. Follow the blue flagging where it crosses the Dixon and EYC double tracks.
Fully refreshed in spring 2026 by the Howe Sound Secondary outdoor leadership students.
