Maintenance in spring 2026 by the Howe Sound Secondary outdoor leadership students.
Easy valley-bottom trail. In spring 2026 SORCA and the Squamish Trails Society replaced its last narrow, rotten bridge and rebuilt the north end, so adaptive mountain bikes can now ride it.

n: Meadow of the Grizzly (Spélhx̱en tl'a Stl'lhalem)
trails.text: Rebuilt by a contractor in fall 2025, with drainage fixes in spring 2026. SORCA's April 2026 report had it open from the top down to Short Circuit, with work continuing below that (Howler).
Gravity Logic finished upgrades on all three parts (Pseudo 1, 2 and 3) in spring 2026, for both beginner and advanced riders. Still bedding in.
First phase of a rebuild by Gravity Logic done in spring 2026; work goes on below the Blindside connector.
Dig for Dave, spring 2026: a small reroute at the end of the last slab, the stump between the two slabs taken out, and repairs in between.
A section hurt by the wildfire was rebuilt in spring 2026: the burnt soil was dug down to the rock bench and the ramp behind the big fir armoured with rock.
New ramp up the steep embankment at the crossing (spring 2026, approved by Recreation Sites and Trails BC).
Dig day and trail crew work before the 2026 SORCA downhill race. Danger is steep and still bedding in; its line was marked better to stop riders braiding around it.

Big reroute in summer 2026 around the chunkiest part of the original trail, near the start: the new line is mostly bedrock and rock armour, with rolls that have options for every level. SORCA said the old line stays open for now; part of one go-around was closed. In fall 2025 the chunky traverse in the first 100 m after Marc My Word (the Pinball) got a new line too, and the old one was kept.
In summer 2026 a stump drop on Word of Mouth was lowered so it can be rolled, with the original builder's input.
SORCA's Climb Trail (once Legacy Climb), ridden uphill. Contractors did repairs and made it more efficient in fall 2025.
Reworked in fall 2025 with the Squamish Nation Youth Mountain Bike team to be friendlier to new riders and small wheels.
Small reroute by Mulgrave School students in fall 2025.
Maintenance by Mulgrave School students in spring 2025.
Also called Smoke-a-Butt. It passes a culturally important Lil'wat site: the plan asks riders to stay on the trail and not build or change anything on it.
Passes a petroglyph site, a protected Lil'wat cultural site: the plan asks riders to stay on the trail. Parts of the trail cross private land.

Mackenzie Basin is deer winter range: the plan asks riders to stay off the trails above the Waco Connector from December to February (a voluntary closure; walkers only). Hunters use the upper part in season.
The club calls it the Bluff's easiest trail, rated blue: flowy singletrack on a moderate grade with small A-frames and log rides, and one large ride-over. Starts at the Q junction.
About 3 km climb to the top of the Bluff, also ridden down as an easier descent. Uphill riders have the right of way, and many hikers use it.
Another way up the Bluff with many switchbacks; downhill it is moderate with a few technical sections. Two-way traffic. Links to All Screwed Up and Soul Stripper.

Fast and flowy. The upper part has technical corners and moderate steeps; the lower part has low boardwalks, a teeter-totter, small A-frames and small jumps, and shares a section with Smoothy. Starts from the P junction.
Fast, flowy finish to a Bluff ride, built in 2016 with funding from the Rotary Club of Smithers. Reached from Auntie Flo, Penetralia or near the start of Uptrack.
A Bluff classic with steeps, berms, drops, stunts and skinnies; some features are large. A double black cutoff branches left partway down. Starts from the P junction.
Rebuilt in 2009: smooth straights, tight berms and small airs. Starts at the Q junction and joins lower Apocalypse; the Bedpost drop is near the bottom.

One of the longest Bluff trails: old-school steeps with rocks and roots, log rides and tricky corners. The top half is much steeper than the bottom, which follows the Old Bluff trail to the pumphouse.

One of the oldest Bluff trails: very steep and rough, which the club says is for riders with solid technical skills. Off-camber turns, a rock drop, a small gap jump and a step-down; a ride-around skips the drop and gaps.
Wooden and dirt gap jumps, a long log ride, a step-up and a technical hip jump. The Bedpost drop near the bottom has a smaller and a larger line.
Steep, old-school trail; most of its old stunts have been removed. Ends at the pumphouse, near where Remembrance Day ends.

Built by WORCA as a blue trail and first ridden in fall 2016. Under Recreation Sites and Trails BC's newer rating standard (a blue trail is no steeper than 25% over any 5 m), WORCA re-signed the upper part black diamond and built a blue ride-around for the last steep ridge of the lower part (finished in early September 2026). Snow can sit around the lake into summer: in 2026 it lingered into late July.
WORCA changed its sign from blue to black diamond in 2026, after Recreation Sites and Trails BC's newer rating standard.
WORCA calls it Mid-Danimal and changed its sign from blue to black diamond in 2026, after Recreation Sites and Trails BC's newer rating standard.
Reworked by WORCA to keep its blue rating under Recreation Sites and Trails BC's newer rating standard.

One of Whistler's oldest trails, named after Wayne Gretzky rather than the highway. In spring 2026 WORCA volunteers built a ride-around to its straight chute, which measures as double black under the newer rating standard, so the trail can stay blue.

Part of the Dessert Platter, a blue route near the valley bottom. In 2025 and 2026 WORCA widened the tread, smoothed bigger obstacles, stretched turns and shortened the steepest bits to keep it blue under Recreation Sites and Trails BC's newer rating standard; the Cherry On Top switchbacks were widened in May 2026.

Short technical descents near the old Industrial Waste crossing. Since June 2026 WORCA's new access climbs the Dessert Platter and turns left halfway up Salted Caramel (before, the way in was the 35% grade of Leftovers or down Working Class). Baby Snakes was built as an all-down exit for Pura Vida.
Water crossings rebuilt in spring 2026, and the trail now joins Cat Scratch Fever properly: WORCA describes the run as a technical black descent that carries on into Mandatory and Mel's.
Upgraded by machine in spring 2026 (Howler Contracting, volunteer work). WORCA plans to keep making it a blue trail down to the towers, so parts may change.

Modernised by WORCA in 2025 and 2026 into a mostly downhill line: tight corners were opened up for longer bikes after work through the fire-thinned forest. Its slab catch berm was rebuilt larger in September 2026.

Part of WORCA's Far Out and Flashback adaptive mountain bike (aMTB) loop: climb Farside, descend Flashback 4 and 5. In fall 2026 the trail crew built a wider bypass on Flashback 2 (about 1.2 m of clear tread) and added berms, rollers and dips on Flashback 3 and 4; fresh tread can stay soft for a while. Flashback 4 now starts straight across the road from the McLaurin suspension bridge access trail.
The climb of WORCA's Far Out and Flashback adaptive mountain bike (aMTB) loop. The Resort Municipality of Whistler's trail crew upgraded lower Farside to the adaptive standard in 2026.
A long-time race test piece. After the dry 2026 summer left new steps on the crux climb, WORCA rebuilt the rockwork there in September 2026.
Bottom section smoothed and tread edges built up in September 2026 (WORCA with the World Indigenous Sports and Health Society).
Reached by the new Al Grey suspension bridge. In April 2026 WORCA rebuilt 5 m of old forestry road and cleared winter deadfall on the way in.

A popular multi-use trail at Alice Lake. SORCA says it was closed for about two years while a debris barrier was built next to it, and its October 2026 dig day worked on it so it could reopen later. Check SORCA for its current status.

In Garibaldi Park, BC Parks lists bikes (and class 1 pedal-assist e-bikes) on this trail from the parking lot as far as Singing Creek, and not past the bridge onto the Helm Creek Trail. Dirt surface. Day-use pass needed in summer.

In Garibaldi Park, BC Parks lists bikes (and class 1 pedal-assist e-bikes) from the Diamond Head parking lot as far as the Elfin Lakes shelter, on the main trail only. Rock and gravel surface; about 11 km and 700 m of climbing (BC Parks' estimates).
SORCA describes it as a progressive blue (intermediate) trail with optional black jump lines.
SORCA describes it as a progressive blue (intermediate) trail with optional black jump lines.

Tourism Squamish rates it Intermediate: a 1.8 km cross-country trail (about 15 to 20 min, their estimate) over rock, through ferns and leafy forest, technical in places, and often part of local races.

Tourism Squamish rates it Intermediate, 1.9 km, and says it suits beginner to advanced riders. Built by Big Red Ted Tempany and volunteers with a mini excavator; they call it Squamish's first government-funded bike trail.

Tourism Squamish rates it Intermediate, 1 km: fast and flowy with rollers; everything can be rolled, with some bigger optional features. Built by the Half Nelson builders, with input from Brandon Semenuk and Anthill Films. It joins Half Nelson about halfway down; reached by the Legacy Climb or Cakewalk.
Tourism Squamish rates it Intermediate, 2.2 km over its three parts: fast and flowy with rollable jumps, bridges and berms.
Tourism Squamish rates it Difficult, 1.2 km: loamy, with frequent roots and ladder bridges over drainages but no big features. It crosses Half Nelson.

Tourism Squamish rates it Intermediate, 1.7 km: short technical climbs to a high point, then a descent with hard root and rock sections that turns fast and flowy. Reached from Darwin's Crossing off Garibaldi Park Road.
Tourism Squamish rates it Easy to Intermediate, 4.1 km: a climbing trail at a mellow grade, an alternative to the forest road.
Tourism Squamish rates it Easy, 1 km: a descent at a gentle grade with many berms, reached from Mashiter Trail.
Tourism Squamish rates it Intermediate, 1.1 km: a short climb, then a bumpy machine-built descent, technical at the top and bermed lower down.
Tourism Squamish rates it Difficult, 1.9 km: downhill mixed with technical climbing, rock rollers, off-camber sections and a viewpoint about halfway.
Tourism Squamish rates it Intermediate, 1.3 km of cross-country singletrack with granite slabs, wood features and rollers.
Tourism Squamish rates it Difficult, 1.5 km of old-school technical cross-country: rock, roots and hard climbs.
Tourism Squamish rates it Difficult and calls it an easy black, with optional intermediate lines marked by plastic chicken signs.
Tourism Squamish rates it Expert, 1.1 km (10 to 15 min, their estimate).

Tourism Squamish rates it Intermediate, 1.2 km: a long singletrack climb from Jack's up to Mike's Loop. Its second part leads on to Leave of Absence, Rupert, Marc My Word, Pleasure Trail and Entrails.
Tourism Squamish rates it Easy, 1.3 km: a short trail along an old logging road through alder forest. It links with High Trail East.
Tourism Squamish rates it Difficult to Expert, 1 km: four or five granite slabs, a cross-country climb and a viewpoint over the Squamish Valley toward the Chief.
Tourism Squamish rates it Difficult, 1.3 km (15 to 20 min, their estimate): narrow, rocky and rooty singletrack with some granite slabs, wooden bridges and tight corners. It links with Half Nelson.
Tourism Squamish rates it Easy to Intermediate, 2.5 km (20 to 30 min, their estimate): old-style cross-country with many wooden bridges and rocky descents. Section 57 leads to it.
Tourism Squamish rates it Expert, 0.4 km: steep rock slabs with many hard rock rolls.
Tourism Squamish rates it Difficult, 1.6 km: woodwork, steep rocky sections, berms and some features with ride-arounds. It starts off Debeck's Grind above Alice Lake, at its north end.
Tourism Squamish rates it Difficult, 0.9 km: part singletrack, part machine-built, with flow and some jumps. It crosses several other trails on the way down.
Tourism Squamish rates it Difficult, 1.1 km: cross-country style with some rock rolls, woodwork and wood carvings.
Tourism Squamish rates it Expert, 0.6 km: a run of steep, grippy rock slabs.
Tourism Squamish rates it Difficult, 0.8 km: singletrack mixed with rollers, doubles and jumps.
Tourism Squamish rates it Difficult to Expert, 0.4 km, down one large rock slab.
Tourism Squamish rates it Easy, 2.1 km (20 to 40 min, their estimate): a forest trail ridden both ways, from Garibaldi Highlands to Alice Lake.
Tourism Squamish rates it Difficult to Expert, 1 km (20 to 30 min, their estimate): many technical granite features; they place it at the hard end of black.
Tourism Squamish rates it Intermediate, 1.3 km: a connector between Mike's Loop, 50 Shades of Green, Rupert, Leave of Absence, Entrails, Value Added and Treasure Trail.
Tourism Squamish rates it Difficult, 1.2 km: technical, with flowing sections. Built by hand over three years (about 3,400 hours) on Squamish Nation land.
Tourism Squamish rates it Easy, 4.8 km (30 to 45 min, their estimate): a large beginner loop with many easy and intermediate side trails, which they suggest for riding with kids.
Tourism Squamish rates it Intermediate, 1.3 km: cross-country with some climbing, woodwork and roots, and a bench with a view near the end.
Tourism Squamish rates it Difficult, 1.3 km: old-school, with short punchy climbs and some tricky features. It leads to Pleasure Trail.
Tourism Squamish rates it Difficult, 0.5 km: slab riding with views.
Tourism Squamish rates it Easy, 1.1 km: nearly flat, with some rocks and roots; they call it family friendly.
Tourism Squamish rates it Difficult, 1.8 km (15 to 35 min, their estimate): a hand-built descent with woodwork, rock slabs and rolls, roots, steep pitches and flow.
Tourism Squamish rates it Difficult to Expert, 0.7 km: a short punchy climb, then down the ridge line, with two optional double black slabs near the bottom.
Tourism Squamish rates it Intermediate, 1.1 km: a connector between Brackendale and the Alice Lake and Highlands trails, built to be ridden both ways.
Tourism Squamish rates it Intermediate, 1.4 km: a flowing connector between Fred and Your Mom.
Tourism Squamish rates it Intermediate, 1.3 km: tight turns through rainforest. It connects to Wonderland.
Tourism Squamish rates it Intermediate, 1 km: berms and flow after a short climb, then bridges and a steeper, more technical finish.
Tourism Squamish rates it Intermediate, 2 km (20 to 30 min, their estimate): ridden in more than one direction, on its own or to reach Cheshire Cat, with a wide wooden bridge.
Tourism Squamish rates it Easy to Intermediate, 3 km (15 to 30 min, their estimate): beginner cross-country with small roots, few rocks and small features, nearly all with ride-arounds.
Tourism Squamish rates it Intermediate, 1.3 km: cross-country with many ups and downs and roots. They call the upper part a black diamond; the two join for a longer ride.
Tourism Squamish rates it Intermediate, 1.1 km: a hand-built descent between Bob McIntosh Memorial and Mashiter Trail with berms and few roots or rocks.
Tourism Squamish rates it Easy, 1 km: a gentle trail under the power lines beside Squamish Valley Road, ridden both ways, with open views of the Tantalus Range. It shortens a Ray Peters Trail loop.
Tourism Squamish rates it Easy, 0.8 km: a short trail through trees beside the highway, ridden either way, on its own from Ray Peters Trail or linked with Live Wire.
Tourism Squamish rates it Expert, 1.6 km (30 to 50 min, their estimate): highly technical, with double black features; some are exposed, with drop-offs and cliffs below.

n: Meadow of the Grizzly (Spélhx̱en tl'a Stl'lhalem)
trails.text: Tourism Squamish rates it Intermediate, 3 km (10 to 20 min, their estimate): a crowd-funded trail known for its berms, often called dark blue for its steep forested slopes.
Tourism Squamish's Diamond Head guide (2020) calls Word of Mouth cross-country with plenty of ups, downs and roots; the upper and lower parts join for nearly 3 km.

Tourism Squamish's Diamond Head guide (2020) likens it to a long pump track with ride-arounds for every level. Parking it lists: the Squamish Adventure Hub on Garibaldi Park Road (bike tools, toilet), and more at the bottom of Half Nelson near the Ring Creek road.
Tourism Squamish's Diamond Head guide (2020) starts its advanced route here from Garibaldi Park Road, then Stl'lhalem Sintl', Angry M and Half Nelson.
On Tourism Squamish's 2026 early season list as a green trail: a wide path with few roots, close to Live Wire and Rusty Bucket.
On Tourism Squamish's 2026 early season list as a green trail ridden either way, with small roots and wooden features that have ride-arounds. They note some parts hold water after rain.
On Tourism Squamish's 2026 early season list (SORCA's pick) as green: used as a climb or ridden down as a mellow descent, from the end of Perth Road into Alice Lake Park, with a few steeper pitches.

SORCA says the Brackendale network (also called the Dump trails or Ray Peters) is mostly on private land, valley-bottom riding with little climbing, and often among the first trails in Squamish clear of snow.
SORCA's Dig Day #7 (September 20, 2026) worked on it, meeting at Carpenter's Son's Bridge.
SORCA's Dig Day on October 18, 2026 worked on it. SORCA puts the top of Brodown at the exit of Low Down 1 (Nightshift).
SORCA calls Low Down 1 Nightshift; it ends at the top of Brodown.
SORCA's Dig Day #10 (October 31, 2026) worked on it, meeting at the Half Nelson parking lot.
SORCA's Dig Day #11 (November 14, 2026) worked on it, meeting at the end of Tantalus Road.
A Valleycliffe trail. SORCA's Dig Day #12 (November 21, 2026) worked on it, meeting at the public washrooms near Squamish Canyon.
SORCA planned its last Dig Day of 2026 (#13, November 28) on it, meeting on Perth Drive at the trail's exit.
Tourism Squamish's 2026 guide calls it a beginner descent with machine-built berms that dries quickly.
Tourism Squamish's 2026 guide calls it an intermediate descent.
Tourism Squamish's 2026 guide calls it intermediate and fairly flat, ridden both ways, with a narrow boardwalk.
Tourism Squamish's 2026 guide calls it intermediate, ridden both ways.
Tourism Squamish's 2026 guide calls it an intermediate descent that can also be climbed.
Tourism Squamish's 2026 guide says it is ridden both ways.

Part of Smoke Bluffs Park's Loop Trail network (outer loop, inner loop and viewpoint trails), which the District calls one of Squamish's most popular short hikes, about 30 min. Mainly for walkers; dogs on leash. The plan says trials motorbikes may not cross the main Loop Trail.

A named trail on the District of Squamish's map of Smoke Bluffs Park. The plan says mountain biking and trials riding are supported only in a marked area in the park's north-east, and signs mark walker-only areas.

SORCA's e-bike rules: class 1 pedal-assist e-bikes (and electric adaptive bikes) may use trails shared with ordinary bikes; class 2 and 3 count as motorized under the provincial policy and generally may not. Riders 16 and older. Riders are asked not to climb trails marked as mainly downhill, and climbers have the right of way.

City of Kamloops trail data: Type III (More Difficult on the City's park maps), in Kenna Cartwright Nature Park. The City's trail types are general park levels that mostly reflect the climbing, not bike grades.

City of Kamloops trail data: Type III (More Difficult on the City's park maps), in Kenna Cartwright Nature Park; dogs on leash. The City's trail types are general park levels that mostly reflect the climbing, not bike grades.

City of Kamloops trail data: Type III (More Difficult on the City's park maps), about 2.1 km in Kenna Cartwright Nature Park; Upper Doc Findlay is Type III too. The City's trail types are general park levels that mostly reflect the climbing, not bike grades.

City of Kamloops trail data: Type IV (Very Difficult, a black diamond on the City's Valleyview Nature Park map), about 1.6 km in two parts, in Valleyview Nature Park next to the Kamloops Bike Ranch; dogs off leash.
City of Kamloops trail data: Type II (Easy on the City's park maps), a prepared surface in Pineview Valley Park; dogs on leash.
City of Kamloops trail data: Type II (Easy on the City's park maps), the 1.5 km natural-surface perimeter trail of Rose Hill Park; dogs on leash.

City of Kamloops trail data: mostly a paved Type I multi-use path, with some natural or prepared Type II parts (Cinnamon Ridge, the airport, the Oak Hills dyke). Dogs are not allowed on the McArthur Island and Riverside Park parts.

Kenna Cartwright Nature Park (City of Kamloops): over 55 km of trails. The City says trails may close during spring snowmelt to limit erosion, the park may close in extreme fire danger, and trails are not cleared in winter. Dogs off leash under control.

Kamloops Bike Ranch (City of Kamloops): closed and not maintained in winter; it reopens in spring when conditions allow, with the date posted by the Kamloops Mountain Bike Trail Association. The City asks riders to stay on designated trails; the silt bluffs next to it are off-limits. The XC Climb can be ridden up.
Tourism Kamloops (2024) calls it a newer green flow descent at Harper Mountain, with Ket-R-Done as the climb.

The City's map gives about 137 m of climbing and 52 m of descent. The City's map marks it the easiest way down and the main way up, a bidirectional multi-use trail; its lower part is shared with Valleyview Nature Park and joins the Sasquatch hiking trail.
The City's map gives about 10 m of climbing and 131 m of descent.
The City's map gives about 1 m of climbing and 47 m of descent.
The City's map gives about 24 m of climbing and 25 m of descent.
The City's map gives about 4 m of climbing and 110 m of descent.
The City's map gives about 0 m of climbing and 74 m of descent.
The City's map gives about 6 m of climbing and 74 m of descent.
The City's map gives about 0 m of climbing and 24 m of descent.
The City's map gives about 1 m of climbing and 43 m of descent.
The City's map gives about 0 m of climbing and 91 m of descent.
The City's map gives about 0 m of climbing and 48 m of descent.
The City's map gives about 1 m of climbing and 73 m of descent.

The Kamloops Mountain Bike Trail Association maintains and manages the Bike Ranch: no dogs, no camping, and no hiking or walking except on the lower XC Trail where it overlaps Valleyview Nature Park. Class 1 e-bikes only; adaptive bikes governed to 32 km/h may ride. Unsupervised; hours are one hour after sunrise to one hour before sunset.
Tourism Kamloops (2021) suggests it as one of the cruisier Bike Ranch descents to start on, before the faster trails and bigger jumps.

Harper Mountain Bike Recreation Site (Recreation Sites and Trails BC), managed by the Kamloops Mountain Bike Trail Association; a small part is in BC Parks' Paul Lake group site. Closed and not maintained from November 1 to May 1. Several trails are downhill only: don't ride or hike up them. Shuttling only in registered, insured vehicles on the main shuttle roads; the upper road is 4x4 only and not maintained. Class 1 e-bikes only. No camping, the ski runs and lifts are off-limits, and cell reception is limited.
KMBTA: one of the network's two main climbing trails, up from the bottom (Paul Lake group site parking).
KMBTA: one of the network's two main climbing trails, from the first hairpin of the Harper Mountain road to the top. Tourism Kamloops (2021) calls it a gentle climb of about 8 km to the summit.

KMBTA: from 2021 to 2023 the trail once called Ramblin' On was rebuilt into Cucwéll, a 5 km beginner-friendly trail. KMBTA renamed it with Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc: cucwéll is the Secwépemc word for trail. OpenStreetMap may still show parts under the old name.
Tourism Kamloops (2021): about 3 km of rolling singletrack on T.E.A. Time leads into Tempus Fugit for a long, flowing descent from top to bottom.
Tourism Kamloops (2024) calls it Harper Mountain's classic fast and flowy descent.
Tourism Kamloops (2024) points to its big jumps.
In June 2026 Tourism Kamloops' Freeride Fund put $10,000 toward rebuilding Gnarwhal and Pimpernot, chosen with KMBTA and KBRA.

Pineview Recreational Trail Network: close to 50 km, maintained by the Kamloops Mountain Bike Trail Association under agreements with ranchers, KGHM, the Province and the City, on a mix of private, ranch and Crown land. Closed and not maintained in winter from December 1; the west side stays closed longer for cattle grazing, with dates posted by KMBTA. Hikers are asked to follow the direction of travel and stay off downhill-only trails. Class 1 e-bikes only; no shuttles, motor vehicles, camping, events or commercial use. Parking: Hugh Allan (main, east side), Lac Le Jeune, and Iron Mask (west side).
Tourism Kamloops (2024): one of Pineview East's high-speed descents. The east side usually opens before the west in spring.
Tourism Kamloops (2021): a wide, non-technical, flowing descent.
Tourism Kamloops (2024): one of Pineview West's descents, ridden once the west side opens.
Tourism Kamloops (2024): part of Pineview West's mix of cross-country and downhill-style trails.
Tourism Kamloops (2021): from the green and blue trails near the Iron Mask parking area, it leads into the larger network of intermediate trails on Pineview's east side.

Lac du Bois Grasslands trails, locally called Batch after the Batchelor Heights neighbourhood, maintained by the Kamloops Bike Riders Association. Tourism Kamloops: mostly south-facing, gentle terrain, often among the first to ride in spring, with open sightlines and very little shade. Riders are asked to stay on the trails, as riding off-trail harms the protected grassland.
Tourism Kamloops (2021) lists it among Batch's gentle green and blue trails for laps.
Tourism Kamloops (2024): one way up to Tower Classic, on the way to Naked Pistol.
Tourism Kamloops (2024): reached from Tower Classic, with wide views, before one of Batch's best-known descents.
Tourism Kamloops (2021) names it among Kenna Cartwright's flowy green and blue trails with wide views.

Tourism Kamloops (2025): washrooms and a bike repair station are at the Tower Trail entrance to Kenna Cartwright Nature Park. The KBRA's Dufferin progression park for kids and new riders is nearby, above Dufferin Elementary School.

Sun Peaks' Mt. Morrisey and valley pedal-access trails: free to ride, built and maintained by the Sun Peaks Recreational Trail Association. Sun Peaks Resort says the network is usually ready to ride in early to mid June and closes when snow arrives in late October.
Sun Peaks Resort: a 6 km singletrack climb, built in three sections, from near the base of the Morrisey Express chairlift to the top of Mt. Morrisey. Shared with hikers.
Sun Peaks Resort: a technical, multi-use out-and-back trail near the top of Mt. Morrisey.
Sun Peaks Resort: a blue descent down Mt. Morrisey, next to the Cedar Twist climb.
Sun Peaks Resort: one of the descents from the top of Mt. Morrisey.
Sun Peaks Resort keeps Family Man for walking, snowshoeing and fat biking in winter, as conditions allow.
Sun Peaks Resort: a blue flow trail they call fun on a trail bike too.
Sun Peaks Resort: a flowy way back to the village; with the lift-access West Bowl XC loop (once called Altitude) it makes a 16 km alpine ride.
Sun Peaks Resort: a green way down from the top of the Sundance chairlift. The Sundance trails opened in 2022 with mellower grades and less vertical than Mt. Tod's.
Sun Peaks Resort: one of the park's classic double-black tech trails, with new wooden features in 2025 and 2026.
Tourism Kamloops names it one of Sun Peaks' iconic technical lines.
School District 73's McQueen Lake Environmental Education Centre: hiking and cross-country ski trails on 640 acres of forest, lakes and grassland, built for its outdoor school programs.

BC Parks shows Deep Lake Loop as a hiking trail on its Lac du Bois Grasslands map; the City of Kamloops lists it as a 4.2 km natural-surface Type III trail from the Ida Lane trailhead. BC Parks asks bikes (and class 1 e-bikes) to stay on established trails, with no shortcuts.

A new connector from Blood Sweat and Fear and Indy 500 to Lower Happy, so these trails no longer end by the CN rail line; PVTA also expects fewer bear encounters near the bottom. Recreation Sites and Trails BC approved it in June 2025: about 300 m of new trail plus about 200 m from Indy to Happy, with about 410 m of old trail to go back to nature. In its 2025 AGM notes PVTA lists finishing it as a 2026 priority.
PVTA's repost of a 2025 Pique article calls Happy the uphill trail in this part of the Mackenzie network.
PVTA's 2025 AGM notes: the Lil'wat referral committee and the Village of Pemberton approved bike safety chicanes at the bottom of Lower K2; PVTA lists adding them as a 2026 project.
One of the Mackenzie trails PVTA paid for trail work on in 2025 (2025 AGM notes).

In February 2023 PVTA said Cream Puff was closed while the Sunstone subdivision was built, and would be rerouted through a wide corridor in the subdivision with two road crossings; the upper part, above Smell the Glove, was to reopen first. Check PVTA for its current status.
A gravel trail paid for by the Sunstone developer, rated green (easiest) and built to be fully accessible (PVTA 2023 AGM notes).

PVTA's Mackenzie Basin road loop upgrade (phase 1, funded by the Whistler Blackcomb Foundation) rebuilt a stream crossing near the Live Like Lisa exit that flooded each season. PVTA says hikers, bikers, horse riders and dirt bikes share the loop.

Formerly Gravitron. PVTA rates it double black, for experts only. The Lil'wat Nation renamed it in 2023 in honour of the late Graham Haywood, and PVTA looks after it. The trailhead is about 9.5 km up the Mackenzie Basin forest road.
About 7 km between Mount Currie and the Village of Pemberton, for bikes, horses and walkers. Run by the Squamish-Lillooet Regional District and part of the Sea to Sky Trail network.
LESS (Lower Elevation Short Squirrels) was built by Howler Contracting and finished in summer 2018, according to WORCA.

WORCA calls it a blue, downhill-only trail carrying riders from Lord of the Squirrels down to the valley. Volunteers and the WORCA crew built the lower half by 2019 and finished the upper 1,100 m in 2020.

In October 2025 WORCA changed Lower Sproatt's signs from blue to black, saying its grades are well past the blue limit in either direction. WORCA's Dessert Platter singletrack bypasses much of the BC Hydro road section.
WORCA rates Industrial Waste blue. Built in 2016, it is part of the blue route from Lord of the Squirrels and Chipmunk Rebellion down to the valley; its Sproatt Creek bridge got railings in 2021.
First made as access to the Foreplay rock slabs on Comfortably Numb. In 2018 and 2019 WORCA volunteers and Whistler Waldorf students replaced its road and steep doubletrack climb with singletrack.
WORCA refers to Out There as a black-rated trail, alongside Billy Epic and Business Time (2026).

A descent from the Flank Trail near the bottom of Lord of the Squirrels. WORCA added ride-arounds in 2020 and 2025 that skip loose chutes; one bypassed chute, which WORCA measured as double-black steep, stays as an optional line.

One of Whistler's oldest trails. When the Stonebridge neighbourhood was built around 2002 it split the Danimals, and a right of way through the lots kept them. WORCA redesigned Danimal North in 2024 with a short reroute.

WORCA rates AM/PM black and says that if its first ride-around feels like a lot, the rest of the trail likely will too. Volunteers rebuilt its exit in 2025 with jumps and a short cool-down section before the forest road.

One of Whistler's oldest trails, beside the Cheakamus River; WORCA has described its character as black diamond. Riders often link Garbage, Rubbish, then Trash, and walkers also use it to reach the Train Wreck site.

WORCA calls Get Over It a technical lower-valley connector with roots, boulders and many wooden bridges. The crew rebuilt much of its woodwork from 2018 to 2023, adding railings at the high creek crossing in 2023.
WORCA says Hot Dog Alley's intended rating is blue (intermediate). Tim Haggerty helped build it under the BC Hydro power lines, and in 2022 the crew added a ride-around for a steep bedrock slab.

WORCA says the old Danimal South line is steep enough to rate black. In 2025 WORCA and volunteers built a blue, all-downhill bypass beside it, running down from Industrial Waste, that now carries the Rock Rabbit name.
WORCA counts Rock Rabbit as part of the blue route from Lord of the Squirrels down to the valley. In 2025 it was extended up to Industrial Waste as an all-downhill blue bypass of Danimal South.
WORCA calls Cut Yer Bars a classic blue descent in the village-side trail maze around Nester's Hill. The trail is named for its tight trees.
The climb into the Sproatt alpine trails. WORCA gives the alpine loop's intended direction as Into the Mystic, then On the Rocks, then Lord of the Squirrels.

WORCA points to Garbage, Rubbish and Trash, ridden in that order, as advanced cross-country riding by the Cheakamus River; the names come from Whistler's old dump nearby. A 2024 bike reroute bypasses the old exit, left for walkers.

WORCA calls Gargamel one of Whistler's most engaging double black trails. It is Tyler Morland's rooty descent, reached via Zanarchy, ridden for over 20 years and part of the 2004 Samurai of Singletrack route.

Built by Dan Swanstrom, it once ran from Emerald to Alpine Meadows. The Rainbow neighbourhood cut through it; Delineator replaced the missing part, and the south end keeps its old No Flow Zone character.
Part of the Sproatt alpine loop. WORCA gives the loop's intended direction as Into the Mystic, then On the Rocks, then Lord of the Squirrels.

WORCA says a 2018 debris flow destroyed the trail's original Sproatt Creek crossing, which was not rebuilt. Parts were renamed: the steep upper section now starts Baby Snakes and the slabby finish is called High Industry.
WORCA traces Kill Me Thrill Me to Chris Markle's original 1998 line; a 2025 bridge rebuild went back to that higher, more direct alignment.
Funded by the Stonebridge development and built in 2018, Scotia Nova serves as the climb back up for laps on the Danimal North descent.
WORCA credits Blake Jorgensen with building it (a 2024 correction). It is a No Flow Zone trail of boulders and drops linked by small bridges, some rebuilt in rock since 2021.
Finished by the WORCA crew in July 2023, Salted Caramel was the last missing link of the Dessert Platter singletrack, joining A La Mode to Whipped Cream away from the BC Hydro road.

WORCA's trail builder made it as his first trail, starting in 2010, across granite slabs with tight, off-camber turns. It leads into Korova Milk Bar and Wizard Burial Ground; the three were renovated in 2023.
Built by WORCA trail crew member Patrick Plante, Working Class descends from the Flank Trail. A ride-around added in 2021 skips its exit chute.

Whistler Waldorf grade 9 students began it with WORCA in 2018 in Lost Lake, linking Central Scrutinizer to Comfortably Numb near the disc golf course; RMOW crews kept working on it. It is named after a Frank Zappa song.
WORCA rates Cheap Thrills double black; a 2020 rebuild of 10 wooden features kept them high and narrow. Eric Barry created the trail, named after the Frank Zappa album nailed to a tree at its start.
WORCA refers to Billy Epic as black rated (2026). It is a long-standing Westside descent that was part of the 2003 Samurai of Singletrack route.
A trail at the far south end of the valley, past Cheakamus. WORCA modernized it in 2021: bridges refreshed, wood replaced with rock and a major washout repaired.

Built in 2017 by the WORCA crew and volunteers (about 350 m) to replace a part of Trash that became a gravel path to the Train Wreck. WORCA called it old-school advanced cross-country; riders go Garbage, Rubbish, then Trash.
The last of three linked trails after A Rockwork Orange and Korova Milk Bar, known for steep chutes under tall trees. WORCA renovated it in 2023, including a smoother chute exit.
WORCA volunteers extended No View across the fire access road to Delineator in 2015, so riders can descend Howler, cross No View to Delineator, and carry on into the No Flow Zone.
A climbing trail built by Howler Contracting with community donations and RMOW matching funds; it was completed in September 2018.
WORCA describes it as a machine-built trail with relentless pitches. Most riders now climb it to close the High Side loop, part of a popular intermediate loop in Cheakamus.

Whistler Secondary School students extended it with WORCA in 2021 and 2022 as an alternative to Shit Happens, so bikes can pedal up toward One Duck Lake. It was redesigned with Creamsicle Rainbow in 2024.
WORCA's lead builder calls it a precision riding test piece. The crew renovated it in 2023 along with A Rockwork Orange and Wizard Burial Ground, armouring holes and reworking transitions.
WORCA calls the Zanarchy and Gargamel pairing one of Whistler's most engaging double black trails.
In 2021 the WORCA crew benched in reroutes to take out the hike-a-bike sections of Azrael.
Sirloin, and later Darwin's, climb above Stonebridge toward the Flank Trail; WORCA's lead builder says they made several westside laps in one ride possible for most riders.
Built by Eric Barry and Dan Raymond (now WORCA's lead builder) on the RMOW trail crew, through terrain once called unbuildable. With Sirloin it forms a westside climbing route.
Built by Tim Haggerty in the Wedge zone, where trail names follow Pink Floyd songs. WORCA and volunteers rehabilitated it in fall 2024 after fire-thinning work nearby.
WORCA built this "Yummy Numby 2.0" in 2018-2019 with volunteers, replacing a road section and a steep, loose doubletrack with forest singletrack toward Comfortably Numb.
Built by Dan Swanstrom, according to WORCA, who also built A River Runs Through It and Shit Happens.
WORCA rerouted two steep, chunky sections in fall 2019 ("Highside 2.0"), adding flowy, pumpy lines with optional jumps. It links with Hi Hi.
WORCA redesigned it in 2019 after forestry work. The club confirmed in 2026 that the sign name is Hi Hi, not High High; it links High Side and Highline.
WORCA's crew armoured it heavily in 2020 to bring it back to what the club calls single-black technicality.
In 2025 WORCA volunteers benched and widened it to Adaptive-MTB black standard, following Tim Haggerty's plan. WORCA says it adds a less technical line in the Wedge zone.
One of the historic singletrack trails in the south Westside zone that the RMOW tasked WORCA with managing after a 2019 land swap, along with Piece of Cake, THC and Danimal South.
WORCA describes it as the climbing trail up to the Blackcomb-side trails. The club upgraded it at an August 2019 volunteer trail day.
WORCA's crew built this 120 m singletrack in Lower Sproatt in 2017 to cut down on steep logging-road riding; the name follows the area's dessert theme.
WORCA's crew and volunteers finished the Green Jello to Beaver Pond connector in September 2025, after starting it the season before.
SORCA's 2025-26 Pseudo-Tsuga upgrade, built by Gravity Logic, rebuilt the Brodown exit and added a reroute of more than 300 m on Pseudo 2 that now joins Brodown.

Built in memory of ski racer Mikayla Martin. Since its 2024 extension by Dream Wizards it is 1.7 km of blue flow, which SORCA says can be lapped on standard and adaptive bikes beside the forest service roads.

SORCA calls Lower Lumbar a blue trail; with All About Yew it forms a descent off Alice Ridge. Volunteers Jim Harvey and Don Hartle built it with full approvals (finished 2023), including Squamish's first two Da Vinci bridges.
Built by volunteers Jim Harvey and Don Hartle under a provincial Section 57 approval. SORCA says it joins Lower Lumbar (finished 2023) to form one descent off Alice Ridge.

SORCA calls Stone Ridge an intermediate (blue) trail in the Alice Lake/Highlands network. Volunteers led by Rob Phoenix built it with Squamish Nation and Crown approval (finished 2023); it is named for its many rock whalebacks.
Built by long-time Squamish volunteer builder Jim Harvey, who names it among about 20 trails he has built in a 2023 SORCA Q&A.
Built by long-time Squamish volunteer builder Jim Harvey, who names it among about 20 trails he has built in a 2023 SORCA Q&A.
A 2025 SORCA board nominee profile credits Cakewalk to Ted Tempany, a long-time Squamish trail builder and freeride course designer.
Part of the original Test of Metal race course: SORCA's history says Ray Peters and Kevin McLane scouted it around 1995, and the first race ran in 1996.
Also called Wild Potato. PVTA's 2025 AGM notes list it among the trails that got paid mountain bike and horse trail work.

PVTA says Recreation Sites and Trails BC granted a Section 57 authorization for Tour de Soo 1 in November 2024. PVTA lists it for mountain biking, horses and hiking (Tour de Soo 2 and 3 are not listed for bikes).
A descent to the valley floor. In 2025 PVTA got Section 57 approval for a connector of about 500 m from its bottom via Indy 500 to Lower Happy, so the trail no longer has to end by the CN rail line.
PVTA's approved connector (2025) links Blood Sweat and Fear and Indy 500 to the Happy uphill trail, so riders no longer end near the train tracks.
PVTA rerouted the Mission Impossible 3 section in 2022 around habitat of the sharp-tailed snake, a species at risk, working with Stewardship Pemberton.
PVTA and PORCA reworked this popular trail in fall 2021 for a more sustainable surface. PVTA also rebuilt a flood-prone stream crossing near its exit on the Mackenzie Basin trail (2023).
PVTA notes that remains of Líl̓wat pit-houses (s7istken) can be seen from this trail on Spel’pul’ (Signal Hill), and asks visitors not to go over the wooden fencing.
PVTA reworked it in fall 2020 (as "Lower Mac") with the goal of keeping it a blue trail, with flow and side hits, to give Pemberton more intermediate riding.
WORCA redesigned Hot Dog Pass in spring 2026, after the 2025 fire thinning buried parts of it, as a flowy low-elevation westside line, and now rates it blue.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Easy, 0.9 km. A wide gravel multi-use trail at Predator Ridge from the Outlook Cabin to Birdie Lake and the main trail parking area.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Easy, 1 km. A multi-use loop around Birdie Lake at Predator Ridge, with a wooden bird-watching platform. Dogs on leash.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 0.5 km. A short trail from the end of Gingerly down into Bear Valley (Kalamalka Lake Provincial Park).
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Most Difficult, 3.4 km. An old-school, very technical trail in the Sovereign Lake bike trails, with a few committing rock slabs.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Difficult, 0.5 km. A short, steep descent in Ellison Provincial Park.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 4.9 km. Mostly ridden as a climb from Upper Stone Free to Be Kind and the King Eddy Plateau trails; it can also be ridden down from the plateau.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 1 km. Tight, rocky riding at low speed. The creek runs over the trail in spring and in wet weather (Kalamalka Lake Provincial Park).

The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 2.8 km. A classic Kalamalka Lake Provincial Park ride: up to The Lookout over Kalamalka Lake and the Cosens valley, then a fast, flowing descent. Climbed by The Wall or Parabola from Comin' Round the Mountain. A busy trail shared with hikers all year.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Easy, 1.1 km. A fast, flowing trail down to Cosens Bay beach, also used as a climb back to Cosens Bay Road after Freaky Creeky.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 1.4 km. A blue trail in Ellison Provincial Park, mostly ridden down from Upper Veedol.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Easy, 2.6 km. A wide path near the bottom of Ellison Provincial Park that narrows further in; mostly used to link other trails.

The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 2.6 km. An easy blue cross-country trail on the King Eddy Plateau between My Crowning Achievement and the Tombstone and Pali Gap junction: a long descent with views over the Vernon valley, gentle climbs with a few short steep bits, then rolling terrain.

The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Most Difficult, 2.3 km. A long, demanding descent on the King Eddy Plateau, from steep and technical to fast and flowing. The map rates it double black partly because it is remote; a few of the hardest moves now have easier main lines.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Easy, 0.3 km. A short forest trail from the High Rim Trail to the pump track (Kalamalka Lake Provincial Park).
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 1 km. Intermediate singletrack beside Corral Trail; the map says it rides best south to north.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 1.9 km. A short climb from the top of Blister's Sister, then a descent toward Home Run or RPM (Ellison Provincial Park).
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 1.2 km. Links the bottom of Hammered Cow and Soup to Nuts back up to the lower parking area on Sovereign Lake Road.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 1.3 km. A mid-level blue descent in Kalamalka Lake Provincial Park that crosses a skid trail and carries on as Crash of '08.

The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Easy, 0.9 km. Smooth and flowing, with a long, wide bridge over a marsh. Past its end the path carries on as a trail on private land that the map says is not sanctioned.

The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 1.8 km. Old-school technical riding in the Sovereign Lake bike trails: tight switchbacks at the start, fast flowing parts, rock sections and some climbing, with a few optional black lines.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 1.2 km. Singletrack between Corral Trail and Cosens Bay Express (Kalamalka Lake Provincial Park).

The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 2.5 km. A newer technical flow trail at the dark-blue end of the scale, from Pali Gap to Rotten Cabin, with side hits along the way. It leads into Flovid.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 1.7 km. One of the busiest trails in Ellison Provincial Park, ridden both as a climb and as a fast, flowing descent.

The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 3.6 km. Technical cross-country singletrack on the King Eddy Plateau with views in every direction (Kalamalka and Okanagan lakes, Silver Star, Swan Lake). Its climbs take work; about a third of it is a long, fast descent.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 0.7 km. A short climbing trail from the lower Sovereign Lake parking area, used instead of the road.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 0.6 km. A technical blue trail reached from the High Rim Trail, or ridden after Jimmy Thang.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 1 km. Links Pali Gap to the lower part of Big Ed.

The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 0.4 km. A short trail off the High Rim Trail climb between the pump track and Twista, with short steep rocky and rooty parts. A connector links it to the bottom of Twista.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 0.5 km. Singletrack that avoids the road between Twisted Sisters or Crash of '08 and Pond Loop or Stone Free.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 0.8 km. A fast, flowing blue trail, almost always ridden down, with two optional black drops near the end.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 0.6 km. Up-and-down cross-country riding with some rock, then a flowing descent to the bog bridges on South Park.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 1.6 km. A machine-built flow trail with optional features, from the end of Be Kind to the High Rim Trail.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Difficult, 0.8 km. Links Tombstone to Upper Ed and Royal Assent on the King Eddy Plateau.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Difficult, 0.6 km. Steep, natural singletrack: another way down after Big Ed instead of Fraidy Cat. Purple Haze leads on to the High Rim Trail.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Easy, 0.8 km. The start of the main climb into the Predator Ridge trails; most riders keep climbing its blue section to the top.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 3.7 km. A cross-country trail on the King Eddy Plateau that leads to Big Ed.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 1.5 km. Smooth, wide, long and steep: Kalamalka Lake Provincial Park's classic climb to The Lookout. Not technical, but hard work.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 0.4 km. A short traverse, often ridden after climbing Crosstown Traffic.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Easy, 2.9 km. A wide multi-use gravel path from the Cosens Bay parking lot to Cosens Bay beach.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 0.6 km. The finish of Twisted Sisters.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 0.4 km. A fast, flowing descent to the Sovereign Lake sign.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Easy, 0.9 km. A very easy singletrack connector in Ellison Provincial Park.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Difficult, 0.4 km. A short, rocky, technical alternate finish to Lookout Trail.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 1 km. Mostly ridden as a singletrack climb to the other trails; often finished on Cabin.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 2.6 km. A flowing blue descent from the top of The Nest at Predator Ridge, with lake views, down to Ellison Provincial Park. Shared with hikers.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Difficult, 1.4 km. Rock slabs in the middle and flowing forest sections, in the Sovereign Lake bike trails. The map suggests it before Hammered Cow.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Easy, 2.1 km. A smooth, easy trail from the Cosens Bay parking lot into the Cosens Creek bike trails, beside Bear Valley.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Difficult, 1 km. Starts at the highest point of Silver Star Provincial Park: tight, with raw rock outcrops. Links with Upper Dagmal or Hammered Cow.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Difficult, 0.5 km. Starts off Serendipity. The first part is intermediate; the last part is steeper and black.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 0.3 km. Not technical, but very steep to ride up.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 0.9 km. A descent with tight corners and natural features; one of the more demanding (dark blue) trails in Kalamalka Lake Provincial Park.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 0.9 km. A technical trail mostly used as a connector, in either direction.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 1.3 km. A climb to My Crowning Achievement and Upper Ed, with a descent over its last third. Views of the Monashees and the Lumby valley.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Easy, 2.1 km. A multi-use trail around the west side of the mountain: mostly doubletrack, singletrack at the switchbacks.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 0.6 km. Ridden both ways at Predator Ridge: down into Ellison Provincial Park (an alternative to lower Granite), or up to lap Rock Garden Playground.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 0.7 km. Links to the Cougar Canyon parking lot; ridden either way.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 1.7 km. Smooth singletrack linking the High Rim Trail, Fraidy Cat, Jimmy Thang and Big Ed.

The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Difficult, 0.6 km. An optional harder section off Upper Rift at Predator Ridge, with some exposure and rock rolls; some features are mandatory, others have ride-arounds.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 3.2 km. A dedicated singletrack climb to the top of SilverStar, with views toward Cherryville and the Monashees. It ends on Paradise.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Easy, 2.2 km. A wide path from the SilverStar village to Silver Shack.

The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Difficult, 1.2 km. A fast, flowing rebuilt trail with steeper lines and dirt and wood jumps; some older features are dated. It can follow Sauce on Side for a longer descent to the valley floor.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Difficult, 1.1 km. Fast and flowing with steeper sections, roots and wood and dirt features; it joins The Baconator.

The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Difficult, 0.6 km. Fast, with wood and dirt jumps (most can be rolled, none have ride-arounds, no gaps) and almost no pedalling. Reached by a forest road and a skid road it crosses several times; dirt bikes and quads use the road. It can get loose in mid-summer.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Difficult. Singletrack descent with root and rock sections in the Sovereign Lake bike trails (spelled Dagamal on the Greater Vernon map).

The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Difficult. Narrower cross-country singletrack with descents, short steep climbs, roots and rocks (spelled Upper Dagamal on the Greater Vernon map). It links with Raw Bones and Dagmal.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate. Technical singletrack with rock gardens; the map calls it one of the harder trails in Ellison Provincial Park.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate. Swooping, rolling trail in Ellison Provincial Park.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 0.3 km. Links Blister's Sister to RPM.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 1.3 km. A nature trail built for hikers in Ellison Provincial Park, with signs along the way, a viewpoint and some rock riding near its end.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Moderate, 0.3 km. From the bike parking lot down to the Ellison campground; steep pitches mean pushing the bike to go up.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Easy, 1.2 km. A climb with easy switchbacks from the Ellison campground to the upper parking lot and the pump track.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Easy, 0.6 km. A wide path with steep parts from the main Kalamalka Lake Provincial Park parking lot to the other trails.

The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Easy, 3.7 km. A multi-use trail around the north and east sides of the mountain in Kalamalka Lake Provincial Park, with short singletrack side loops (the Bunnies) on its north part. It leads to The Wall and Parabola.

The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Difficult, 4.1 km. A favourite at Predator Ridge: a fast descent with smooth rock slabs, berms, short climbs and views. Built as a descent; some of it runs along a cliff edge.
The Greater Vernon trail map rates it Easy, 0.2 km. A wide, fairly steep gravel path down to a beach (Kalamalka Lake Provincial Park).
The main doubletrack climb into the Crawford trails, up to Teddy Bear Junction; singletrack climbing trails branch off it.
About 10 km of doubletrack, about an hour to ride (their estimate).
A climb that turns right at Teddy Bear Junction and leads up toward Boris.
About 4 km, around 20 minutes (their estimate).
Drops in from the Kettle Valley Railway: roots and trees in its lower part, then open granite with drops and technical rock features and views over Kelowna.
One of the area's longest descents, about 4.2 km and 525 m down: a steep chute at the top, then rock rolls with optional drops and ride-arounds, mostly embedded rock with steep, loose sections.
An easy descent with swooping turns through the trees; with Fairlane, the beginner ride in the guide.
Ridden both ways: a direct climb or a quick descent.
Rated blue in the guide: a few slightly steeper sections and two rock features that can be ridden around.
About 5 km of gentle terrain, about 20 minutes (their estimate).
Chunky rock that can be ridden fast; a rock feature about two thirds of the way down is a step from blue toward black trails.
Rated black in the guide: a moderately technical climb to a sunset viewpoint, chunky rock lines, drops and a slab; its lower part is fast with flowing corners.
Lots of rock and some steep rock steps.
A fast descent with smaller rock drops and loose corners.
A fast section with rock jumps, steep rock rolls, a narrow slab into a drop of about 1.2 m (4 ft) and a technical corner with a rock step. Reached by a short climb from Connector.
Flowing, with some big rock jumps that have ride-arounds.
A short black trail with rock rolls, slabs and drops.
About 900 m of blue singletrack; Kelowna.com suggests it as a start for new riders, with Galloping and Fairlane.
A rocky trail; the author suggests it as an easier first run before Vapour.

The Angel Springs and KLO Creek descent, from the Kettle Valley Railway (by the Myra Bailout) or June Springs Road: rocky ponderosa forest, a side-hill descent through Catapult Canyon into cedar forest, four or five creek crossings, ending at McCullough Road. About 7 km and 750 m down (her figures).
The first, roughed-in part of the climbing trail MTBCO was building in Gillard in 2023, to reach the lower trails.
Rated blue in the guide: fast singletrack with berms and rock gardens through young forest along the edge of a small canyon.
Berms and rock gardens, with a couple of technical features: a ladder bridge and a drop.
Rated blue in the guide: flowing, with optional rock slabs and wooden A-frame jumps.
Rated blue in the guide: flowing, with optional rock slabs and wooden A-frame jumps (two A-frames near the bottom).
Re-rated from blue to black: a rough rock garden near the bottom with no ride-around.
Rated black in the guide: wood stunts and gap jumps from the Kettle Valley Railway, a rocky flat pedal part-way, then fast, rough rock gardens.
Rated double black in the guide: dirt gap jumps and medium to large wood-to-dirt gaps, with optional ride-arounds.
Short: a rock drop, then gaps and big jumps that finish on the dirt road.
Rated black in the guide: woodwork, drops, slabs and berms, with two optional double-black features (a wood drop and a slab into a tight corner). It ends at the parking lot.
A Gillard classic with natural and wooden features and ride-arounds; some features are double black.
A mix of flowing sections and small features.
A fairly mellow climb with switchbacks through sagebrush and long grass; Boyce Trail links it to Knox Mountain Drive.
Rated blue in the guide: a machine-built flow descent with tables, hips, doubles and fast berms.
Rated blue in the guide: a machine-built descent from the top with rock rolls, fast berms, jumps and drops (locals call it The Berms). The black line beside it is Shale Trail Direct.
A climbing and descending loop with one steep, loose section part-way.
A mellow cross-country trail.
About 2.5 km of cross-country riding with some rocky sections and gentle slopes.
A twisty climb with optional technical parts, about 585 m up to the top of the network; lookouts and connectors branch off it.
Uphill only: about 7.4 km and 416 m of climbing, with tight switchbacks, rocky sections and a lookout over Okanagan Lake.
Rated black in the guide: a fast, flowing descent with berms, jumps and drops, and steep whoops in the lower gully.
About 3.1 km down: wide, steep off-camber berms half-way, rock drops near the top and middle, and near the bottom a wooden roll-down or a drop of about 1 m into a hip.
Rated blue in the guide: a descent with turns and an optional wood feature between trees; it feeds into Feel the Love.
Flowing, with winding berms, one mellow wooden A-frame and small rollable jumps; it leaves Feel the Love before its technical lower part.
Rated blue in the guide, about 1.1 km: quick corners, berms, jumps and drops of 0.3 to 1 m with ride-arounds. It leaves Feel the Love about 2 km down.
A descent that mixes technical and flowing parts, with many wooden features on its lower part.
Fast, with large berms and gap jumps of about 1.5 to 9 m (tables, doubles and a big step-up at the bottom); narrower than a bike park line. Reached from the climb.
A descent with berms, jumps and technical terrain.
A popular, smooth flow trail.
A fairly flat, simple dirt trail for beginners that leads into Trail on the Edge.
A descent with rock and switchbacks, less steep lower down: about 2 km and 295 m down (her figures, 2018).
Rated double black in the article: a short, steep chute with a sharp right turn, reached from Jabbarocky.
Built into the mountainside across scree fields with exposure, with tricky switchbacks, rock sections and views of the reservoir.

n: City on the Edge of Forever
trails.text: Very steep, with what the author calls the hardest switchbacks in the Okanagan; loose in summer, with a chute under a rock formation. Its bottom part is easier.
Rock rolls, chutes and scree with switchbacks, and a fair amount of climbing.
A mildly steep side-hill trail.
One of the climbs of the guide's Campbell Mountain ride, from the main trailhead at Reservoir and Spiller roads. The guide says Campbell Mountain has no black-diamond trails.
A climb, named for an old Dairy Queen table at a lookout at its top.
Fast and flowing, after the climbs.
Flowing, with berms, toward the canyon trails.
Narrow singletrack with some exposure beside it and big canyon views.
Narrow singletrack with some exposure beside it and big canyon views; Burnt Rock Rise joins it past the most exposed part.
Campbell Mountain's main descent: fast bermed corners, jumps and rollers, with ride-arounds for every feature. It ends near the parking lot.
A steep climb, in the longer version of the guide's Campbell Mountain ride.
A climb with switchbacks toward the top of the Three Blind Mice trails, after Yellow Brick Road.
Winding dirt and flowing corners.
Rated black in the guide: chunky rock, roll-downs and technical sections, with ride-arounds at most technical spots. Part of a BC Bike Race stage in 2021, nicknamed Flat Tire Alley.
Short, mellow climbing between descents.
Rated black in the guide: large slabs and rock rolls; the guide calls it more intermediate than many rocky black trails on the coast.
One of the most flowing trails mid-mountain, with some of the best views in the network.
PACA's flow trail, finished in 2019: nearly 2 km of berms, rollers, doubles and jumps. All of it can be rolled, with ride-arounds at a few bigger features, including a road gap.
A short trail down to the Riddle Road entrance.
Some technical riding that suits intermediate riders.
Flowing, with the odd chunk of rock.
Rated black in the guide: a rocky, loose, dusty descent with tight corners on shifting shale, and wide views of Okanagan Lake.
Views like Jose's with much less technical riding; the main trail ends near the top of Riddle Road.
Traverses across the top of the Three Blind Mice trails.
Big views on the way down toward the lake.
Many drops. Before the climbing trails were built, riders used to climb beside it.
Short, rocky and technical; the guide calls it gnarly, with consequences.
Rated black in the guide: more a freeride area than one trail, with drops, gaps and jumps to choose from; some of the cliffs there are just cliffs.
Fast and flowing, with a feature called Compression Redemption.

Through trees burned in the 2020 Christie Mountain fire, with small rock slabs for beginners. The guide names the Gillies Creek corridor as the sanctioned mountain bike area of Skaha Bluffs Provincial Park.
A few short, steep climbs at the start lead to big views, then flat, dusty corners, flow and a few odd rocks.

Summerland's most popular trail: a hand-built loop of about 10 km on Cartwright Mountain with about 290 m of climbing, flowing berms, rollers and fast descents. Ridden one way; they call it moderately challenging.
A short pump-track-style section, mostly downhill, about 330 m.
Rated black, downhill only: exposure, steep sections, small features and loose scree side-cuts; about 1.1 km and 118 m down.
Reached from Joyride-K2 or Hairway to Steven, toward a pond and Roxy Roller: steep, loose corners, small jumps that can be skipped and a rollable rock jump; about 480 m.

Much of the trail network there crosses private land and Líl̓wat option lands.

One of the 20 favourite trails named in the 2018 community survey for the Pemberton trails master plan (2020). The Rutherford area around it also has a hydro plant, soil composting and active logging, and the plan recommends re-routing and improving its bottom section.

The Pemberton trails master plan (2020) says the sharp-tailed snake (a federally listed species at risk) and the rubber boa have been found low on the slopes between this trail and the Wetlands trail.
The Pemberton trails master plan (2020) says the sharp-tailed snake (a federally listed species at risk) and the rubber boa have been found low on the slopes between Moby Dick and this trail.
The Pemberton trails master plan (2020) calls it the kids' trail at the south end of One Mile Lake.
In spring 2023 Xet̓ólacw school students working on this trail suggested Ucwalmícwts names for renaming it (PVTA spring newsletter).
Tourism Pemberton lists it as a black diamond ride: a 7.6 km advanced loop up One Mile Hill with views of the Green River below Mount Currie.
Tourism Pemberton lists it as a blue (intermediate) ride and one of Pemberton's popular routes.

Coast Range Heli-Skiing flies riders by helicopter to its Hidden Peak trail, between Whistler and Pemberton, and rates it expert (black diamond): about 8.3 km and 1,200 m down from the lower helipad, or 12 km and 1,500 m down from the top one, which adds a climb of about 1.1 km. The operator says it has no mandatory drops, bridges or gaps, but some mandatory rock rolls and steep sections.

Alberta Parks: 2.9 km with about 250 m of elevation change, past Jewell Falls with views of Barrier Lake (3.9 km from Barrier Dam to the pass). Reached from Barrier Dam along Stoney Trail; often joined with Prairie View Trail as a loop.

Alberta Parks: also called the Barrier Fire Lookout trail, 6.6 km (one way) to the viewpoint with about 421 m of elevation change, switchbacking up an old forestry road to a view over Barrier Lake. From the top it goes on to the lookout or down towards Jewell Pass, on a fainter trail near the top.

Alberta Parks: a long, open 22.5 km trail (one way) that follows the power line, with equestrian camping at Jewell Bay Backcountry Campground. Alberta Parks lists a yearly closure from April 15 to June 15 from Jewell Bay Campground south to Lorette Creek.
Alberta Parks: a 0.8 km connector from the Silvertip area to Montane Traverse (east) or Montane Cutoff (west).

Alberta Parks: 1.6 km (one way) between Montane Traverse and the parking area near the Canmore cemetery. Alberta Parks lists a yearly closure from December 1 to June 15 for wildlife, later than the May 15 in the map's trail name.

Alberta Parks: a 19.3 km forest trail (one way) with about 150 m of elevation change, crossing Goat Creek and the Spray River to the Spray River Fire Road and Banff townsite; most of it lies in Banff National Park.
Alberta Parks calls it a challenging trail: 8.0 km with about 323 m of elevation change along the slopes of the Ehagay Nakoda Range, mostly in forest with a few views at creek crossings.

Alberta Parks: a 4.8 km loop with about 147 m of elevation change, from the Cougar Creek trailhead on the east side of the creek (or from the Alpine Club house); used by mountain bikers, walkers and riders on horseback.
Alberta Parks: 1.5 km with about 200 m of elevation change, linking Montane Traverse with Highway 1A in Canmore.
Alberta Parks: a 1.6 km connector east of Stoneworks Creek between Montane Traverse and Douglas Fir Bench or the bottom of Johnny's Trail, with steep pitches through old Douglas fir forest.
Alberta Parks: 7.7 km with about 275 m of elevation change, from the Cougar Creek parking lot to Harvie Heights, with views of the Rundle range.
Alberta Parks says its preferred use is downhill mountain biking: 1.6 km and about 151 m down, steep with a few short flat parts, ending at the Grassi Lakes parking lot. Riders may come down it fast.

Alberta Parks says its preferred use is downhill mountain biking: a steep, loose and rocky 1.6 km (about 272 m of elevation change) from Whiteman's Pond to the Quarry Lake parking lot, crossed by the Highline trail at its middle and near the bottom.

Alberta Parks: a paved, 3 m wide trail beside the highway linking Canmore and Banff (about 26 km in all; 20 km listed on the Alberta side), built from 2010 for Parks Canada's 125th anniversary, with mountain views.
Alberta Parks: a 4.3 km loop with about 120 m of elevation change, climbing through pine woods with a short side trip to a foothills lookout.
Alberta Parks: 4.6 km, listed for bikes, e-bikes, hikers and horses in summer; in winter Alberta Parks lists fat biking only from Allen Bill Day Use Area to the Snagmore trail.

Alberta Parks: half of the Elbow Loop, 23 km (one way) with about 400 m of elevation change on an old fire road along the Little Elbow River and over Tombstone Pass to Tombstone Backcountry Campground, with views of Mounts Romulus, Remus, Glasgow and Tombstone. The trailhead is at the west end of the equestrian campground.

Alberta Parks: 7.3 km (one way) with about 470 m of elevation change, on an old fire road along Moose Ridge and up Moose Dome; the last kilometre to the lookout is steep singletrack on loose rock. The trailhead is at the end of Moose Mountain Road.
Alberta Parks: 6.2 km (one way) with about 510 m of elevation change up the narrow Powderface Creek valley; gently rolling in the east half, steeper and rockier further west.
Alberta Parks: 9.2 km (one way) with about 180 m of elevation change; the first 2 km climb the edge of a shaded canyon, then the trail drops to Prairie Creek.

Explore Cariboo describes it as flowy blue singletrack through tight trees, ending back near the start of What the Huck.
Tourism Quesnel: a wide, machine-built, downhill-only flow trail on the Wonderland network, berm to berm, with jumps.
Explore Cariboo describes it as a blue flow trail with berms, rollers and some jumps.

Tourism Quesnel: a technical, downhill-only trail on the Wonderland network that winds back and forth across a wide gully, with ladder bridges and bermed corners. What the Huck, the climbing trail next to it, leads back to the top.
Tourism Quesnel names it the climbing trail on the Wonderland network, next to Sluice Box.
Explore Cariboo describes it as a two-way trail, ridden up and down, that tops out at the start of Woodbury's Way.
Explore Cariboo: it starts at the top of What the Huck on the Wonderland network, and is named in memory of a rider, Dick Woodbury.

Tourism Quesnel: with Rock in the Park, a gradual 7.1 km climb to the top of Dragon Mountain. The first 3 km are wide and machine-built, and it gets narrower and more technical higher up. It crosses the road at 1.6 km.
Explore Cariboo describes it as a two-way green trail on Dragon Mountain, built to be fun both up and down.
Tourism Quesnel: the upper part of the 7.1 km climb to the top of Dragon Mountain that starts with Walk in the Park.
Explore Cariboo calls it a blue square climb to the top of Dragon Mountain.
Tourism Quesnel names it one of Dragon Mountain's fast, technical downhill lines, reached by shuttle or by climbing the access road or Walk in the Park.
Explore Cariboo describes it as a black diamond downhill trail with committing drop-ins, rock work and slabs, built by the Gold Rush Cycling Club and First Journey Trails.
Tourism Quesnel names it one of Dragon Mountain's fast, technical downhill lines, reached by shuttle or by climbing the access road or Walk in the Park.
The City's trail page says Fox Mountain's trails can be reached by climbing Jimmy's Fox or by shuttling up Fox Mountain Road. The network has 28 trails and over 45 km of singletrack.
Explore Cariboo rates it green, with gentle climbs and small features that can be rolled or jumped.
Explore Cariboo rates it green, with gentle climbs and small features that can be rolled or jumped.
The Village of Burns Lake describes it as an 18 km all-mountain trail from the Bike Park to the top of Boer Mountain.
The Village of Burns Lake describes it as a 10 km down-country trail from the top of Boer Mountain.
The Village of Burns Lake lists it among the trails down from the top of Boer Mountain, rated black diamond.
The Village of Burns Lake lists it among the trails down from the top of Boer Mountain, rated black diamond.
The Village of Burns Lake lists it among the blue runs down from the top of Boer Mountain.
The Village of Burns Lake calls it the network's signature blue run, built by Gravity Logic.
The Village of Burns Lake describes it as a wall ride of more than 2,000 square feet, next to the Kager Lake parking lot.
The Village of Burns Lake lists a four-cross track among the Bike Park's features, with jumps, drops, wall rides and boardwalks.

The club rates it a black diamond trail. A double black feature sits just off the main line: a dirt step-up onto a wooden deck, then a 2.4 m (8 ft) drop to a dirt landing. It is signed and needs intent to hit.
The 2023 field study counted 35 technical features, mostly jumps, along its 2.4 km. Repairs it suggested may have been done since.
Tourism Terrace lists the Johnstone/Walsh trailhead as the way into Flathead on Terrace Mountain, and rates it black.
Tourism Terrace lists the Spring Creek Road trailhead as the way into Steinhoe Ridge, rated green and blue.

Alberta Parks: from the southwest corner of Beaver Creek Campground past a beaver pond to near the bottom of Old Baldy Campground. The first 0.6 km, to the wooden bridge, is wheelchair and stroller accessible; the west half is flowy singletrack that ends at Horseshoe Canyon Trail.
Alberta Parks: a hiking and biking trail that carries on from the end of Beaver Creek Loop up to Plateau Trail, with about 179 m of elevation. Listed for fat biking in winter.
Alberta Parks: a green flow trail meant for kids and beginners working on their skills.

Alberta Parks: a blue flow trail with berms, jumps and wall rides, starting just off the main ski run at the top of Hidden Valley. The park lists it as the only trail of its kind in southeastern Alberta, and has noted trail work that can change it.
Alberta Parks: starts off Rangers Trail, climbs a ridge (the first part can be a little steep), crosses Tower Trail and winds through the pines. Roots and rocks.
Alberta Parks: a winding trail in two sections through the trees, with views of Elkwater Lake.

Alberta Parks: from across the road south of the West-Central Day Use Area to loop D of Firerock Campground. A steep climb to a grassy area past a large glacial erratic, then a gentle climb through poplar and spruce; it meets Horseshoe Canyon and Old Baldy trails about halfway.

Alberta Parks: a short black trail that mixes flow and technical riding (berms, jumps, a gap jump, roots), reached from the south end of the Hidden Valley resort, taking the left option at the intersection in the trees.
Alberta Parks: links the top of the Sorry climbing trail to the start of the Hidden Valley descents.
Alberta Parks: a 4 m wide trail through lodgepole pine, reached from Rodeo Loop or Spruce Coulee Trail, for bikes, hikers and horses.

Alberta Parks: climbs an old road from the Old Baldy Campground road through fields and mixed forest to a view of the Horseshoe Canyon landslide, linking up with Beaver Creek Trail at the top. About 241 m of elevation.

Alberta Parks: a black technical trail down the Hidden Valley T-bar line, from where the T-bar line meets Canadiana. Technical features, flowy berms, and a step-up near the bottom; about 127 m of descent.
Alberta Parks: runs along the base of Hidden Valley and collects the downhill lines, back to the parking lot and Sorry. Rollers, berms and jumps.
Alberta Parks: from near the Spruce Coulee Reservoir boat launch through spruce and lodgepole pine along the west shore and back to the campground. Parking at Spruce Coulee Campground.
Alberta Parks: the park's first downhill-only, bike-only trail. A black machine-built flow trail: steep berms first, then jumps, drops and berms.

Alberta Parks: a short connector from Cobble Miner to Mystery Trail with a viewpoint at its north end, an easier way up than Tower Trail to Upper Mystery. Part of the park's 15 km loop (Rangers, Cobble Miner, Lower Mystery, Mystery, Plateau, Beaver Creek).
Alberta Parks: a blue flow trail with berms and jumps that joins the lower two thirds of Mitt Nibbler. From the south end of Hidden Valley, take the middle option at the intersection.
Alberta Parks: a descent through mixed forest with views.
Alberta Parks: links Ferguson Hill Road and Elkwater Campground to the Mitchell Creek trailhead.

Alberta Parks: a steady climb of about 187 m from the south end of Elkwater Campground to Murray Hill Road on the plateau, with an informal viewpoint over Elkwater Lake a third of the way up. Ridden point to point or as a loop with Mystery Trail.
Alberta Parks: a green flow trail down the Hidden Valley ski area with berms, jumps and rollers, from the top of the Magee run (stay right at the intersections).

Alberta Parks: a tight, twisty trail on old overgrown forestry roads across the top of the hills, from the top of Mitchell Creek Trail to the top of Lower Mystery. Reached by climbing Tower, Mitchell Creek, Beaver Creek or Horseshoe Canyon trails.

Alberta Parks: a smooth, flowy side loop with views of the lake and Elkwater, starting about 100 m up Horseshoe Canyon Trail (the entrance is not well marked). Ridden west to east, it is a fast flow trail back down to the campground.

Alberta Parks: through grassland, aspen and lodgepole pine on the Cypress plateau, joining Horseshoe Canyon, Beaver Creek, Mitchell Creek and Mystery trails. Passes the free, outdoor Tom Trott Forestry Museum.

Alberta Parks: circles the south side of the Elkwater townsite. Part of a 3.5 km loop (Rangers, Soggy Bottom, Shoreline) and of the park's 15 km loop (Rangers, Cobble Miner, Lower Mystery, Mystery, Plateau, Beaver Creek).
Alberta Parks: a narrow, difficult technical trail with berms, drops, jumps and a rock garden, starting just north of the top of the Magee run.

Alberta Parks: a 19.8 km one-way trail for hiking, biking or horses, from the Trans Canada Trail just west of Reesor Viewpoint east along the hills and ridges on the park's north edge, past some of its best lookouts. About 533 m of elevation.
Alberta Parks: meets the Reesor Hills TCT trail halfway, for shuttles or shorter loops.
Alberta Parks: through aspen, pine and spruce. Groomed for cross-country skiing in winter.
Alberta Parks: links the Hidden Valley ski area to Rangers Trail.
Alberta Parks: an asphalt path with boardwalks along the south shore of Elkwater Lake, between the West End and East End day use areas. Wheelchair friendly.
Alberta Parks: a packed, smooth climbing trail, the easiest way to the top of Hidden Valley. Bikes ride it uphill; hikers may use it both ways. About 166 m of climbing.

Alberta Parks: follows an old road from near the Rodeo Grounds parking lot through woods and fields to Bull Trail Road and Spruce Coulee Campground. The park recommends it for experienced mountain bikers. About 251 m of elevation.
Alberta Parks: from beside the park administration office, across the road from the east end of Soggy Bottom, to Highway 41 and Spruce Coulee Trail.
Alberta Parks: a popular way up to the radio tower and the plateau, from behind the old water tower along an old forestry doubletrack. About 173 m of climbing.
