Alberta Parks: a green loop linking the Elkwater, Old Baldy, Lakeview and Beaver Creek campgrounds, the skills park, pump track and Visitor Centre.
Alberta Parks: through lodgepole pine; the park suggests riding it as part of a longer loop.
Parks Canada: a figure-8 for hiking and biking, a 2.2 km short loop or 4.1 km long loop; the long loop reaches Kinosao Lake.
Parks Canada: 1.9 km one way, rolling alongside Brûlé Trail to Kinosao Lake, then northwest to Grey Owl Trail. For hiking and biking.
Parks Canada: 14.8 km return to Grey Owl's cabin at Beaver Lodge Lake, for hiking and biking (Parks Canada calls it a better bike trip than a hike). A ski trail with a warming hut in winter.
Parks Canada: a gently rolling hiking and biking trail to a backcountry campsite beside Cowan Lake.
Parks Canada: for hiking, biking, horses and wagons, linking to Bald Hill, J.E.T. and Reeve's Ravine for loops, with backcountry campsites at Breezy Hill and East Deep Lake.
Parks Canada: 10.1 km return on an old logging road that climbs steadily up the escarpment; for hiking, biking and horses.

Parks Canada: a 6.1 km loop on the ridge above Edwards Creek, for hiking and biking. The east side crosses wetlands and is a winter trail (groomed for skiing and fat biking); the west side is a 3.0 km link between the Crawford Creek trailhead and the Northgate trails next to the park.
Parks Canada lists it for hiking only and says biking is not permitted. A one-way trail with creeks and narrow paths between the escarpment base (Birches trailhead) and the top.
Parks Canada lists it for hiking only: a 0.5 km loop on a floating boardwalk through the marsh.

Parks Canada: built with the Manitoba Escarpment Trail Society for mountain biking, a flowy singletrack along the ravine's edge in the East Escarpment network, in three parts (2.5 km trailhead to junction, 2 km to J.E.T., 2.6 km to Bald Hill).

Parks Canada: for hiking, biking and horses through prairie and forest to the Tilson Lake and Birdtail backcountry campsites (west section 14.5 km, east section 21.5 km). Parks Canada says to expect bumps along the way.

Tourism Dauphin: the Co-op Community Family Trail section at the Northgate trailhead, for hiking, biking and play, connects to harder trails in the 26 km stacked-loop system on Riding Mountain's North Escarpment. Parking and washrooms at the trailhead.
Travel Manitoba names Bobsled, with Auto Alley and the pump track, among Northgate's faster trails.
Travel Manitoba describes this Northgate trail as winding through large ferns.
The Contagious Mountain Bike Club suggests it as a first black on Grey Mountain; locals often call it an “easy” black.
The Contagious Mountain Bike Club rates it black. Reached via The Dream; the club says to expect some hiking, out of the forest into low alpine plants near the summit.
The Contagious Mountain Bike Club names it as the way to the black Grey Mountain Summit Trail.

The Contagious Mountain Bike Club lists it as one of Grey Mountain's two double blacks, from the summit. Shuttles start at the Grey Mountain towers; the club describes the road past the Grey Mountain Lookout as unmaintained, narrow and rough.
The Contagious Mountain Bike Club finished it in 2025: it runs along Grey Mountain Road from the base of RIP (across the road) to the Magnusson parking lot, so riders can stay off the road.
The Contagious Mountain Bike Club reworked some loose flat corners in 2025, with support added for more grip.
The Contagious Mountain Bike Club names the Quickie loop among the most popular routes in the Hillcrest and Copper Ridge network, which is mostly green and blue.
An alpine trail on Mount McIntyre, reached from Copper Haul Road by climbing McIntyre Ascent (Contagious Mountain Bike Club).
Travel Yukon describes a long, technical run that starts after a bigger climb.
An alpine trail on Mount McIntyre, reached from Copper Haul Road by climbing McIntyre Ascent (Contagious Mountain Bike Club).
The Contagious Mountain Bike Club names it as the climb from Copper Haul Road to Mount McIntyre's alpine trails (Starbuck's Revenge, Upper/Lower Goat).
A Mount McIntyre trail built by volunteers. The Contagious Mountain Bike Club says a new drop was built and opened on it in 2025.
Travel Yukon suggests it, with Caribou and the Porcupine climb, as a place for beginners to start on Montana Mountain, Carcross. Most Montana Mountain trails are downhill only, with a few up-tracks.
Travel Yukon suggests it, with Lower Dei Kwaan and the Porcupine climb, as a place for beginners to start on Montana Mountain, Carcross.
Travel Yukon lists it among Montana Mountain's intermediate trails (Carcross). Most Montana Mountain trails are downhill only; shuttles up the road are common.
Travel Yukon names Goat and Wolf as Montana Mountain's hardest descents (Carcross).

The Contagious Mountain Bike Club says the Mountain Hero loop on Montana Mountain (Carcross) is an IMBA EPICS-designated backcountry ride, a full day out. The club asks riders to support Carcross/Tagish First Nation by registering at the Carcross Visitor Centre.
Tourism Saskatchewan: part of the bike park area next to the Buffalo Pound visitor centre, with drop lines, tabletops and a dirt pump track for building skills.
Manitoba Parks lists it as a hiking trail with red markers, about 2.5 km, along the Assiniboine River.
Manitoba Parks lists it as a hiking trail with yellow markers, about 3.4 km.
Manitoba Parks lists it as a hiking trail with white markers, about 5.0 km, reached from Highway 1.
Manitoba Parks lists it as a hiking trail, about 2.0 km.
Manitoba Parks lists it as a hiking trail, about 2.5 km, reached from Highway 1.

hikes.text: Tourism Fernie's figures: 8 to 11 hours one way to Island Lake Lodge, 1,450 m up and 1,585 m down, over Three Sisters Pass and Windy Pass. Built by Heiko Socher (finished 2003, once the Mountain Lakes Trail). Hiking only, no bikes. Backcountry with no cell coverage; the trailhead road needs high clearance. Island Lake Lodge access only on some days.

n: Swine Flu Access / Mount Proctor Trail
Swine Flu Climb / Mount Proctor Trail
hikes.text: Tourism Fernie's figures: a 20 km loop, 8 to 11 hours, 1,500 m of climbing, from the Fernie Visitor Centre to the 2,393 m summit. The top is loose, rocky and exposed, with some scrambling; Tourism Fernie describes the loop counter-clockwise, with the scramble on the way up. No dogs (cattle grazing). Usually late June to September.

Tourism Fernie's figures: 2 to 3 hours to the peak, 910 m of climbing. The first 3 km climb to the base of Ghostrider Peak; the rest is steep and rugged, with scrambling on loose rock. Trailhead on Hartley Lake Road (high clearance suggested), limited parking, no water. Usually July to October.

Tourism Fernie's figures: 8 km return, 3.5 to 5 hours, 910 m of climbing. Rebuilt by Heiko Socher in place of the older Moccasin Trail. Steep, with loose, rocky and exposed sections and some scrambling near the top; a bench three quarters of the way up looks at the Three Sisters. Trailhead at the end of Canyon Trail road. Usually mid-June to early October.

Tourism Fernie's figures for Castle Mountain: about 12 km return, 5 to 6 hours, about 648 m of climbing from the Montane trailhead by Montane Blue, Roots, Hyper Ventilation and Southern Comfort. Gentle at first, steeper higher up, with several viewpoints. Shared with mountain bikes.

Tourism Fernie's figures: 7 km return, about 3 hours, 521 m of climbing, from the parking by Gorby Bridge in Mount Fernie Provincial Park. A gentle first kilometre, then steep climbing through old red cedars; can be slippery when wet. Usually July to October.

Tourism Fernie's figures to the viewpoint: about 8 km return, 5 hours, 350 m of climbing from the Montane trailhead by Montane Blue and Roots, then about 800 m up Hyperventilation to a bench looking over the Lizard Range. Shared with mountain bikes.

Tourism Fernie's figures: about 7 km return, 2 to 3 hours, about 188 m of climbing to Montane Hut (bench, picnic tables, outhouse). The grade stays under 5%. Tourism Fernie lists it year-round, shared with bikes, dogs on leash. On private land.

Tourism Fernie's figures: 3 to 4 hours one way from the Fernie Aquatic Centre to the suspension bridge (opened June 2026), 301 m up and 92 m down, with several short, steep climbs. Interpretive signs (2026) on the old Coal Creek mining town; old mine portals along the way. Matheson Falls is a short hiking-only side trail past the bridge.

Nelson Kootenay Lake Tourism's figures: 3.6 km return (a fairly steep 1.8 km each way), 338 m of climbing, with views of Nelson and Kootenay Lake. The Flagpole is a further 2.2 km and 317 m up. Spring to fall. Dog-friendly.
Nelson Kootenay Lake Tourism's figures: 2.2 km and 317 m of climbing past Pulpit Rock to the Flagpole viewpoint over Nelson.

Tourism Rossland's figures: 17 km return, 7 to 9 hours, best late June to early September. Climbs through old forest and alpine meadows to the highest peak of the Rossland Range, the site of an old weather station.
Tourism Rossland's figures: an easy 3 km loop through big trees off Highway 3B, with a carved bench about halfway. Popular for snowshoeing in winter.
20 min. A short, easy loop by the Summit Lodge with views of Howe Sound, Sky Pilot and Goat Ridge. Starts at the top of the Sea to Sky Gondola (ticket).
30 to 60 min. Through old-growth forest to viewing platforms over Howe Sound. Starts at the top of the Sea to Sky Gondola (ticket).
30 to 60 min return. A nature trail with a boardwalk around the lake. Starts at the top of the Sea to Sky Gondola (ticket).
1 to 2 h. Steeper single track through old-growth forest, passing under the gondola. Starts at the top of the Sea to Sky Gondola (ticket).
30 to 45 min. A kid-approved trail by the Summit Lodge. Starts at the top of the Sea to Sky Gondola (ticket).
30 to 60 min. Short but harder, with some steep scrambles. Starts at the top of the Sea to Sky Gondola (ticket).
30 to 45 min. A harder side trip off the Wonderland Lake Loop. Starts at the top of the Sea to Sky Gondola (ticket).

n: Sea to Summit / Shannon Basin Loop
hikes.text: One way, 3 to 5 h, about 900 m up from the gondola base to the Summit Lodge. Steep stairs, fixed ropes and chains, mud, rock and roots. First time: leave before 11 am, carry a headlamp and at least 1 litre of water; phone signal is patchy. Ride down for $19 online ($25 at the window).
One way, 3 to 5 h. A steep, direct way up to the Summit Lodge with fixed ropes and exposed steps. Leave before 11 am; ride down for $19 online.

2 to 3 h. A winding loop around the Shannon Creek watershed with views of Goat Ridge, Shannon Creek and Mount Habrich. Phone signal isn't reliable. Starts at the top of the Sea to Sky Gondola (ticket).

Return, 3 to 4 h (the Sky Pilot Valley Trail). Along the access road and an old logging road up the valley below Mount Habrich, then steep single track to treeline near the base of Sky Pilot. Past the end of the marked trail you need mountaineering gear and skills (glacier, exposed rock). Starts at the top of the Sea to Sky Gondola (ticket).

Return, 3 to 6 h. The gondola's flagship backcountry hike: old-growth forest, glacial rock, creeks and waterfalls, with big views of Howe Sound and Sky Pilot. Numbered markers; snow comes early up high (micro-spikes past marker 33 in fall). Starts at the top of the Sea to Sky Gondola (ticket).

1 to 2 h loop from marker 58 of Al's Habrich trail (4 to 8 h with it): up through old-growth forest to Neverland Falls, best in spring and fall (dry in summer). Starts at the top of the Sea to Sky Gondola (ticket).

Out and back, 6 to 8 h. Straight up the centre ridge of the upper Shannon Creek watershed to the alpine between Sky Pilot and Goat Ridge, with views of Goat Ridge, Mount Habrich and the Sky Pilot peaks. Starts at the top of the Sea to Sky Gondola (ticket).
The gondola's Backcountry Access Road from the Summit Lodge, the way to the Sky Pilot Valley, Skyline Ridge and Shannon Basin trails. Groomed for Nordic skiing in winter.
About 30 min, 30 m of climbing. A gravel loop from the far side of the Cloudraker Skybridge back to the top of the Peak chair, with signs on local First Nations history. Lift ticket needed.
About 10 min, 63 m of climbing. Gravel trail from the Roundhouse Lodge to the Peak Express chair.
About 60 min, 20 m of climbing. An easy walk off the Harmony Lake trail with views of Blackcomb, Garibaldi Park and the Spearhead Range.
About 90 min, 120 m of climbing. Drops through alpine forest away from the Roundhouse Lodge to Harmony Lake.
About 45 min, 81 m of climbing. A steep link from High Note and Harmony Lake back to the Roundhouse Lodge, with views of the Fitzsimmons valley.

About 4 hours, 420 m of climbing. Whistler Blackcomb calls it the best hike on Whistler Mountain: from the top of the Peak Express over rugged ground with views of Black Tusk and Cheakamus Lake, then easier rolling trail; turn north at the junction (away from Flute and Singing Pass) to loop back to the Roundhouse Lodge.
About 75 min, 136 m of climbing. A shorter way back from High Note, joining Pika's Traverse to the Roundhouse Lodge.
Up to 3 hours, 119 m of climbing. Out and back to Flute Summit, or on into Garibaldi Park (BC Parks puts Flute Summit to the Singing Pass junction at about 3.5 km).
About 60 min, 272 m of elevation change. A mountain road back from Half Note to the Roundhouse Lodge, with some steep parts.
About 45 min, 82 m of climbing. A mountain road with wide views up to the summit of Whistler Mountain. Whistler Blackcomb asks hikers not to enter glacier areas.
About 40 min, 20 m of climbing. Singletrack around the summit of Whistler Mountain from the top of the Peak Express.
About 40 min, 80 m of elevation change. A mountain road linking Half Note, High Note and Musical Bumps; its lower part becomes singletrack.
About 30 min, 72 m of climbing. A gentle walk from the Rendezvous Lodge on Blackcomb to the Fitzsimmons lookout, with alpine signs along the way.
Seal Bay Nature Park (CVRD), west side of Bates Road: a level creek-side walk to Melda's Marsh, named for Melda Buchanan, who campaigned for the park. Dogs must be leashed on this loop all year.

Seal Bay Nature Park (CVRD): follows an old rail or logging grade once used to haul logs; its new sign also gives its aýaĵuθəm (Coast Salish) name. The CVRD says bikes are welcome on trails signed with brown or blue tops; purple marks hike-only trails.

Seal Bay Nature Park (CVRD), water side of Bates Road: one of three trails down to the park's nearly 1 km of beach, through a steep ravine with big sword ferns. Dogs must be leashed on the water side.
Seal Bay Nature Park (CVRD), water side of Bates Road: one of three trails down to the park's nearly 1 km of beach. Dogs must be leashed on the water side.
Seal Bay Nature Park (CVRD), water side of Bates Road: reaches the beach where a small Japanese camp and a sawmill once stood. Dogs must be leashed on the water side.

Nymph Falls Nature Park (CVRD), 61 ha of second-growth forest on the north side of the Puntledge River: the falls are an easy half-kilometre stroll from the main entrance, with fish ladders where salmon can be seen in October and November.

CVRD: a multi-use trail on the old Comox Logging and Railway grade through farm country (Agricultural Land Reserve), named after the first locomotive on the line. Sections include Tsolum South (8.5 km) and Tsolum North (8 km). Dogs must be leashed on all sections.
CVRD: links Burns and Brazier Roads and connects the Wildwood Interpretive Forest trails to the One Spot Trail. Named for a local rider who kept up the trail for horses for many years.

Wildwood Interpretive Forest: 276 ha of Crown land about 7 km from Courtenay, with trails on logging roads, old rail grades and narrow dirt paths, managed by the CVRD with Recreation Sites and Trails BC. Outings range from short walks to a three-hour loop.

BC Parks: the Paradise Meadows loop, 4.2 km return, about 1.5 hours. An easy walk through sub-alpine meadows on wide boardwalk and hard-packed gravel, built for wheelchair access with grades around 5%. Starts at the Mount Washington Nordic area parking lot, 25 km from Courtenay.

BC Parks: about 16 km one way from the Paradise Meadows trailhead (32 km return). Beyond the Circlet Lake junction the route is unmaintained, rougher and steeper, and its last 4 km follow a bare rock alpine ridge with no trail tread. BC Parks installed tall waymarking posts in 2020 at the turn off the ridge back toward Circlet Lake, and says it is the second busiest hike for search and rescue on Vancouver Island.
BC Parks: 3 km, about 2 hours one way, 100 m elevation change. Starts just past Westmin and follows a gravel road for 700 m before turning into forest trail, with old-growth forest and a waterfall.
BC Parks: 5 km, about 4 hours one way, 1,250 m elevation change. Starts at Highway 28; views open above 1,300 m.

BC Parks: 6.6 km, about 6 hours one way, 1,250 m elevation change. Starts at Phillips Creek marine campsite on Buttle Lake, reached by boat from Auger Point or Karst Creek. Viewpoints, alpine meadows and limestone formations.
BC Parks: 6 km, about 4 hours one way, 800 m elevation change. A well-graded trail from the trailhead just past Westmin to Arnica Lake, with a camping area at the lake's north end.

BC Parks: 6 km, about 5 hours one way, 1,250 m elevation change. Starts on Buttle Lake Road. BC Parks says the trail is steep and rough until the open alpine ridge and water can be scarce; open ridge hiking with viewpoints.

BC Parks: 6 km, about 3.5 hours one way, 600 m elevation change. Starts from Jim Mitchell Lake Road; camping in designated areas only, no campfires. Routes to Cream Lake and Bedwell Sound leave from this area.

BC Parks: about 8.5 km and 7 hours one way to Cream Lake, 1,200 m elevation change. Starts at the south end of Buttle Lake on a gravel road for 3 km, then a rough trail up the valley; past Price Creek it becomes a very steep, rough route to Cream Lake.

BC Parks: 11 km, about 5 hours one way, 600 m elevation change. Starts at Highway 28 and follows the Elk River valley for 10 km before climbing to Landslide Lake. Campsites at Butterwort Flats (6 km) and the upper gravel bar (9 km); no camping at Landslide Lake.
BC Parks' Strathcona trail report of June 5, 2026 listed the Karst Creek trail as closed, with a rockfall hazard upstream. Check BC Parks for its current status.
BC Parks' Strathcona trail report (June 2026) says the Castlecrag route is not maintained. There is no camping at Moat Lake (core area of the park); the nearest campsites are at Circlet Lake.
The City of Nanaimo gives the lake loop as about 5.5 km and calls it an easy, groomed walk apart from a steep knoll near the west end, and lists bikes as permitted on it.
The Regional District of Nanaimo says mountain bikers use this route on Crown land to ride from the Benson View Road parking lot to the Westwood bike trails.
A trail in Mount Benson Regional Park (Regional District of Nanaimo map). In 2023 the RDN and the Nanaimo & Area Land Trust named it after park advocate Gail Adrienne.
The Regional District of Nanaimo maps it as a Mount Benson Regional Park trail climbing toward the summit area (1,019 m).
The Regional District of Nanaimo maps it as a Mount Benson Regional Park trail toward the summit area.
The Regional District of Nanaimo maps it as a short loop to a viewpoint in Mount Benson Regional Park, off the gravel road.
The Regional District of Nanaimo maps it as a Mount Benson Regional Park trail running toward the summit from the gravel road.

The Regional District of Nanaimo rates it difficult: 1.6 km one way from Weigles Road (about 45 minutes) or 2.4 km from Creekside Place, with steep pitches, stairs and uneven footing. Its parking gates close overnight.
A Trans Canada Trail section, 5 km from Harewood Mines Road to Virostko Road, passing the Abyss, a narrow fissure in the rock (Regional District of Nanaimo).
A Trans Canada Trail section, 5.3 km from Bramley Road to the north bank of the Nanaimo River (Regional District of Nanaimo).
A Trans Canada Trail section, 1.6 km from the south bank of the Nanaimo River to Spruston Road. The RDN notes there is no bridge across the river at its end.
A Trans Canada Trail section, 3 km from the Spruston Road trailhead to Timberland Lake (Regional District of Nanaimo).
A Trans Canada Trail section, 6.5 km from Timberland Lake to the Timberlands Road parking lot, crossing Haslam Creek canyon on a suspension bridge 48 m above the creek (Regional District of Nanaimo).
The City of Nanaimo lists it as a paved multi-use trail; biking is one of its listed uses.
The City of Nanaimo describes a 1 km loop around Lost Lake with gravel sections.
The City of Nanaimo says its part of Linley Valley Cottle Lake Park has groomed trails and boardwalks; other parcels in the valley have other owners.
The District of Lantzville's Copley Ridge Recreation Trail: 8.6 km in a working woodlot, with easy, moderate and hard parts. No motor vehicles; parts may close during harvesting.
BC Parks' Newcastle Island map shows about 2 km from the dock to Mallard Lake. BC Parks calls the island's trails easy hikes.
BC Parks' Newcastle Island map shows about 2 km from the dock to Kanaka Bay, part of a 22 km trail network on the island.
The Regional District of Nanaimo maps it in Englishman River Regional Park, near the Middlegate Road entrance and the hatchery. The Allsbrook Road gate closes overnight.
The Regional District of Nanaimo describes about 7 km of 3 m wide compacted-gravel trail along the E&N rail line from Springwood Park to Coombs. No motor vehicles.
The Alberni-Clayoquot Regional District manages km 3 to 21: km 3 to 7.9 is non-motorized, and km 7.9 to 21 is shared with registered off-road vehicles. The ACRD lists its hours as 6 am to 10 pm.

The Alberni-Clayoquot Regional District rates Stage 1 (Ship Creek Road to China Creek) moderate: 14 km, about 6 hours one way, about 1,400 m of total climbing, on private working forest. Non-motorized; it may close in fire season or for logging. Stage 2 adds 9.8 km to Franklin River.
The Alberni-Clayoquot Regional District rates it moderate: 2.5 km, about 2 hours, 60 m climb, from Stirling Arm Road past a suspension bridge and Fossli falls to a beach on Sproat Lake.

The Alberni-Clayoquot Regional District rates the Stamp Long River Trail (Sayachlas t'a saa'nim) moderate: 7.5 km, about 3 hours one way, along the Stamp River from Stamp Falls park, with no access between its two ends.
The Alberni-Clayoquot Regional District rates the Maplehurst trails easy: about 4 km of linked loops, about 2 hours, 100 m climb, partly beside Kitsuksis Creek, with two steep bank sections.
The City of Port Alberni lists the Kitsuksis Dyke Trail as 4.6 km (about 75 minutes on foot), mostly paved along Kitsuksis Creek, with a dirt spur north to a waterfall.
Port Alberni Parks lists it as 1.13 km of soft surface for walking, dogs and bikes, gentle except near the west creek crossing. Part of the meadow beside it is private land.
Port Alberni lists it as 2.1 km across the Roger Creek ravine. On January 13, 2026 the City posted that it is closed at Roger Creek until further notice.
BC Ministry of Forests, Beaver Lodge Forest Lands map (2022): the main trail from the South McPhedran Road kiosk; part of it is marked wheelchair accessible.
BC Ministry of Forests, Beaver Lodge Forest Lands map (2022): the Beaver Pond Trail, marked wheelchair accessible, near the Trask Road and South McPhedran Road kiosks.
Destination Campbell River: the Beaver Lodge Rail Trail is a wide, level former logging grade, rated easy and usable with wheelchairs and strollers.

Parks Canada: an 800 m boardwalk loop over a bog, with no stairs and benches along the way; the boardwalk floats on the bog and can be uneven. Its October 2026 conditions report lists trail work, limited access and no dogs.
Parks Canada: 500 m one way (1 km return), gravel and then boardwalk with steps down to the beach. Dogs are not permitted on this trail or beach from April 1 to October 1.

Parks Canada: 1.8 km one way including the Willowbrae Trail, branching off it 1.3 km from that trailhead, with steep stairs and handrails down to a small beach. Parking is limited, with no space for RVs.

Parks Canada: 1.4 km one way on a historic route, wide gravel and then a long, steep boardwalk staircase to Halfmoon Bay and Florencia Bay South. Its October 2026 conditions report notes limited access, some sections in poor condition and no dogs.

The Wild Pacific Trail Society rates most of the trail easy, with some moderately steep hills, from the 2.6 km Lighthouse Loop to the 8 km marker at Rocky Bluffs. The society and the District of Ucluelet say bikes are not permitted on it.

The Wild Pacific Trail Society rates the Artist Loop section moderate to challenging, with small hills and stairs (a stroller bypass avoids the stairs): from the 4 to the 6.75 km markers past viewing decks and painters' perches, about 45 to 60 minutes.
The Wild Pacific Trail Society: a loop of about 1 km through old-growth cedars off the Rocky Bluffs section, about 15 minutes. Built in 2013 and upgraded in 2025.
The Wild Pacific Trail Society map shows a 300 m interpretive loop near the Whale parking lot on the Lighthouse Loop, about dwarf trees and carnivorous bog plants.

n: Terrace Beach First Nations Interpretive Trail
hikes.text: The Wild Pacific Trail Society map shows this interpretive trail of about 15 minutes from the Otter lot in He-Tin-Kis Park; its signs share Yuułuʔiłʔatḥ First Nation knowledge.

The District of Tofino: a moderate gravel trail of about 3 km, plus 800 m of boardwalk and stairs, from the Community Hall to Tonquin, Third and Middle beaches. Some steep sections; dogs must be leashed.
The District of Tofino: a 1 km wide gravel connector from the Community Hall and bike park to Industrial Way, suitable for biking.

Tla-o-qui-aht Tribal Parks: a boardwalk on Meares Island (Wanachus-Hilthuuis Tribal Park), reached only by boat and maintained by the Tribal Park Guardians. Tourism Tofino gives about 2.4 km return and notes the boardwalk can be slippery when wet and the island has no facilities.
Tourism Tofino: a steep trail of about 2.7 km with more than 700 m of climbing on Meares Island, reached by boat.
The Capital Regional District's 2025 map lists it at 2.2 km around Lower Thetis Lake; the CRD notes some parts are steeper than 8%, with rocks, roots and narrow spots.
The Capital Regional District's 2025 Thetis Lake map lists it at 2.6 km; the CRD rates the park Moderate overall.
The Capital Regional District's 2025 Thetis Lake map lists it at 4.0 km; the CRD says Scafe Hill has spring wildflowers.
The Capital Regional District's Sea to Sea map lists it at 0.8 km and marks it as a bike push-up to Mount Brule.
The Capital Regional District's Sea to Sea map lists it at 5.6 km to the Mount Manuel Quimper fire lookout; the top part is marked as a bike push-up.
The Capital Regional District's Sea to Sea map lists Charters Trail at 1.8 km, rated Easy for bikes.
The Capital Regional District's Sea to Sea map lists it at 5.0 km, rated Easy for bikes.
The Capital Regional District's Sea to Sea Lakes map lists it at 5.4 km in a signed wilderness area, with a 0.4 km spur to the 682 m summit.
The Capital Regional District's Sea to Sea Lakes map lists it at 3.2 km to a Sheilds Lake viewpoint, in a signed wilderness area.
The Capital Regional District's Sea to Sea Lakes map lists it at 2.7 km to a Crabapple Lake viewpoint.
The Capital Regional District's 2026 Sooke Hills Wilderness map lists it at 13 km as a hiking and cycling trail, past a suspension bridge near Goldstream, with gates along the way.
The Capital Regional District's 2026 Sooke Hills Wilderness map lists it at 3.3 km as a hiking trail to Sugarloaf (358 m).
The Capital Regional District's East Sooke map lists it at 5 km; the CRD says the Anderson Cove trails are mostly steep and uneven, and bikes are not permitted in the park.
The Capital Regional District's East Sooke map lists Copper Mine Trail at 2.5 km, past an old mine site, as a hiking trail. Bikes are not permitted in the park.
The Capital Regional District's East Sooke map lists Interior Trail at 6.5 km as a hiking trail. Bikes are not permitted in the park.
The Capital Regional District: an old 1.5 km logging road with gravel and a gentle grade to a meadow, then a short steep bit to Iron Mine Bay.
The Capital Regional District's 2025 map shows the 10 km trail around Elk and Beaver lakes with km markers, open to hikers, cyclists and horses.
The Capital Regional District's 2026 Witty's Lagoon map lists Lagoon Trail at 1.9 km along the lagoon.
The Capital Regional District calls the Summit Trail a challenging, exposed climb across Mount Work Regional Park; its 2025 map lists it at 5 km.
North Cowichan and the Cowichan Trail Stewardship Society list it as a 1.7 km hiking-only trail from Kaspa Road through Garry oak meadows with Cowichan Bay views.
North Cowichan and the Cowichan Trail Stewardship Society list Awesome Trail as a 1.7 km hiking-only route on Mount Tzouhalem's western ridge, with steep, loose and exposed parts.
North Cowichan and the Cowichan Trail Stewardship Society call it the easiest hike on Maple Mountain: 0.6 km, marked with green paint.
North Cowichan and the Cowichan Trail Stewardship Society list it as Maple Mountain's longest hike, 5.2 km from Maple Bay toward Crofton, above Sansum Narrows.
North Cowichan and the Cowichan Trail Stewardship Society describe it as a 4 km coastal hiking route, often used as a return from the Blue Trail.
North Cowichan and the Cowichan Trail Stewardship Society call it Maple Mountain's most accessible trail: hard-packed gravel from Osborne Bay Park, suited to wheelchairs.
Cowichan Valley Regional District: the trestle is about 187 m long and 44 m above the Koksilah River, on flat crushed gravel about 1.2 km from the south parking lot.
BC Parks: about 20 km from Glenora to Skutz Falls, about 6.5 hours. Bikes are not permitted on the park's hiking trails, and parts cross private land.

60 to 80 min, 124 m of climbing. Blackcomb's main hiking trail, reaching into Garibaldi Park past wildflowers and glacier-fed lakes, with views of the Overlord Glacier; it leads to the Lakeside and Decker loops.
About 60 min, 183 m of climbing. A narrow singletrack through the tree line back to the Rendezvous Lodge; Whistler Blackcomb suggests starting from Overlord.
About 40 min, 72 m of climbing. A short climb to wildflower meadows above Blackcomb Lake. The loop is hiked clockwise, back down to Overlord.
About 75 min, 214 m of climbing. Hiked clockwise from Overlord into Garibaldi Park, with views of the Overlord Glacier and Decker Tarn. Whistler Blackcomb's pick for advanced hikers on Blackcomb.
First part of the Blackcomb Ascent Trails (74 m of climbing), between ski runs up to Base 2. Lift tickets apply on the mountain; no dogs on the Ascent Trails.
Second part of the Blackcomb Ascent Trails: 435 m of climbing to the Blackcomb Gondola midstation. No dogs on the Ascent Trails.

Last part of the Blackcomb Ascent Trails: 667 m of climbing through old-growth forest to the Rendezvous Lodge. The three trails together are about 6.2 km and 1,200 m from the base; they are the summer route between the valley and Garibaldi Park on Blackcomb. No dogs.

BC Parks' estimates: Rubble Creek parking lot to the Garibaldi Lake and Taylor Meadows junction 6 km and 770 m of climbing (strenuous, steep switchbacks; shortcuts can knock rocks onto people below), then 3 km and 130 m to the Garibaldi Lake campground (moderate). Free day-use pass needed at Rubble Creek on summer weekends and holidays.

BC Parks' estimates: the 6.5 km junction to Taylor Meadows campground is 1.5 km and 180 m of climbing; Taylor Meadows to the Garibaldi Lake campground is 2.3 km and 50 m (easy), and to the Black Tusk junction 2 km and 180 m.

BC Parks' estimates: Black Tusk junction to the viewpoint is 4.4 km and 300 m of climbing, very steep. BC Parks doesn't maintain the trail past the viewpoint kiosk and advises against climbing the Tusk itself (loose rock, fall hazard).

BC Parks' estimates: Helm Pass to Panorama Ridge is 3.2 km and 330 m of climbing on a steep, poorly defined trail (Black Tusk junction to Helm Pass adds 2 km and 100 m). BC Parks asks hikers to follow the orange markers and main trail to protect the meadows.
BC Parks' estimates: Cheakamus Lake trail junction to Helm Creek campground is 7 km and 600 m of climbing, then 5 km and 240 m to Helm Pass. Bikes stop at the bridge over the Cheakamus River.

BC Parks' estimates: parking lot to Cheakamus Lake campground 3.5 km and 90 m of climbing (easy), then 4 km and 50 m to Singing Creek (moderate). Reached by 7 km of rough gravel road (Cheakamus Lake FSR). Day-use pass needed in summer; no fires.
BC Parks' estimates: parking lot 5 in Whistler to the Singing Pass and Musical Bumps junction is 11.5 km and 1,200 m of climbing. There is no bridge over Harmony Creek.
BC Parks' estimates: Singing Pass and Musical Bumps junction to Russet Lake is 3 km and 250 m of climbing. Campground reservations required.

BC Parks' estimates: 6 km and 1,200 m of climbing from the parking lot to Wedgemount Lake, very steep. The 2 km gravel road to the parking lot isn't plowed in winter. BC Parks asks hikers to follow the orange markers and main trail.

BC Parks' estimates: Diamond Head parking lot to Red Heather Meadows is 5 km and 450 m of climbing (strenuous), then 6 km and 250 m to Elfin Lakes (moderate). 4x4 recommended on the road up. Day-use pass needed on summer weekends and holidays.

BC Parks' estimates: Elfin Lakes to Opal Cone is 6.5 km and 460 m of climbing on a lightly maintained wilderness trail. In May 2026 BC Parks said the trail past Zig Zag Creek toward Rampart Ponds was closed by a bridge washout.
BC Parks' estimates: Elfin Lakes to the Saddle, Gargoyles and Columnar Peak is 2.5 km and 330 m of climbing on a steep, unmaintained trail.
BC Parks' figures: First Peak 1.5 km and 540 m of climbing, Second Peak 1.7 km and 590 m, Third Peak 1.8 km and 630 m. BC Parks says rockfall can happen and stairs and tread can be icy in winter.

Tourism Squamish rates the Chief hikes Difficult: about 4, 5 and 7 km return to the First, Second and Third Peaks (2 to 4, 4 to 5 and 5 to 7 h, their estimates), with chains and ladders on the First and Second Peaks. They list March to October as the season.

BC Parks: about 6 km. Bikes are never allowed between Edith Lake and Alice Lake (South Beach) or around Alice Lake, and the rest of the trail is closed to bikes from May 1 to September 15. Tourism Squamish calls it an easy 6.5 km loop of 2 to 3 h.
Tourism Squamish: 11.5 km, 5 to 7 h (their estimate), best March to October, dogs on leash.
Tourism Squamish: 3.5 to 10 km depending on the loop, 1 to 2 h, steeper parts on rock bluffs, more than 10 km of trails in all; dogs on leash.

Tourism Squamish: 11 km, 4 to 5 h (their estimate). Steep, with near-scramble sections, chains, fixed ropes and unprotected drops; it climbs the canyon to a logging road, then about 5 km back down the road. They say it is very hard when wet or icy.
Tourism Squamish: 2.3 km, 1 to 1.5 h (their estimate), with unprotected cliff edges.
Tourism Squamish: 4.3 km, 1 to 2 h (their estimate), dogs on leash.

Tourism Squamish: 0.5 to 5 km depending on the loop, 2 to 3 h (their estimate), to a lookout over the Tantalus Range. Their loop from the Brohm Lake lot: Bridge Trail, High Trail and Tantalus View Trail, back by the Connector Trail and Brohm Lake Trail. Dogs on leash.

Tourism Squamish: 4.5 km, 1.5 to 2 h (their estimate), through ferns on boardwalks, then along The Covenant to a bridge just in front of a waterfall. A loop can come back by an old logging road and Trestle Trail.

Tourism Squamish: 6.5 km, 3 to 5 h (their estimate), more than 600 m of climbing on a rough, bouldery trail with some scrambling and route finding, to Tony's Lookout. It starts from a pull-out about 2 km along the Mamquam River FSR. They note unprotected cliffs and that it is very hard when wet or icy.
BC Parks: 13 km one way from Westsyde to McQueen Lake, multi-use, no motorized use. BC Parks says ticks are common in spring.
BC Parks: a 3.5 km loop that they list as walked counter-clockwise.
BC Parks: 4.25 km in Lac du Bois Grasslands.
BC Parks: 5.7 km with a steep climb.
Sun Peaks Resort's 2026 hike map: a lift-access alpine hike, 2.4 km and about 45 min one way (their estimate); part of the resort's 7.1 km Tod Lake route.
Sun Peaks Resort's 2026 hike map: a lift-access alpine hike, 1.5 km and about 45 min one way (their estimate).
Sun Peaks Resort's 2026 hike map: three short multi-use (hike and bike) trails, not lift access: Lower 0.6 km, West 0.4 km, East 0.7 km, each about 10 to 15 min one way (their estimate).
Tourism Kamloops: about 3 km return in Kenna Cartwright Nature Park, a steady climb through ponderosa pine and open hillside to a wide view of the Thompson Valley.
Tourism Kamloops: a loop of about 1.7 km along the ridge of Valleyview Nature Park, with some climbing and views over the city.
Tourism Kamloops: about 4 km return in Dallas-Barnhartvale Nature Park through ponderosa pine and sagebrush, mostly packed dirt and gravel with a few rocky parts and wooden steps.
Tourism Kamloops: about 5.6 km return in Peterson Creek Nature Park, climbing through open hillside, then into canyon terrain with switchbacks.

Tourism Kamloops (2018): 4.2 km return, about 2 hours, with one steep part. The bluff stands about 360 m above Kamloops Lake, in the Tranquille Ecological Reserve. The trailhead is reached from Dewdrop Flats by Tranquille-Criss Cross Road and Frederick Road, where they recommend a 4x4.

n: Isobel Lake Interpretive Low Mobility Trail
Isobel Lake Interpretive Low Mobility Tr
hikes.text: Tourism Kamloops (2021): a family trail of about 3.2 km they list as stroller-friendly, with interpretive signs about the forest and a picnic spot.
Tourism Kamloops (2021): about 2.8 km at the north end of Kenna Cartwright Nature Park, with no major climbs and wide views; not stroller-friendly. Dogs may be off leash.
Tourism Pemberton: a 1.45 km loop that they list as wheelchair accessible, with a dog beach on the north end.
Tourism Pemberton: a 9 km loop from One Mile Lake, mainly a bike trail that hikers use to reach the top of Signal Hill.
Tourism Pemberton calls it a challenging 21 km hike for experienced hikers.
An out-and-back trail, mostly in trees, to the top of the Cougar Canyon climbing area, with views of the cliffs and Kalamalka Lake.
A hiking trail at Predator Ridge with steep parts, from Longspoon Drive through forested ravines, with views of Okanagan Lake. It joins Ellison Connector toward the Outlook Cabin.
A wide paved path down to a beach in Kalamalka Lake Provincial Park.
A one-way trail around the former BX Ranch farmland, past Mutrie Dog Park and the BX Ranch dog park.
A loop around Birdie Lake at Predator Ridge with a wooden bird-watching platform. Dogs on leash.
Dead Horse Creek to the end of the canyon, about 5 hours (BC Parks' estimate). Settlers once used a route through the canyon, and the Salish used it as a wild horse trap.
Dead Horse Creek to the Pinnacles, about 1.5 hours (BC Parks' estimate).
From the Wildhorse Canyon Trail to Good's Creek, about 45 minutes (BC Parks' estimate). Named for Dave Good, who supplied the Kettle Valley Railway survey crews.
North part: Rimrock Gate to Divide Lake on a restricted-access road, 8 km, about 3.5 hours. South part: from the Wildhorse Canyon junction, 5 km, about 2 hours (BC Parks' estimates).
Old C.N. Trail to Dead Horse Creek, about 2 hours (BC Parks' estimate).
North parking lot to Divide Lake Road, about 2 hours (BC Parks' estimate).
To Divide Lake, about 3 hours (BC Parks' estimate).
About 2.5 hours (BC Parks' estimate); it continues to Baker Lake (4 km) and Good's Creek (4 km).
Divide Lake to Baker Lake, about 1.5 hours (BC Parks' estimate); Victor Lake is 1 km further.
Off the Wildhorse Canyon Trail, about 45 minutes (BC Parks' estimate); BC Parks names its views among the park's best.

A short gravel path beside the railway from Urdal Road to the Lillooet River. In 2016 the landowners gave the SLRD a right of way so the public can use it, and the riverfront by their land, for non-motorized recreation.

BC Parks: a gravel trail along the lake to Birkenhead Lake Estates at the south end, used by hikers and cyclists, with horses possible on the west half up to Sockeye Creek. Motor vehicles are not permitted. About 1 km from the trailhead it crosses a 50 m stretch of loose rock and a stream that can run high in heavy rain.

BC Parks: a short trail on the south side of the valley, rough and steep in places, ending at a view of the lake. Mountain goats may be seen on the cliffs above the campground in spring and fall. From April to June Phelix Creek can rise over the log bridge near the start, and the trail may close then.
Tourism Pemberton: Tenquille Lake has a volunteer-maintained cabin (reservations required), used for summer hiking and winter ski touring. They note a 4x4 vehicle is needed to reach the trailhead.

n: Nairn to One Mile Lake Trail (Part of Sea To Sky Trail)
hikes.text: Tourism Pemberton: a shaded trail through the forest and along the Green River between One Mile Lake and Nairn Falls, part of the Sea to Sky Trail.
Tourism Pemberton: an easy 6 km network of short trails by the Soo River, just off Highway 99 south of Pemberton, with examples of different forest practices.
Tourism Pemberton: a short, quieter hike near town to Pemberton Creek Falls, a waterfall in the forest.
Alberta Parks: a 2.1 km scenic walk (one way) along the Bow River between Whitefish Day Use Area and Bow Valley Campground.
Alberta Parks rates it easy: 1.9 km (one way) through forest and meadows with views.
Alberta Parks rates it easy: a 2.0 km return walk with mountain and Kananaskis River views, a lookout over a beaver pond and signs about the water cycle.
Alberta Parks rates it intermediate: 1.3 km (one way) up a narrow creek canyon over seven bridges to a waterfall. Alberta Parks says it can be icy in the colder months.

Alberta Parks: 2.9 km with about 250 m of elevation change, past Jewell Falls with views of Barrier Lake (3.9 km from Barrier Dam to the pass). Reached from Barrier Dam along Stoney Trail; often joined with Prairie View Trail as a loop.
Alberta Parks: a 1.3 km loop around a wetland basin with uncommon plants, an observation deck over the springs and interpretive signs.
Alberta Parks rates it easy: 2.0 km through forest and meadows along Middle Lake.
Alberta Parks rates it easy: a gentle 1.5 km through forest and meadows, with signs about the montane forest.
Alberta Parks rates it intermediate: 1.1 km (one way) along the top of a glacial ridge with mountain views and signs about glacial features.

Alberta Parks: also called the Barrier Fire Lookout trail, 6.6 km (one way) to the viewpoint with about 421 m of elevation change, switchbacking up an old forestry road to a view over Barrier Lake. From the top it goes on to the lookout or down towards Jewell Pass, on a fainter trail near the top.

Alberta Parks: 5.7 km (one way) from the trailhead to Quaite Valley Backcountry Campground, passing the Heart Creek trail 0.8 km in; beyond the campground it climbs to Jewell Pass and meets the Jewell Pass and Prairie View trails.

Alberta Parks: a long, open 22.5 km trail (one way) that follows the power line, with equestrian camping at Jewell Bay Backcountry Campground. Alberta Parks lists a yearly closure from April 15 to June 15 from Jewell Bay Campground south to Lorette Creek.
Alberta Parks: a 0.97 km link between Crocus Loop and Old Mill North in Brown-Lowery Provincial Park.
Alberta Parks: 0.54 km from the Brown-Lowery Provincial Park parking area down a hill to the rest of the park's trails.
Alberta Parks calls it Brown-Lowery Provincial Park's signature trail: 1.9 km climbing to viewpoints over the foothills and Front Ranges.
Alberta Parks: 1.5 km through the trees between Pine Hill and Old Mill North, with views of the open fields where the old mill stood.
Alberta Parks: 1.1 km east to west through the middle of Brown-Lowery Provincial Park, linking Red Willow with Raven and Wildrose.
Alberta Parks: 0.6 km through forest to the south end of Brown-Lowery Provincial Park, linking Pine Hill and the Lookout trail.
Alberta Parks: a 0.7 km old seismic line across the south end of Brown-Lowery Provincial Park, between Lookout and Red Willow.
Alberta Parks: 0.8 km through mixed forest beside Old Mill West; the two can make a loop.
Alberta Parks: 1.4 km on the east side of Brown-Lowery Provincial Park, partly along Pothole Creek, linking Pine Hill and Old Mill North.
Alberta Parks: 0.6 km; often joined with Old Mill West, Pine Hill and Lookout for a loop with views on the west side of Brown-Lowery Provincial Park.
Alberta Parks: 0.7 km from the west side of Crocus Loop, often used to reach the Lookout trail; it links to Wildrose East over the South Wildrose Bridge.
Alberta Parks: a short 0.4 km piece past the south Wildrose Bridge that reaches Old Mill West.
Alberta Parks: 5.0 km with about 332 m of elevation change, listed for bikes, e-bikes and hikers.
Alberta Parks: a 0.8 km connector from the Silvertip area to Montane Traverse (east) or Montane Cutoff (west).

Alberta Parks: 1.6 km (one way) between Montane Traverse and the parking area near the Canmore cemetery. Alberta Parks lists a yearly closure from December 1 to June 15 for wildlife, later than the May 15 in the map's trail name.

Alberta Parks: a 19.3 km forest trail (one way) with about 150 m of elevation change, crossing Goat Creek and the Spray River to the Spray River Fire Road and Banff townsite; most of it lies in Banff National Park.

Alberta Parks rates it intermediate: 1.9 km with about 125 m of climbing, the steeper of the two routes to Grassi Lakes (left at the fork near the start), with a waterfall and views over Canmore and signs about Lawrence Grassi. The easier route to the right follows an old road.
Alberta Parks: only a short part near the start is a maintained trail; most of the 2.7 km is a scramble route, with about 1,425 m of elevation change.

Alberta Parks: a maintained trail for 3.5 km to the saddle below Ha Ling Peak; the last 400 m and 103 m of climbing to the summit are on an unmaintained trail over loose, rocky ground. About 810 m of elevation change.
Alberta Parks: a short 1.0 km trail from the Tibbits Quarry trail to Meander Trail.
Alberta Parks calls it a challenging trail: 8.0 km with about 323 m of elevation change along the slopes of the Ehagay Nakoda Range, mostly in forest with a few views at creek crossings.

Alberta Parks: a 4.8 km loop with about 147 m of elevation change, from the Cougar Creek trailhead on the east side of the creek (or from the Alpine Club house); used by mountain bikers, walkers and riders on horseback.
Alberta Parks: 1.5 km with about 200 m of elevation change, linking Montane Traverse with Highway 1A in Canmore.

Alberta Parks: a short, very steep 3.2 km trail from the Cougar Creek trailhead up to the ridge of Mount Lady Macdonald and the site of an old tea house, with about 1,200 m of elevation change and little water on the way.
Alberta Parks: 2.0 km to Montane Traverse, just east of Harvie Heights.
Alberta Parks: a 1.6 km connector east of Stoneworks Creek between Montane Traverse and Douglas Fir Bench or the bottom of Johnny's Trail, with steep pitches through old Douglas fir forest.
Alberta Parks: 7.7 km with about 275 m of elevation change, from the Cougar Creek parking lot to Harvie Heights, with views of the Rundle range.
Alberta Parks says its preferred use is downhill mountain biking: 1.6 km and about 151 m down, steep with a few short flat parts, ending at the Grassi Lakes parking lot. Riders may come down it fast.

Alberta Parks says its preferred use is downhill mountain biking: a steep, loose and rocky 1.6 km (about 272 m of elevation change) from Whiteman's Pond to the Quarry Lake parking lot, crossed by the Highline trail at its middle and near the bottom.

Alberta Parks: a paved, 3 m wide trail beside the highway linking Canmore and Banff (about 26 km in all; 20 km listed on the Alberta side), built from 2010 for Parks Canada's 125th anniversary, with mountain views.
Alberta Parks: a short 1.6 km interpretive trail with signs about the forest and foothills.

Alberta Parks: the east half of the Elbow Loop, 26.5 km (one way) with about 350 m of elevation change on an old fire road up the Elbow River past Big Elbow and Tombstone backcountry campgrounds, with views of Threepoint and Cougar Mountains, Mounts Glasgow and Cornwall and Banded Peak. It also reaches Elbow Pass Day Use Area on Highway 40 (6.0 km more from Tombstone to Elbow Lake).
Alberta Parks: a 4.3 km loop with about 120 m of elevation change, climbing through pine woods with a short side trip to a foothills lookout.
Alberta Parks rates it easy: a short 0.8 km paved loop to viewpoints over Elbow Falls; the upper (left) part is wheelchair accessible. Signs describe water erosion.
Alberta Parks: 4.6 km, listed for bikes, e-bikes, hikers and horses in summer; in winter Alberta Parks lists fat biking only from Allen Bill Day Use Area to the Snagmore trail.
Alberta Parks: a 4 km loop with about 235 m of elevation change, climbing through trees on the north side and coming down through open meadows with views down the Elbow River valley.

Alberta Parks: a 4.0 km loop (6.8 km with the access trail from Allen Bill Day Use, rerouted after the 2013 flood), with about 213 m of elevation change. It climbs either the ridge edge or the gentler valley behind, with views of Moose Mountain and the Elbow River from the top.

Alberta Parks: half of the Elbow Loop, 23 km (one way) with about 400 m of elevation change on an old fire road along the Little Elbow River and over Tombstone Pass to Tombstone Backcountry Campground, with views of Mounts Romulus, Remus, Glasgow and Tombstone. The trailhead is at the west end of the equestrian campground.

Alberta Parks: 7.3 km (one way) with about 470 m of elevation change, on an old fire road along Moose Ridge and up Moose Dome; the last kilometre to the lookout is steep singletrack on loose rock. The trailhead is at the end of Moose Mountain Road.

Alberta Parks: 2.5 km (one way) with about 390 m of elevation change, switchbacking to the shoulder of Nihahi Ridge, across an open saddle and up the ridge edge, with views down the Elbow and up the Little Elbow valleys. It starts on the Little Elbow trail, 0.5 km west of Little Elbow Campground.
Alberta Parks: 6.2 km (one way) with about 510 m of elevation change up the narrow Powderface Creek valley; gently rolling in the east half, steeper and rockier further west.
Alberta Parks: a strenuous 7 km climb (one way, about 640 m of elevation change) from either end, with views and flower meadows on top. It starts at the end of Highway 66 or from Three-trail Pass.
Alberta Parks: 9.2 km (one way) with about 180 m of elevation change; the first 2 km climb the edge of a shaded canyon, then the trail drops to Prairie Creek.
Alberta Parks: a 3.2 km cut-off over the saddle between the Powderface Creek and Prairie Creek trails, about 85 m of elevation change; it shortens a 24 km route to 11 km.
Alberta Parks: about 8.4 km out and back, with about 675 m of elevation change, across Highway 66 from Elbow Falls in the Kananaskis Public Land Use Zone.

Alberta Parks: 2.7 km (one way) with about 102 m of elevation change, through aspen and mixed woods up the escarpment above the Elbow River, with views of the river canyon and wildflowers. It starts at the west end of the Paddy's Flat interpretive trail.
Alberta Parks: through pine, spruce and aspen forest with views of the Elbow River and the eastern slopes; 8.5 km as a loop from the Fullerton trailhead.
Alberta Parks: 5.2 km with about 215 m of elevation change; the west end climbs the escarpment over Canyon Creek through aspen, then winds through spruce down to the Elbow Valley Trail.

Alberta Parks: a 2.5 km connector (one way, about 275 m of elevation change) between Ford Creek Trail, Powderface Trail road and the Powderface Creek and Powderface Ridge trails, climbing through forest to Three-trail Pass with views of Nihahi and Compression ridges.

Alberta Parks: 15.8 km (one way) with about 357 m of elevation change, from the Little Elbow Suspension Bridge around the north side of Forgetmenot Ridge and up the valley to the east, joining Volcano Creek Trail with links to Hog's Back and Threepoint Creek trails.
Alberta Parks: 1.4 km from Bowbend Trail, with views of the Bow River valley and a climb west towards the Windmill Lookout.
Alberta Parks: 4.8 km south of the railway in Glenbow Ranch Provincial Park, with a west loop and an east loop; reached by Glenbow Trail across the tracks.
Alberta Parks: the main paved trail west from Glenbow Trail, 4.7 km, linking to the Cochrane Gleneagles pathways.
Alberta Parks: a 3.9 km gravel trail from Badger Bowl or the west end of Bowbend Trail.
Alberta Parks: a 2.5 km gravel loop from Glenbow Trail with high viewpoints over the Bow River valley and a link to Scott Trail on the east side.
Alberta Parks: 1.8 km on cross-country ski trails through forest near Kananaskis Village, with meadows and views of the Kananaskis Valley.

Alberta Parks says it is popular with downhill mountain bikers and hikers: 13.7 km from Baldy Pass Trailhead (or 15.9 km from Wasootch Day Use Area) to Lusk Creek Day Use Area, with about 490 m of elevation change. It climbs steadily to a forested pass; from Lusk Creek it passes a logged area with views of Barrier Lake. It can make a loop with Highway 40.
Alberta Parks: a short uphill hike (2.5 km one way from the lower Barrier Lake parking, shorter from the upper lot, about 100 m of climbing) to a ridge with views of both ends of Barrier Lake.

Alberta Parks calls it the highest maintained trail in the Canadian Rockies: 6.8 km from Ribbon Creek over the top of Mount Allan (2,819 m) and 17.5 km to Wind Valley, with about 1,340 m of elevation change. Alberta Parks gives 4 to 6 hours to the summit and lists a yearly closure from April 1 to June 21 for bighorn sheep.
Alberta Parks: 2.3 km (one way) with about 246 m of elevation change, from 0.4 km along Hidden Trail through forest to a reclaimed coal mine (1947 to 1952) with views.

Alberta Parks: an old fire road, 14 km (one way) to Evan-Thomas Pass. It links to Wedge Connector, but Alberta Parks says the bridge over Evan-Thomas Creek is gone and the crossing can be hard in high water.
Alberta Parks: 1.6 km (one way) with about 230 m of elevation change, between Ribbon Lake and Lillian Lake backcountry campgrounds, with wide views; reached from Ribbon Lake or Galatea Creek trails.
Alberta Parks: 1.5 km (one way) close to the Kananaskis River, past the eagle migration viewing site; with Troll Falls Trail it makes a 4 km loop.
Alberta Parks: 1.4 km (one way, about 70 m of elevation change) to the Nakiska day lodge, with the turn to Centennial Trail 0.4 km in.

Alberta Parks: a 1.7 km self-guided walk about forest management and history, with four viewpoints, joining Baldy Pass Trail 1.7 km from Lusk Creek Day Use Area. With the Lusk Pass connector it can make an 8 km loop.
Alberta Parks: 5.1 km between Kananaskis Village and Ribbon Creek Day Use, with some hard hills up or down.
Alberta Parks: a short 0.8 km trail through mature forest between the Kovach and Ribbon Creek trails.

Alberta Parks: 8.8 km (one way) up a valley between the cliffs of Mount Kidd and Mount Bogart to Ribbon Falls and its backcountry campground, then 2.0 km more to Ribbon Lake up a cliff with fixed cables and rungs. About 350 m of elevation change to the falls and 250 m more to the lake. Alberta Parks lists bikes on part of it only.
Alberta Parks: a short 0.4 km link between Troll Falls and Skogan Pass trails.

Alberta Parks: 10.2 km from Ribbon Creek Day Use Area to Skogan Pass and 19.4 km to Highway 1 near Dead Man's Flat, with about 624 m of elevation change. It follows a power line, so views are often partly blocked and the route is sunny.

Alberta Parks: 1.2 km (one way, about 400 m of elevation change) from Skogan Pass Trail to the old Hummingbird Plume Fire Lookout site; with High Level and Skogan Pass trails it makes a 12.8 km trip with views of the Kananaskis Valley.
Alberta Parks: a short 1.0 km link between Terrace Trail and Kovach Trail.

Alberta Parks: 7.2 km (one way) south of the Kovach junction, a hike and bike trail with views of the Kananaskis Valley and golf course, often used to link the Ribbon Creek and Lillian Lake backcountry campgrounds.

Alberta Parks: a 1.4 km trail through mixed forest to Troll Falls, shared with many hikers. Alberta Parks says bikes are not permitted on the short narrow part before the falls, and the side paths around the falls are closed for rockfall.
Alberta Parks rates it easy: a 1 km walk to the Wasootch Slabs climbing area.

Alberta Parks rates it difficult: 1.6 km (one way, about 321 m of elevation change) from the top of the Wasootch Day Use parking, steep in places with some loose rock and views early on. The maintained trail ends on the ridge; past that an informal route goes on over smaller peaks.
Alberta Parks: 2.0 km (one way) along the Kananaskis River, with views of paddlers and rafters.

Alberta Parks: 7.4 km (one way) with about 470 m of elevation change, through forest and willow flats by the Burstall Lakes, then steeply up to alpine meadows and the pass. Water may cover the trail in the willow flats. Alberta Parks lists bikes only to the end of the old logging road (2.7 km).

Alberta Parks: 4.6 km (one way) with about 300 m of elevation change, through forest to an alpine meadow and the lake below Mount Chester. Alberta Parks lists bikes only on the first 2 km (logging road). Alberta Parks lists a yearly closure from May 1 to June 29 while the area dries.
Alberta Parks: 6.6 km return with about 183 m of elevation change, climbing through old-growth forest to views from the ridge.

Alberta Parks calls it easy: 7.4 km (one way) with about 390 m of elevation change from Sibbald Lake Day Use Area through open foothills to the north edge of Kananaskis Country, with views of Cox Hill and the Bow Valley.
Alberta Parks: an 8.5 km loop crossing Highway 68 at both ends, with views of the Sibbald hills, popular with hikers and mountain bikers early in the season when other trails still have snow.
Alberta Parks: 13.2 km (one way) along the ridge, reached from several points on Powderface Road, with wide views and ways to make it longer or shorter.
Alberta Parks: a short, steep 2.5 km (one way, about 350 m of elevation change) through forest to the high point of the ridge, from Powderface Road.

Alberta Parks: 10.2 km (one way) with about 350 m of elevation change, mostly in forest with a wildflower meadow near the middle; the current route uses part of Baldy Pass Trail and the Baldy-Lusk connector. The first 650 m with Baldy Pass and the forestry interpretive trail make a loop of about 5 km. Alberta Parks says the old direct alignment is no longer maintained.

Alberta Parks: a former 3.5 km return interpretive trail through mature forest from the Jumpingpound Demonstration Day Use Area. Alberta Parks says it is not currently maintained, with missing bridges and signs that may be wrong.
Alberta Parks: a 3.6 km return loop (about 168 m of elevation change), 1 km along the Sibbald Reforestation interpretive trail, with views of Moose Mountain.

Alberta Parks: the main 27.3 km link between the Elbow River and Sibbald Creek valleys around the north side of Moose Mountain, about 210 m of elevation change, used mostly for mountain biking and horseback riding.

Alberta Parks: 7.5 km (one way) to the pass with about 671 m of elevation change, a steady climb through trees into alpine terrain; it goes on over the pass to Ribbon Lake (10.1 km to the campground).
Alberta Parks: part of the Trans Canada Trail, 63 km from Goat Creek to Peninsula Day Use (80 km to Elk Pass), for bikes, e-bikes and hikers.
Alberta Parks: 0.8 km (one way) through trees to a spring that pours out of a rock wall, branching off Watridge Lake Trail 3.9 km from the Mount Shark trailhead.
Alberta Parks: 4.2 km at West Bragg Creek, for bikes, e-bikes, hikers and horses.
Alberta Parks: 5.2 km at West Bragg Creek, for bikes, e-bikes, hikers and horses.
Alberta Parks: 0.7 km at West Bragg Creek, for bikes, e-bikes, hikers and horses.
Alberta Parks rates it intermediate: 3.1 km at West Bragg Creek.
Alberta Parks: 2.3 km at West Bragg Creek; in winter it is part of the north winter equestrian route.
Alberta Parks: 1.6 km at West Bragg Creek, for bikes, e-bikes, hikers and horses.
Alberta Parks rates it easy: a short 0.3 km loop at West Bragg Creek.
Alberta Parks: 1.9 km at West Bragg Creek, for bikes, e-bikes, hikers and horses.
Alberta Parks: 8.6 km at West Bragg Creek, for bikes, e-bikes, hikers and horses.
Alberta Parks: 6.1 km, for bikes, e-bikes, hikers and horses; in winter only its southern 0.7 km is part of the winter equestrian route.
Alberta Parks: 1.5 km from Merlin View along the north side of Moose Loop, a link to Tom Snow off the ski trails.
Alberta Parks rates it intermediate: 1.5 km at West Bragg Creek, for hikers and horses in summer.
Alberta Parks rates it intermediate: 3.8 km at West Bragg Creek, for hikers and horses in summer.
Alberta Parks: 1.5 km at West Bragg Creek, for bikes, e-bikes, hikers and horses.
Alberta Parks: 4.2 km at West Bragg Creek, for bikes, e-bikes, hikers and horses.
Alberta Parks: 1.4 km at West Bragg Creek; in winter it is part of the north winter equestrian route.

Alberta Parks: 8.8 km, machine and hand built and looked after by the Calgary Mountain Bike Alliance, with smooth dirt, roots, rocks, berms, boardwalks and views. Built as an alternative to Tom Snow, it crosses Tom Snow three times, splitting it into four sections. Alberta Parks lists it for all users and says it is mostly ridden by mountain bikers.
Alberta Parks: 4.6 km at West Bragg Creek, for bikes, e-bikes, hikers and horses.

Alberta Parks: the part east of Telephone Loop is not recommended from April 1 to November 30 because it is wet, with no biking or horses on that part; Alberta Parks lists bikes on the west part (2.4 km).
Alberta Parks: a 0.6 km shortcut at West Bragg Creek.
Alberta Parks: a 3.6 km narrower trail between Strange Brew and Snagmore.
Alberta Parks: a 3.5 km rooty trail linking Strange Brew and Elbow, mostly ridden by mountain bikers.
Parks Canada: a figure-8 for hiking and biking, a 2.2 km short loop or 4.1 km long loop; the long loop reaches Kinosao Lake.
Parks Canada: 1.9 km one way, rolling alongside Brûlé Trail to Kinosao Lake, then northwest to Grey Owl Trail. For hiking and biking.
Parks Canada: 14.8 km return to Grey Owl's cabin at Beaver Lodge Lake, for hiking and biking (Parks Canada calls it a better bike trip than a hike). A ski trail with a warming hut in winter.
Parks Canada: a gently rolling hiking and biking trail to a backcountry campsite beside Cowan Lake.
Parks Canada: for hiking, biking, horses and wagons, linking to Bald Hill, J.E.T. and Reeve's Ravine for loops, with backcountry campsites at Breezy Hill and East Deep Lake.
Parks Canada: 10.1 km return on an old logging road that climbs steadily up the escarpment; for hiking, biking and horses.

Parks Canada: a 6.1 km loop on the ridge above Edwards Creek, for hiking and biking. The east side crosses wetlands and is a winter trail (groomed for skiing and fat biking); the west side is a 3.0 km link between the Crawford Creek trailhead and the Northgate trails next to the park.
Parks Canada lists it for hiking only and says biking is not permitted. A one-way trail with creeks and narrow paths between the escarpment base (Birches trailhead) and the top.
Parks Canada lists it for hiking only: a 0.5 km loop on a floating boardwalk through the marsh.

Parks Canada: built with the Manitoba Escarpment Trail Society for mountain biking, a flowy singletrack along the ravine's edge in the East Escarpment network, in three parts (2.5 km trailhead to junction, 2 km to J.E.T., 2.6 km to Bald Hill).

Parks Canada: for hiking, biking and horses through prairie and forest to the Tilson Lake and Birdtail backcountry campsites (west section 14.5 km, east section 21.5 km). Parks Canada says to expect bumps along the way.
Manitoba Parks lists it as a hiking trail with red markers, about 2.5 km, along the Assiniboine River.
Manitoba Parks lists it as a hiking trail with yellow markers, about 3.4 km.
Manitoba Parks lists it as a hiking trail with white markers, about 5.0 km, reached from Highway 1.
Manitoba Parks lists it as a hiking trail, about 2.0 km.
Manitoba Parks lists it as a hiking trail, about 2.5 km, reached from Highway 1.

BC Parks' trail map: 4.7 km one way to Upper Joffre Lake, about 3.5 h one way (their estimate). The map gives 490 m of climbing, the park page about 400 m. Lower Joffre Lake's viewpoint is a few minutes from the parking lot; the trail then climbs through old-growth hemlock and spruce and across talus to Middle Joffre Lake, and is narrower and rougher on the last part to Upper Joffre Lake, below Matier Glacier and Joffre Peak. Camping only at the Upper Lake campground (reservation). BC Parks says day-use passes are often needed in peak season, and that vehicle access depends on the weather from November to May.
BC Parks: a short side trail off the Brandywine Falls Trail, starting just before the rail crossing. A bit rough, with one short steep climb, to a small lake with no beach or dock.
BC Parks: part of the Sea to Sky Trail through Brandywine Falls Park, shared by hikers and cyclists.

BC Parks' estimates: Elfin Lakes to Rampart Ponds, on the way to Mamquam Lake, is 11 km and 570 m of climbing on a narrow, lightly used wilderness trail with infrequent maintenance. BC Parks' trail sheet of May 19, 2026 reported a washed-out bridge at Zig Zag Creek, about 9 km from Elfin Lakes, with the trail past it and Rampart Ponds campground closed until further notice; no camping at Mamquam Lake. BC Parks advisories have the current status.

BC Parks: a 2 km barrier-free interpretive loop, about 1 h, from near the alpine ski area through subalpine meadows, with a short side loop through old-growth forest. No dogs when the trail is snow-free (sensitive marsh); guide dogs welcome.

BC Parks: 2.5 km, a little over 90 min, about 100 m of elevation change, across the Black Mountain plateau past several small lakes. Their figures include side trips to the Yew Lake viewpoint and the Vancouver lookout.

BC Parks: about 7 km return and 3 h from the ski area parking lot (the Cabin Lake trail itself is 1 km), with about 275 m of elevation change. Reached by 2.7 km of the Baden-Powell Trail up Black Mountain; it passes small lakes, the Yew Lake lookout and Black Mountain's south summit, then rejoins the Baden-Powell Trail.

BC Parks: about 8 km return and 4 h from the Nordic area parking lot (the peak trail itself is 1.3 km), with about 400 m of elevation change, by the powerline road and the Baden-Powell Trail to the top of Hollyburn Mountain. In winter BC Parks marks a 6 km return route to Hollyburn Peak and says it crosses avalanche terrain.

BC Parks: in winter, a marked 3.5 km return route from the ski area's backcountry access corridor past the Yew Lake meadows to Bowen Lookout. It needs a free backcountry access tag from the Black Mountain Lodge, and BC Parks says it crosses avalanche terrain.

BC Parks: 29 km one way from the Cypress ski area north past the Lions and Deeks Lake, down to Highway 99 just south of Porteau Cove. Remote and rugged, with cliffs, scree and exposed ridges; orange markers can be far apart, and the trail can be hard to follow in poor weather. BC Parks lists no reliable water between Strachan Meadows and Magnesia Meadows. Wilderness camping, with no set sites, at places such as Magnesia Meadows, Brunswick Lake and Deeks Lake. No bikes; the Capilano watershed is no entry.

BC Parks: 4 km one way, about 2.5 h, 450 m of elevation change (summer figures), from the north end of the top parking lot over Brockton Point and First and Second Pump to the summit, with views over Vancouver and, on clear days, the Gulf Islands and Vancouver Island.

BC Parks: 1 km to First Lake (about 30 min), then 2 km on to Dog Mountain (about 40 min), with little elevation change, through subalpine old-growth fir to a view over Greater Vancouver and the Seymour River valley.
BC Parks: a 3 km loop from First Lake (about 45 min, 60 m of elevation change) that joins the Mount Seymour Trail back down to the parking lot.
BC Parks: 1.5 km, about 45 min, 180 m of elevation change, from the north end of Parking Lot 4 along the chairlift line to the lake. BC Parks notes there are no fish in it.

BC Parks: a self-guided interpretive loop of about 2 km from the parking lot, about 1 h, with little elevation change, past the Goldie rope tow area to Goldie Lake. It links to the Flower Lake and Perimeter trails.
BC Parks: 1.5 km, about 45 min, 150 m of elevation change, starting 500 m along the Goldie Lake trail, through subalpine bogs and ponds with many kinds of birds.

BC Parks gives 17 km, 9 to 10 h return (their estimate), and about 500 m of elevation change. It leaves the Mount Seymour Trail just before First Pump, and past Gopher Lake it narrows and is marked with flashers and tape. BC Parks calls it rugged and easy to lose in poor weather, and lists its season as late June to October. The shelter at the end is for emergencies only.

BC Parks: 5.5 km to the Perimeter Trail junction (about 2 h), with about 670 m of elevation change, or 2.3 km to the Baden-Powell junction (about 45 min), on the grade of an old logging road from near the park entrance.
BC Parks: 1 km, about 30 min, with little elevation change, from the Vancouver picnic area parking lot to the Old Buck Trail.
BC Parks: 750 m, about 15 min, with little elevation change, from across the road from the Vancouver picnic area parking lot, through some of the mountain's early ski-area history.
BC Parks: 1.5 km, about 45 min, 240 m of elevation change, from the Deep Cove lookout up to the Goldie Lake access trail junction.

Metro Vancouver: 2.5 km one way, about 800 m of climbing, 2 h or more (their estimate). A steep climb through second-growth forest, often crowded on weekends and in summer. No dogs. Metro Vancouver lists AEDs at markers 10, 20 and 30.
Metro Vancouver: 2.9 km, about 750 m of climbing, 2 h or more (their estimate). A steep climb through second-growth and old-growth forest, rougher than the Grouse Grind. No dogs.

Metro Vancouver lists Lynn Loop and the longer Lynn Loop and Cedars Mill loop as easy, well-marked trails suited to families. Lower Lynn Loop and Cedars Mill are leash-optional for dogs; the park map has distances and times.
Metro Vancouver lists it as an easy, well-marked trail suited to families.

Metro Vancouver lists the Cedars Mill and Headwaters Trail loop and Norvan Falls as intermediate, with steep parts and rough, uneven ground. Norvan Falls is the Headwaters Trail's destination. North of the third debris chute, the Headwaters Trail is leash-optional for dogs.

Metro Vancouver calls it a hiking route, steeper and rougher than its trails, in the park's backcountry toward Grouse Mountain. Dogs are not allowed on the Grouse Mountain Skyride. Metro Vancouver closes the backcountry beyond Norvan Falls for part of the year; its park page has the current notice.

Resort Municipality of Whistler: a 16 km round trip from the Alta Lake Road trailhead by the Rainbow Falls Loop to Rainbow Lake, about 850 m of climbing; they suggest at least 6 h. It is Whistler's water supply area: no dogs, bikes, swimming, fishing or camping (campsites 2.2 km further on at Hanging Lake). Grizzly, black bear and cougar country. RMOW lists the alpine trails as closed to hiking and biking from November to May.

Resort Municipality of Whistler: a 13.8 km hiking-only route that starts off the Flank Trail where it crosses 19 Mile Creek, at about 1,100 m. Often reached from the end of Mountain View Drive (no parking there; RMOW suggests Meadow Park). Side trails lead to Iceberg Lake and Screaming Cat Lake. Grizzly, black bear and cougar country. RMOW lists the alpine trails as closed to hiking and biking from November to May.

BC Parks: about 12 km and 1,500 m of elevation change from the West Canyon parking lot to the Golden Ears, about 7 h one way (their estimate), by Alder Flats and an old logging road up to steep Panorama Ridge. BC Parks says water can be scarce past Alder Flats and snow can stay on Panorama Ridge well into July; the shelter on the ridge is for emergencies only. Wilderness camping at Alder Flats and Panorama Ridge, no fires.

BC Parks: about 11 km of trails from Mike Lake to Alouette Mountain, by the Incline and Alouette Mountain fire access trails, 9 to 10 h return (their estimate), with wide views from the top. BC Parks calls it a long, strenuous hike and says to expect snow well into June.
BC Parks' 2008 guide: 1.2 km one way, about 1 h, 150 m of climbing, up the old incline loggers used to skid logs down to Mike Lake. It leads on toward Alouette Mountain.

BC Parks' 2008 guide: 5 km one way, about 2.5 h, 250 m of climbing, on an old logging grade for 3.2 km, then uphill before dropping to Lower Falls. It is the start of the Golden Ears Trail; wilderness camping at Alder Flats.
BC Parks' 2008 guide: 1.5 km one way, about 45 min, 175 m of climbing, to views over the valley, with waterfalls in the wet season.

BC Parks' trail guide: 21 km one way from the end of Blackwall Road to Nicomen Lake, about 7 to 9 h (their estimate), 292 m of elevation change. Along Lone Man Ridge and past the Three Brothers through subalpine meadows that flower after the snow melts, often late June and July. Camps at Buckhorn (5 km) and Kicking Horse (about 13.5 km), backcountry permit needed. A 1 km side trail climbs First Brother (2,272 m) over loose rock. It can link with the Grainger Creek and Hope Pass trails to Cayuse Flats.

BC Parks' trail guide: 10.4 km one way from Lightning Lake, or 14.2 km from the Windy Joe trailhead, 27 km as a full loop, 1,150 m of elevation change, 4 to 6 h one way or 11 h for the loop (their estimates). Through forest and an old subalpine larch stand to a 2,408 m sub-peak of the park's highest mountain. BC Parks says it is one of the park's last trails to lose its snow, with cornices on the ridge in early summer, and gives mid-July to the first big snowfall (often late September or October) as its usual season. Backcountry camp at Frosty Creek (6.5 km).

BC Parks' trail guide: 9 km return around Lightning Lake, about 3 h, little elevation change, or a shorter figure-eight loop over Rainbow Bridge. Starts at the Lightning Lake day-use area or Spruce Bay parking, past the campgrounds and a picnic area.

BC Parks' trail guide: 12 km one way, about 4 h, little elevation change, from Spruce Bay past Lightning, Flash and Strike lakes to Thunder Lake, out and back. The last part crosses rock slides. Strike Lake backcountry campsite.

BC Parks' trail guide: 14.6 km one way, about 6 h, 775 m of climbing, from Strawberry Flats to Lightning Lakes; with the Lightning Lakes Chain and South Gibson trails it makes a 19.6 km loop. Much of it is an exposed ridge with no water, and meadows flower mid-June to late July.

BC Parks' trail guide: 18.6 km one way, 7 to 9 h, 500 m up and 1,350 m down to the Silver-Skagit Road in Skagit Valley Park. It leaves Skyline I at Despair Pass, crosses meadows below Snow Camp and Lone Goat mountains to Mowich camp, then descends to the Skagit. BC Parks notes several kilometres of meadow with no water past Mowich.

BC Parks' trail guide: 8 km one way, about 4.5 h, 525 m of climbing, on an old access road to the Windy Joe fire lookout at 1,825 m, restored as an interpretive site. It starts on the West Similkameen trail off Gibson Pass Road.

BC Parks' trail guide: 8 km one way, 3 to 4 h, 435 m of climbing, from Strawberry Flats past the ski area and Nepopekum Falls to Poland Lake, below Grassy Mountain. Rated difficult for its remoteness and steep parts. Backcountry camp at the lake; bikes and horses use the old fire road and stop 200 m short of the lake.

BC Parks' trail guide: 4.5 km one way, about 2.5 h, little elevation change, starting with 2 km of the Strawberry Flats trail. Past Shadow and Nepopekum falls to Derek Falls, with viewing landings; back the same way.

BC Parks' trail guide: 2 km one way, about 45 min, little elevation change, on an old fire-access road to the bottom of the ski area, where it meets the Three Falls trail. Wild strawberries in late July.

BC Parks' trail guide: a 1.5 km loop, about 30 min, little elevation change, from the lower or upper alpine parking lots off Blackwall Road. White and yellow flowers in late spring and a second bloom from mid-July.
BC Parks' trail guide: about 500 m, 15 min, through a bog made by beavers, 1.5 km down Gibson Pass Road. Flowers from June; the white rein orchid in July.

BC Parks' trail guide: 2 km one way, about 45 min, little elevation change, from the Headwaters Corral Camp east beside the Similkameen River to the Beaver Pond nature trail, a 500 m loop by a beaver pond.

BC Parks' trail guide: 2 km one way, about 45 min, 50 m of elevation change, beside the Similkameen River from Coldspring Campground to Gibson Pass Road, where it links to the Little Muddy, Similkameen and Windy Joe trails.

BC Parks' trail guide: 300 m one way, about 20 min, 125 m of climbing, to a rocky knoll at 1,725 m with views of Frosty Mountain and Lightning Lake. The trailhead is 500 m up the road from the Cascade Lookout. Flowers bloom early on this south-facing slope.
BC Parks' trail guide: 2.5 km one way, about 1 h, 100 m of elevation change, linking the Lightning Lake day-use area (from the Twenty Minute Lake parking lot) with Manning Park Resort.

BC Parks' trail guide: 3.4 km one way, 125 m of elevation change, about 2.5 h as a loop with South Gibson (3.8 km). A wide cross-country ski trail north of the road between Strawberry Flats and Lightning Lakes campground, a little harder than South Gibson.

BC Parks' trail guide: 3.8 km one way, 125 m of elevation change, about 2.5 h as a loop with North Gibson (3.4 km). A wide cross-country ski trail south of the road between Strawberry Flats and Lightning Lakes campground.

BC Parks' trail guide: 17 km one way, 8 to 10 h, 950 m of climbing, from behind the park's Eastgate sign up to the Heather Trail, then 7 km more to the lower alpine parking lot on Blackwall Road. BC Parks puts the last reliable water at about 7 km; the last 2 km cross subalpine meadows.

BC Parks' trail guide: 25 km one way from the Cascade parking lot to Paddy's Pond on the Whipsaw FSR, 14 to 16 h, 1,131 m of climbing. Up Snass Creek past Dry Lake to Paradise Valley and the Tulameen meadows below Snass Mountain. Popular with horse riders. It can loop with the Whatcom trail (about 20 km) or with the Hope Pass and Skagit Bluffs trails.

BC Parks' trail guide: 9.5 km one way, about 5 h, 1,082 m of climbing. It leaves the Dewdney Trail 2.5 km from the Cascade parking lot, climbs to Punch Bowl Pass and Lake below Mount Snass, then drops to Snass View camp on the Dewdney Trail.
BC Parks' trail guide: 9.2 km one way, about 4 h, 952 m of climbing, from Grainger Creek camp on the Hope Pass trail (7 km from Cayuse Flats) up to Nicomen Lake and the Heather Trail.
