BC Parks' trail guide: 24 km one way, about 10 h, 1,000 m of climbing, from Cayuse Flats up the Skaist River to the Whipsaw FSR. Built by the Royal Engineers in 1861 as a route between Hope and Princeton. Camps at Grainger Creek and Marmot City.
BC Parks' trail guide: 7.5 km one way, about 2.5 h, 300 m of elevation change, through subalpine meadows from Nicomen Lake to the Hope Pass trail. Remote; the rustic Fido camp is 1 km from the lake.
BC Parks' trail guide: 16 km one way, about 5 h, 850 m of climbing, from the Monument 78/83 parking lot through old burn to Holdover Peak on the Canada-US border, with two old fire lookouts.

BC Parks' trail guide: 12 km one way from the Monument 78/83 parking lot, 4 to 5 h, 200 m of elevation change, to Monument 78 camp near the Pacific Crest Trail's northern end. Brushy and only maintained from time to time past the East Similkameen junction; the guide notes the Castle Creek bridge on the Similkameen side is out. Backcountry permit for camping.

BC Parks' trail guide: the Canadian end of the Pacific Crest Trail, 12.2 km one way, 4 to 5 h, 450 m of elevation change, from the Windy Joe trailhead past the PCT camp down to Castle Creek and Monument 78 at the border. BC Parks' notice warns of heavy snow and avalanche conditions on it in late spring and early summer, and that crossing the border here needs permission from both countries.
BC Parks' trail guide: 5.7 km one way, about 2.5 h, 225 m of climbing, between the Cascade parking lot and Cayuse Flats, with steep parts high above Highway 3.

BC Parks' trail guide: 14.3 km one way, 4 to 6 h, little elevation change, from the Sumallo Grove parking lot along the Skagit River through rainforest into Skagit Valley Park, to the Centennial trail. DeLacey camp at 4 km.
BC Parks' trail guide: about 500 m, 15 min, wheelchair accessible, through old-growth western red cedar and Douglas fir, 9.5 km east of the park's west entrance.
BC Parks' trail guide: about 500 m, 15 min, off the eastbound side of Highway 3 about 9 km east of Westgate. Red rhododendrons usually bloom around mid-June.
BC Parks' trail guide: about 500 m, 20 min, from the parking lot before the Lightning Lakes day-use area. Named for the walk from the old park centre.
BC Parks' trail guide: 9 km one way, about 4 h, 450 m of climbing, from the Allison Pass highways yard to Poland Lake (park outside the gate). Used in winter to reach backcountry ski terrain.

BC Parks: 16 km one way to the core area, 6 to 8 h, 1,300 m of elevation change, from km 13 of the Ashnola Forest Service Road (23 km from Highway 3). The most direct trail in, still rated difficult. BC Parks' hiking page notes closures on some trails after the 2023 Crater Creek wildfire; its advisories have the current status.

BC Parks: the Wall Creek trail is 20 km one way to the core area, 7 to 9 h, 1,100 m of elevation change, from km 38 of the Ashnola Forest Service Road, over a footbridge and up through open forest to Red Mountain meadows.

BC Parks: 28 km one way to the core area, 10 to 12 h, 1,740 m of elevation change, the hardest of the three trails in, often split with a camp at Twin Buttes. BC Parks' hiking page notes closures on some park trails; its advisories have the current status.

BC Parks: from Quiniscoe Lake, 1 km and about 30 min each to Lake of the Woods (30 m of elevation change) or Pyramid Lake (very little). The Quiniscoe, Lake of the Woods and Pyramid loop is 2 km and about 1 h, on a wide, firm path with bridges and boardwalk.
BC Parks: 3 km return, about 1 h, 60 m of elevation change, a short side trip from the Diamond Trail to a small lake.
BC Parks: 8 km return around Scout Mountain, about 4 h, 250 m of elevation change, past flowers, rock bluffs and a small rock glacier, with BC Parks' pick of views over the Ashnola valley.

BC Parks: 7 km return, about 3 h, 200 m of elevation change, through larch and spruce with views of Grimface, the Matriarch and Macabre Tower. BC Parks calls Ladyslipper Lake the best spot in the park for fishing.

BC Parks: 10 km return, 4 to 5 h, 150 m of elevation change, along the valley bottom and the outlet creek through wetlands. BC Parks' hiking page notes closures on some park trails; its advisories have the current status.

BC Parks: 12 km return, 7 to 10 h, 600 m of elevation change, to the park's highest point, with views over the park and Snowy Protected Area. BC Parks' hiking page notes closures on some park trails; its advisories have the current status.

BC Parks: about 1 km and 45 min, 200 m of climbing, through old subalpine forest to the Trophy Mountain meadows, flowering in July and August. The trail goes on about 1.25 h over rock to Sheila Lake, and a further climb reaches Skyline Ridge (12 km return from the parking lot). The trailhead is up 11 km of gravel road off Clearwater Valley Road. BC Parks gives late June to early October as the trail's usual season. No bikes.
BC Parks: from the parking lot at the bottom of Green Mountain Road, past big cottonwoods and old-growth cedar to Placid Lake, a fen turning into a bog, with nearly 50 kinds of dragonflies.

BC Parks: from a sharp bend on the Green Mountain lookout road, about 40 min through young birch and aspen to the south face of White Horse Bluff, an old volcanic formation with views of the Clearwater valley.
BC Parks: about a 45 min walk from the Green Mountain viewing tower to Foot Lake, through forest with many nesting songbirds in summer.

BC Parks: 20 km return from the parking lot on the west side of the road at km 30.6, into a network with the Trout Creek, Hoodoo Rim, West Rim and Clearwater River trails. Past Hemp Creek Falls, the Green Mountain hoodoos and a volcanic cave. BC Parks says it is the one trail system in Wells Gray where horses need no letter of permission.

BC Parks: a short walk from the parking lot to the viewing platform over the Bailey's Chute rapids, where chinook salmon try to jump the chute from late August to early September. The trail goes on upstream through old cedar and hemlock past Marcus and Myanth falls.

BC Parks: an easy gravel path from the parking area past mineral springs to the 1920s Ray homestead, with split-rail fences and barns. The farmhouse collapsed in 1998, and BC Parks asks visitors not to go in the buildings. A second way in from Alice Creek parking passes the bubbling Ray mineral spring cone.

n: C.W. Shook Trail to Dragon's Tongue
hikes.text: BC Parks: a 17 km loop from the trailhead east of Falls Creek and Clearwater Lake campgrounds, or shorter trips to the Dragon's Tongue lava beds and Sticta Falls. BC Parks says the route beyond the Dragon's Tongue to Kostal Lake (24 km) needs wilderness travel experience.

BC Parks: a backcountry trail from the end of Kinney Lake Road near the Welcome Centre to Berg Lake below Mount Robson and Robson Pass, where BC Parks finished four years of repairs. Their trail map puts the campgrounds at about Kinney Lake 7 km, Whitehorn 11 km, Emperor Falls 16 km, Marmot 19 km, Berg Lake 21 km, Rearguard 22 km and Robson Pass 23 km. Campground reservations in peak season; no permit for day hikes. Bikes only to Kinney Lake, dogs on leash for day hikes only, no fires, and a permanent boil-water advisory. No cell service.
BC Parks: the Snowbird Pass part of the Berg Lake Trail heads southeast from Robson Pass. No dogs, and BC Parks closes it each year from May 1 to July 1 for wildlife calving.

BC Parks: a user-maintained route, not a formal trail, 5 to 7 days as a loop through Jasper National Park and back on the Berg Lake Trail (66 km from the trailhead to Berg Lake campground), or 49 km one way to the Alberta border. Rustic camps along it, 16 river crossings, and parts with no visible trail. BC Parks suggests late summer and early fall. BC Parks asks hikers to register at the trailhead kiosk; Berg Lake and Jasper camps need their own bookings.

BC Parks: from the Yellowhead Lake parking lot, 1.2 km along the pipeline to the trailhead kiosk, where BC Parks asks hikers to register, then 600 m of climbing on a firm trail to the main campground at 7.2 km by Rockingham Creek. Past the creek the trail is rough, poorly defined and can be wet, up a headwall at 11 km to a second campground at the first alpine lake about 2.5 km on.
BC Parks: 5.6 km of easy hiking from Assiniboine Lodge to the Wonder Pass viewpoint.
BC Parks: 5.7 km from Assiniboine Lodge, a strenuous climb to Windy Ridge.
BC Parks: 4.8 km from Assiniboine Lodge, a strenuous uphill hike to Mount Cautley.
BC Parks rates Assiniboine Lodge to the Nub as moderately demanding, and lists day hikes from Sunburst Lake to Elizabeth Lake (1.7 km), Wedgwood Lake (5.1 km) and Rock Lake (11.3 km).

BC Parks: from the parking lot past the Shark Mountain turn-off on the Smith-Dorrien road, by Watridge Lake and Bryant Creek in Banff National Park, 21 km and about 6 h to Assiniboine Pass, then 4 km and about 1 h more to Magog Lake: 520 m of elevation change, high point 2,195 m. Parks Canada asks for a backcountry permit to camp on the Banff part.
BC Parks: the other way in from Bryant Creek, past Marvel Lake to Wonder Pass (22 km, about 6 h), then 4.5 km and just over 1 h to Magog Lake: 700 m of elevation change, high point 2,378 m.

BC Parks' guide: 7.2 km, about 2.5 h, with steep parts, from Slocan City north along the lake to Evans Creek. BC Parks points to parking just south of the Slocan River bridge (residents only north of it). An early-season trail with flowers, swimming and fishing. BC Parks' park page notes wildfire closures along Slocan Lake; its advisories have the current status.

BC Parks' guide: from Evans Beach, 4 km and 500 m up to Emerald Lake (4 tent pads), 2 km and 215 m on to Cahill Lake (6 tent pads), then 2.5 km and 215 m to Beatrice Lake (no camping), about 5.5 h in all by their times. BC Parks calls it prime grizzly habitat and allows pets on leash only as far as Beatrice Lake.

BC Parks' guide: 8.8 km, 8 h or more each way, 1,900 m of climbing, from the west shore of Slocan Lake (boat access) past waterfalls to views of New Denver Glacier. Only maintained from time to time; no facilities.

BC Parks' guide rates it easy to moderate and gives 4 km, about 4 h and 905 m of climbing, from the west shore of Slocan Lake (boat access) past the Rock Castles, a historic cabin and big old cedar and hemlock. The short Nemo Falls loop is 1 km. Upper Nemo Creek is prime grizzly habitat; pets only as far as the Rock Castles.

BC Parks' guide: 2 km and 300 m from the trailhead to Drinnon Lake (3 tent pads), 1.3 km and 125 m on to Drinnon Pass and Wicca Lake, then 2.7 km (250 m up, 125 m down) to Gwillim Lakes (12 tent pads), about 3.5 h in all by their times. Reached by the Little Slocan and Hoder Creek forest service roads. No fires or pets; camping only on the tent pads.

BC Parks: from the Gibson Lake parking lot (16 km of gravel road off Highway 3A), 4.5 km and 445 m up to Kokanee Lake (about 2 h, no camping), then on to the Kokanee Glacier Cabin at 8 km or the Slocan Chief Cabin at 9.3 km, about 4 h, 590 m up and 100 m down. Camping only on the tent pads near Kaslo Lake.
BC Parks: an easy 2.5 km loop, about 1 h, at the Gibson Lake trailhead (1,536 m), with views of the peaks and old mine workings. No camping or fires.
BC Parks: 3 km, about 1.5 h, 193 m of climbing, from Woodbury Creek, starting with 2 km of the Scranton Mine Road. No camping or fires.
BC Parks: 8 km, about 4 h, 762 m of climbing, from the Woodbury Creek trailhead (1,321 m) to the 8-person Woodbury Cabin north of Woodbury Glacier, with tenting nearby.
BC Parks: 7 km, about 5 h, 1,016 m of climbing on steep switchbacks, from Woodbury Creek to the 10-person Silver Spray Cabin below Sunrise Mountain, through old mining sites and flower meadows.

BC Parks: 9.8 km, about 5 h, 950 m of climbing, from the Lemon Creek trailhead to Sapphire Lakes (no camping there), or 14.3 km and about 7.5 h to the Slocan Chief Cabin. Old-growth forest, waterfalls and an old mine cabin. BC Parks says it is only semi-regularly maintained.
BC Parks: 4.5 km, about 2.5 h, from Sapphire Lakes over Lemon Pass by Kaslo Lake to the Slocan Chief Cabin, 105 m up and 320 m down.
BC Parks: 10.2 km, about 5 h, 759 m up and 107 m down, from the Enterprise Creek trailhead (1,340 m) to the Slocan Chief Cabin, reached from Highway 6 north of Slocan City.
BC Parks: 6.4 km, about 3 h, 540 m of climbing, from Enterprise Creek to Blue Grouse Basin. No facilities.
Sépaq: a 2.6 km loop, about 45 min, from km 0 of the park road, under tall maples and birches.
Sépaq: 3.4 km return, about 1 h 15, from km 0, over a footbridge across the Cachée River to a view of the Jacques-Cartier River, with a 120 m height difference.
Sépaq: a 2.9 km loop, about 1 h, from km 3, past a peat bog, a fir stand and yellow birch forest.
Sépaq: a 5.4 km loop, about 2 h 15, from km 3, along the river with views of the valley and L'Épaule mountain, with a 220 m height difference.
Sépaq: a 2.2 km loop, about 45 min, from km 10, beside the Belleau brook.
Sépaq: a 4 km loop, about 1 h 30, from km 10, beside a brook with a string of cascades.
Sépaq: 14.8 km return, about 5 h, from km 10 or km 18, through forest along the Jacques-Cartier River.
Sépaq: a 10.4 km loop, about 3 h 30, from km 10, up the Belleau brook valley to a viewpoint, with a 210 m height difference.
Sépaq: an 11.2 km loop, about 4 h, from km 10: 2.6 km on Les Coulées, then a steady climb to a viewpoint over the valley, with a 360 m height difference.
Sépaq: 4.8 km return on foot, about 1 h 30, from km 12.5, along the Sautauriski River, an Atlantic salmon river. Sépaq also lists a 10 km return by bike from km 10.
Sépaq: 1.2 km return, about 25 min, from km 12.5, to a river delta with wetland and forest habitats.
Sépaq: from km 16, 5 km return (about 2 h) to the first lookout or 11 km return (about 3 h 30) to the second, over the Jacques-Cartier and Sautauriski valleys, with a 456 m height difference.
Sépaq: a 5.4 km loop, about 1 h 45, from km 18: a steep climb at the start, then Buvard Lake and maple stands.
Sépaq: 24.8 km return, about 8 h 30, from km 18 or km 30, along the Jacques-Cartier River with valley views and rock walls.
Sépaq: 16 km return, about 5 h 15, from km 30, up a stream valley to the western plateau and the top of Mont Andante, with a 497 m height difference.
Sépaq: 15.8 km return, about 4 h 30, from km 33, with views of the river and the valley's steep walls.
Sépaq: 1.4 km return, about 40 min, 96 m of climbing, from the Chute-du-Diable parking lot 7 km north of the Discovery Centre, to a 15 m waterfall on the Rivière du Diable.
Sépaq: 0.7 km return, about 20 min, 25 m of climbing, from the Chutes-Croches parking lot 5 km north of the Discovery Centre, to cascades and a whirlpool on the Rivière du Diable.
Sépaq: 5.4 km return, about 2 h 25, 340 m of climbing, from the Discovery Centre to a lookout over the Lac Monroe valley and the Mont Tremblant highlands.
Sépaq: an 8.3 km loop, about 3 h 30, 482 m of climbing, linking the La Roche and La Corniche lookouts. It starts on either of those trails and comes back by the Boucle-des-Chutes-Croches.
Sépaq: 3.4 km return, about 1 h 30, 223 m of climbing, from the La Corniche parking lot 1.7 km north of the Discovery Centre, to a lookout over the Lac Monroe valley.
Sépaq: 7.4 km return, about 3 h 40, 392 m of climbing, from the Discovery Centre by the La Roche trail, past rock faces to a lake and a cascade.
Sépaq: an 8.7 km loop, about 3 h 30, 277 m of climbing, from the Pointe-aux-Bouleaux parking lot 2.3 km south of the Discovery Centre, through hardwood forest past La Hutte hut and a lakeside stop.
Sépaq: 5.9 km return, about 2 h 40, 305 m of climbing, from the Discovery Centre up to Lac à l'Ours, coming back by La Renardière.

Sépaq: 15.6 km return, about 7 h 35, 960 m of climbing, from La Sablonnière parking lot 7 km south of the Discovery Centre, past the Ruisseau des Pruches cascades to Johannsen Peak, the highest point in the Laurentians. The Ruisseau des Pruches waterfall alone is 3 km return.

Sépaq: a 9.5 km loop, about 3 to 5 h, 634 m of climbing, from La Sablonnière parking lot 7.5 km south of the Discovery Centre, with views of the Diable River. Adding the Vache Noire trail from the Centenaire summit makes 14.5 km, 5 to 8 h and 1,151 m of climbing, rated Very difficult.
Sépaq: a 2.8 km loop, 120 m of climbing, near the Lac-Monroe visitors centre, through forest with views of Lac des Femmes and signs of beavers.
Sépaq: 7.2 km return, about 2 h 20 on foot (40 min by bike), 125 m of climbing, from La Cachée registration centre to the Chute-aux-Mûres falls.

Sépaq: 4.3 km return, about 1 h 50, 266 m of climbing, from the L'Envol parking lot near the Pimbina-Saint-Donat registration centre, through maple and yellow birch to a lookout over the La Pimbina valley.
Sépaq: 3.2 km return, about 1 h, 76 m of climbing, from the Lac-des-Sables campground along an old forest path to the Lac-des-Sables hut.

Sépaq: 4.6 km return, about 2 h, 268 m of climbing, from the Grandes-Vallées parking lot 9.4 km north of the L'Assomption registration centre, through maples to a view of the Lac de L'Assomption valley.
Sépaq: a 7 km loop, about 2 h 35 on foot (45 min by bike), 216 m of climbing, from the Lac-de-L'Assomption picnic area 15 km north of the L'Assomption registration centre.

n: Sentier de belvédère de la Lucarne
hikes.text: Sépaq: a 2.5 km loop, about 1 h, 80 m height difference, from the Discovery and Visitor Centre, with a view of the Sainte-Anne River valley.
Sépaq: 4.2 km, about 1 h 45, 190 m height difference, from the Discovery and Visitor Centre, with views of the McGerrigle Mountains, the Gîte du Mont-Albert and the Sainte-Anne River valley.

Sépaq: up to a bare ridge with views of Mont Albert and the Sainte-Anne River valley. From the Discovery and Visitor Centre: 11.4 km, about 4 h, 460 m height difference, rated Difficult. From the Ruisseau-Isabelle parking lot: 8.8 km, about 3 h 30, 375 m, rated Intermediate.
Sépaq: 4.6 km, about 2 h, 155 m height difference, from the Ernest-Laforce parking lot to a summit with a 360-degree view of Mont Albert and the peaks around it.
Sépaq: 11.6 km, about 6 h, 710 m height difference, from the Mont Richardson parking lot to a summit with a 360-degree view.
Sépaq: 14.2 km, about 5 h, 430 m height difference, from the Lac Cascapédia camping station, with views of the Chic-Choc Mountains and the St. Lawrence valley.

Sépaq: one way to Le Draveur visitor centre, 10.8 km from the Félix-Antoine-Savard visitor centre, 10.2 km from Du Cran campground or 8.8 km from the Des Érables bridge, about 2 h 30 to 3 h 30, with a 160 to 170 m height difference. Mostly fine gravel along the west shore of the Malbaie River, with picnic tables. Sépaq lists the way back on the same trail, on Les Rapides or by the park shuttle when it runs.
Sépaq: 7.6 km one way from Du Cran campground, about 2 h, 20 m height difference, past several rapids, with several exits to the park road.
Sépaq: a 2.5 km loop, about 1 h, 20 m height difference, from the Des Érables bridge, under the Cran des Érables cliff. Reaching it adds 2.4 km return on a forest road along the Malbaie River.
Sépaq: 0.4 km return, about 15 min, 55 m height difference, to a lookout over the valley.
Sépaq: a 0.7 km loop, about 15 min, 35 m height difference, from Le Draveur visitor centre (km 8), to a lookout facing Mont Félix-Antoine-Savard above the dam.

Sépaq: 1 km return, about 30 min, 78 m height difference, to the foot of a 45 m waterfall in the L'Équerre sector. Its start is 7 km from Le Draveur visitor centre, by the multi-use trail along the Malbaie River or on the river (14 km return, about 4 h, not included).

Sépaq: 11.2 km return, about 4 to 6 h, 800 m height difference, from Pin-Blanc campground (km 6), through forest to a summit with rare arctic-alpine plants. Sépaq's season for this trail runs from the second Friday of June to Thanksgiving (mid-October), and a park ranger closes it 3 hours before sunset. Sépaq asks hikers to stay on the marked trail.
Ontario Parks: a 2.1 km loop, about 1 h 30, at km 7.2 of Highway 60, along the Oxtongue River to Whiskey Rapids. Its trail guide covers the river's ecology and history.
Ontario Parks: 1 km, about 45 min, at km 13.8 of Highway 60, through hardwood forest to a view of Smoke Lake and the hills around it.
Ontario Parks: 10.8 km, about 6 h, at km 15.4 of Highway 60, past nine ponds and small lakes with some of the corridor's best chances to see wildlife. Ontario Parks lists no dogs on this trail.
Ontario Parks: 2.3 km, about 1 h 30, at km 19.2 of Highway 60, around the shore of Peck Lake.
Ontario Parks: a 7.5 km loop, about 4 h, at km 25 of Highway 60, with a lookout over Cache Lake and an optional 5.5 km side trip on an old railway to Mew Lake.
Ontario Parks: 3.5 km, about 2 h, at km 27.2 of Highway 60, through mixed forest to a view of Jack Lake.
Ontario Parks: a 5.8 km loop, about 3 h 30, at km 30 of Highway 60, through a hemlock stand to a lookout and acidic Bat Lake.
Ontario Parks: a 2.1 km loop, about 1 h, at km 31 of Highway 60, with a climb to a pine-covered cliff.
Ontario Parks: a 10 km loop, about 3 to 4 h, at km 37.6 of Highway 60, along two high ridges with wide views.
Ontario Parks: 2.9 km, about 2 h, at km 40.3 of Highway 60, past large old-growth white pines and the remains of an 1880s logging camp.
Ontario Parks: 5.1 km, about 3 h, 9 km south of Highway 60 on the Rock Lake road (from km 40.3), past two lakes and a lookout, coming back on an old railway.
Ontario Parks: a 1.5 km loop, about 1 h, at km 42.5 of Highway 60, with boardwalks through two black spruce bogs.
Ontario Parks: 2.4 km, about 1 h 30, from the Visitor Centre parking lot at km 43 of Highway 60, with short steep climbs from the lake to hilltop views.
Ontario Parks: 2 km, about 1 h 30, at km 45.2 of Highway 60, with views of two beaver ponds.
Ontario Parks: 1.3 km, about 1 h, at km 54.5 of Highway 60, with exhibits on the area's logging history, a re-created camboose camp and a steam-powered amphibious tug called an alligator.

Ontario Parks: 1.5 km, about 45 min, along the north rim of the 100 m deep Barron Canyon, with six trail guide stops, 10 km from the Sand Lake Gate. Ontario Parks notes the trail passes an unfenced cliff.
Ontario Parks: 4.5 km around Berm Lake, about 1 h 30, from Achray Campground, through pine and oak forest.
Ontario Parks: 1.6 km, about 45 min, near Achray, to the place where Tom Thomson sketched The Jack Pine.
Ontario Parks: 2 km, about 1 h 30, from the Brent Road: an observation tower over the meteorite crater, then down to its floor and back, with six stops on its geology and history.
Ontario Parks: 3 km, about 1 h 30, along the park's southern edge over small ridges to a point on Georgian Bay, with iron mooring rings from the logging days and history plaques.
Ontario Parks: 4 km, about 2 h 30, past bogs, marshes and swamps with pitcher plants and beaver feed piles, and rock smoothed by glaciers.
Ontario Parks: 2 km, about 1 h, through old fields and forest up to a ridge with two lookouts over the La Cloche Mountains and Georgian Bay.
Ontario Parks: a 3.5 km loop around Lake of the Woods, about 3 h, from old-growth forest to rocky outcrops with views toward Silver Peak, and a short boardwalk to the lake's island.
Ontario Parks: 6 km, about 4 h, up through a jumble of large boulders to the top of Killarney Ridge, with wide views over the white cliffs of the La Cloche Mountains.

Ontario Parks: an 80 km loop, 7 to 10 days, from two trailheads in George Lake Campground. The west section is moderate, over rolling forested hills to Acid and Lumsden lakes; the east section climbs over rocky ridges and large boulders to the Crack.

Parks Canada: 3 km, about 3 h, from the Cyprus Lake area: the Georgian Bay Trail to the shore and the Bruce Trail, Halfway Rock Point, Indian Head Cove, the Natural Arch and the Grotto, coming back by Marr Lake. Parks Canada notes the Marr Lake side crosses rough shoreline boulders.
Parks Canada: 1 km, about 30 min, along Horse Lake through marsh and woodland to a boulder beach on Georgian Bay, where it meets the Bruce Trail.
Parks Canada: 5 km around Cyprus Lake, about 2 h 30, past charred stumps from forest fires of the early 1900s.
Parks Canada: 1 km, about 30 min, from the parking lot to a cobble beach under sheer cliffs on the Bruce Trail. Parks Canada notes the Grotto is about 3 h each way from here, over very rugged ground.
Parks Canada: 3 km, about 1 h 30, through woods and dunes along Dorcas Bay to rare alvar habitat.
Parks Canada: 2 km return, about 1 h.
Parks Canada: 1 km return, about 30 min.
Parks Canada: 6 km return, about 1 to 2 h.
Parks Canada: 6 km return, about 1 to 2 h.
Parks Canada: a 2 km loop, 30 min to 1 h.
Parks Canada: 10 km return, about 2 to 3 h.
Parks Canada: 1.5 km return, 30 min to 1 h.

Parks Canada: 17 km return, at least 6 to 8 h 30, about 1,000 m of climbing to the 806 m summit. The Approach Trail (9 km return, 463 m, rated Moderate) follows Crow Gulch Brook to a viewing platform at the base of the mountain; the Summit Trail (an 8 km loop, 537 m, rated Difficult) climbs a scree slope, crosses the rocky plateau and comes down through Ferry Gulch. Parks Canada closes the summit trail every year from May 1 to June 27 to protect wildlife.
Parks Canada: a 5.8 km loop, about 2 to 3 h.
Parks Canada: 4 km return, about 1 to 2 h.

Parks Canada: 9 km return, about 3 to 4 h, from Route 431 (3 km from Trout River): over the Tablelands' serpentine barrens and down through boreal forest, 4.5 km to the coast at Old Man Cove, then north along cliff-top meadows to Steve's Cove, with sea stacks and a sea cave. The way back is mostly uphill and steep in places. Parks Canada's page has notes on the sections beyond Steve's Cove.
Parks Canada: 14 km return, about 4 to 5 h.
Parks Canada (Stuckless Pond): a 9.5 km loop, about 2 to 3 h.
Parks Canada: 4 km return, about 1 to 2 h.
Parks Canada: an 8.4 km loop, 3 to 4 h, from 20 m up to 365 m above the Chéticamp River, with views of the Acadian coast, the river valley and the highland interior, and benches along the way.
Parks Canada: 9.5 km return, 3 to 4 h, between 15 and 110 m, a level trail along the floor of the Chéticamp River canyon under cliffs almost 400 m high. The First Pool is about 3.6 km in.
Parks Canada: 4.6 km return, about 1 h 30, between 25 and 65 m, on an old Acadian cart path to Chéticamp, past open fields and old foundations.
Parks Canada: a 1.6 km loop, 30 to 45 min, between 0 and 55 m, a self-guiding trail over a small hill above the Chéticamp River with old Acadian homestead sites.
Parks Canada: 6.5 km return, about 2 h, between 30 and 170 m, along a brook through hardwood forest to a small waterfall at the end of a box canyon. Check Parks Canada's page for the brook crossings.

Parks Canada: 6.5 km return (about 2 h) or an 8.2 km loop (2 h 30 to 3 h), between 290 and 405 m, to a headland boardwalk high above the Gulf of St. Lawrence with steps at the end. Parks Canada may require a parking booking for this trail in its busy season.
Parks Canada: a 0.5 km boardwalk loop, about 15 min, at 410 m on the highland plateau, with signs about pitcher plants, orchids and other bog life. Parks Canada lists it as wheelchair accessible.
Parks Canada: 3 km return, 1 to 1 h 30, at about 400 m on the plateau, across wet barrens and evergreen forest to a small lake, with boardwalk in places.
Parks Canada: 12 km return, 5 to 6 h, from 355 m about 6 km down to a small ocean cove, the park's only designated wilderness campsite.
Parks Canada: 1.7 km return, 30 to 45 min, between 30 and 65 m, a fairly level walk along a brook through hardwood forest to a waterfall.
Parks Canada: a 0.6 km loop, about 15 min, through a forest of sugar maples about 350 years old, with a replica of a Scottish crofter's hut at the start.
Parks Canada: 9.6 km return, 3 to 4 h, between 60 and 450 m, along the Aspy fault through Acadian and mixed forest, with stream crossings.

Parks Canada: a 7.9 km loop, 3 to 3 h 30, between 260 and 410 m, through mixed forest and stunted taiga to the plateau, with views of the barrens and the Aspy fault, and a narrower path on to quartz and mica outcrops.
Parks Canada: a 2.3 km loop, about 1 h, between 0 and 50 m, above the Atlantic coast through a jack pine stand that grew back after a 1921 fire, with history panels.
Parks Canada: 2.5 km return, 45 to 50 min, between 0 and 45 m, through boreal forest to the quieter end of Neil's Harbour beach by an estuary.
Parks Canada: 0.2 km return, about 10 min, onto a granite headland over the ocean, with wind-twisted trees.
Parks Canada: 13.9 km, between 8 and 166 m, on part of the old Cabot Trail route to Mary Ann Falls, with stairs to the base of the falls and remains of an old iron bridge.
Parks Canada: 2.3 km return, about 1 h, between 35 and 180 m: switchbacks through softwood forest, 168 m up in 1.6 km, to views of the Atlantic coast, Middle Head and Cape Smokey.

Parks Canada: a 4.7 km loop, about 1 h 30, a level trail around the park's largest lake, from the Warren Lake picnic area or a 1.6 km connector from Broad Cove Campground. Check Parks Canada's page for the suspension bridge.

Parks Canada: a 13 km full loop (5 to 6 h, from 17 m up to 423 m) or a 4.5 km lower loop (1 h 30 to 2 h, up to 170 m), from the end of Franey Road, to a summit with views of the Clyburn Brook canyon and the coast from Cape Smokey to Ingonish.
Parks Canada: 8.5 km, 2 to 3 h, between 5 and 50 m, along the river past hardwood stands, huge boulders, old beaver ponds and the remains of an old gold mine, under Franey Mountain.
Parks Canada: 5.3 km return, about 1 h 30, between 10 and 55 m, along a narrow peninsula between two bays to headland cliffs facing Cape Smokey and Ingonish Island.

Parks Canada: 1.7 km return, between 0 and 15 m, a short level trail by the ocean along a lake that was once a bay, with a viewing deck and a 1.6 km return side trail on the cobble beach. Parks Canada lists bikes on this trail.
Parks Canada: a 2.1 km loop, 1 to 1 h 30, past bog plants and beaver ponds. Parks Canada lists wheelchair access.
Parks Canada: 1 km return, about 30 min, with views of the estuary and the covered bridge.
Parks Canada: a 5.6 km loop, 2 to 2 h 30, through forest.
Parks Canada: 2.8 km return, about 1 h 30, with stairs into a steep-walled valley where the stream disappears underground.
Parks Canada: a 4.4 km loop, 1 h 30 to 2 h, past an old mine site, with coastal views.
Parks Canada: a 1.5 km loop, 30 to 45 min, on boardwalk and stairs past tumbling cascades.
Parks Canada: 1 km return, about 30 min, with stairs down to the beach.
Parks Canada: 1 km return, about 30 min, under tall red spruce to the beach. Check Parks Canada's page for the Point Wolfe covered bridge.
Parks Canada: a 4.4 km loop, 1 h 30 to 2 h, past old homestead foundations, with a view of the bay. Parks Canada lists bikes on this trail.
Parks Canada: 3.5 km one way, 1 h 30 to 2 h, through open hardwood forest. Parks Canada lists bikes on this trail.
Parks Canada: 2.5 km one way, 1 to 1 h 30, to a curtain waterfall and a pool.
Parks Canada: 7 km one way, about 2 h 30, with wet sections, pitcher plants and backcountry camping.
Parks Canada: 7.4 km return, 3 to 4 h, to the park's highest waterfall (16 m).

Parks Canada: two sections, both rated Difficult and part of the Trans Canada Trail. Coastal East is 3 km one way, about 2 h, with ridge-top views and fern glades; Coastal West is 6.7 km one way, 2 h 30 to 3 h, with steep sections and coastal views.
Parks Canada: 11.4 km one way, 2 h 30 to 3 h, to backcountry camping at Goose River. Part of the Trans Canada Trail; Parks Canada lists bikes on it.
Parks Canada: 13 km return, 5 to 6 h, with steep switchback climbs, a river crossing, a dam and fishway, and a waterfall.
Parks Canada: 8.5 km one way, 2 h 30 to 3 h, to a lake with trout, moose and beaver, and backcountry camping.
Parks Canada: a 4.5 km loop, 1 h 30 to 2 h, with coastal views and a sea stack.
Parks Canada: 5.7 km one way, 2 to 2 h 30, with several small brook crossings. Parks Canada lists bikes on this trail.
Parks Canada: 3 km one way, 1 h 30 to 2 h, through a beech grove.
Parks Canada: 1.85 km one way, 1 h 30 to 2 h, past an old beaver pond to a view over the forest.
Parks Canada: 4.4 km one way, 1 h 30 to 2 h, through shaded forest with a river crossing and backcountry camping.
Parks Canada: 4.5 km one way, 2 to 3 h, a steep descent and climb back, with a waterfall. Part of the Trans Canada Trail.
Parks Canada: 3.2 km one way, 1 h 30 to 2 h, a steep descent and climb back to deep pools, with a river crossing. Part of the Trans Canada Trail.
Parks Canada: 8.2 km one way, about 3 h 30, past salmon pools and rapids, with a river crossing. Part of the Trans Canada Trail.

Parks Canada: a 1.9 km loop, about 20 m of climbing, about 40 min (their estimate). A self-guided interpretive trail through old spruce forest at the edge of Banff, on hard soil with patches of roots.

Parks Canada: 0.9 km one way, about 85 m of climbing, about 40 min return (their estimate). It leaves the Rockbound Lake Trail 300 m from the trailhead and ends on an open hillside below a waterfall that drops over narrow ledges. Narrow in places, with roots and rock.

Parks Canada: 1.1 km one way to the Lower Falls (about 1 h return) and 2.4 km to the 30 m Upper Falls (about 215 m of climbing, 2 h return). An uneven paved path with narrow railed bridges into the canyon; it gets busy. Check Parks Canada's page for current closures here.

Parks Canada: 5.1 km one way, about 180 m of climbing, 3 to 4 h return (their estimate). Through forest to a large lake ringed by peaks; a bumpy path with rocks, boulders, roots, wet spots and small streams.

Parks Canada: Sunshine Meadows is a network of about 10.3 km of paths around alpine lakes and meadows, about 580 m of climbing, 4 to 5 h (their estimate). The busiest one crosses the Continental Divide to a viewpoint over Rock Isle Lake, with the Larix Lake and Grizzly Lake loop beyond. Gravel paths with rocks, roots and steps. Parks Canada lists the paid gondola from the Sunshine Village parking lot for early July to early September.

Parks Canada's Upper Stoney Trail: a 4.4 km loop, about 210 m of climbing, about 1 h 30 (their estimate). It climbs through thick forest from the Mount Norquay parking lot to the Stoney Lookout, with views of Cascade Mountain and the Bow Valley, and comes back down past old ski runs. Narrow, twisty and rocky, with roots.

Parks Canada: 2.3 km one way, about 275 m of climbing, about 2 h return (their estimate). Switchbacks to a low summit above the town of Banff, with views of the Bow Valley and Mount Rundle. Roots, rock and a few concrete steps.

Parks Canada: 4.4 km one way, about 115 m of climbing, about 3 h return (their estimate). Below the cliffs of Tunnel Mountain and along the Bow River to the Hoodoos viewpoint, with views to Mount Rundle. Many roots, a few short steep climbs and some steps.

Parks Canada: 9.5 km return from Cave and Basin, about 190 m of climbing, about 3 h (their estimate): 3.7 km of paved trail (bikes can lock up at its end), then a 2.1 km hiking-only loop up and around the canyon, steep and narrow with rock steps.

Parks Canada: 3.8 km one way, about 440 m of climbing, about 3 h return (their estimate). Past foundations and vents of the old Bankhead coal mine to a large glacier-carved bowl in the north face of Cascade Mountain. Steep and rutted in places.

Parks Canada: 4.8 km one way to the top of the gondola, plus 0.5 km of boardwalk with many shallow steps to Sanson Peak; about 655 m of climbing, about 4 h return (their estimate). Steady switchbacks with roots and rock from the Upper Hot Springs parking lot.

Parks Canada: 8.8 km one way, about 650 m of climbing, 6 to 7 h return (their estimate), from the Sunshine Village parking lot. Rooty and rocky along Healy Creek to open meadows above the trees. Parks Canada says wildflowers bloom from mid-July to late August and larches turn gold in late September.

Parks Canada: 6.8 km one way, about 740 m of climbing, about 6 h return (their estimate). From the Mount Norquay lodge up the gravel road to the Mystic chairlift, then a forest trail to a meadow inside a natural amphitheatre on Cascade Mountain.

Parks Canada: 8.5 km one way, about 765 m of climbing, 6 to 7 h return (their estimate). A long steady climb through forest behind the cliffs of Castle Mountain to meadows and Tower Lake (7.5 km), then up a low cliff band to Rockbound Lake. Many roots and rocks.

Parks Canada: 4.6 km one way to Arnica Lake, about 580 m of climbing, about 5 h return (their estimate). Down to Vista Lake first (1.4 km), then a long switchback climb through larches to Arnica Lake below Storm Mountain. It carries on to the Twin Lakes: 7.4 km and about 700 m of climbing to Lower Twin Lake.

Parks Canada: 6.7 km one way to Bourgeau Lake, about 730 m of climbing, about 6 h return (their estimate); Harvey Pass is 2.2 km more on a rough, rocky trail (8.9 km and about 1,010 m of climbing from the trailhead). A steady forest climb with roots, rock and stream crossings to a lake in a glacier-carved amphitheatre.

Parks Canada: an 11.7 km loop, about 930 m of climbing, about 6 h (their estimate), from the Fireside day-use area. Steep, rocky and exposed with narrow sections, up to a pass below Mount Louis; the loop comes back through the Gargoyle Valley and Edith Pass. Parks Canada says route-finding skills are needed.

Parks Canada: 11.6 km one way from the Lake Minnewanka day-use area, about 770 m of climbing, 7 to 8 h return (their estimate). Along the Lake Minnewanka shoreline for 7.8 km, then uphill to a former fire lookout over the lake. Roots, rocks and narrow sections. Parks Canada sets a group rule here from July 10 to September 15 each year: see its page.

Parks Canada: 13.1 km one way from the Lake Minnewanka day-use area, about 970 m of climbing, 8 to 9 h return (their estimate). Along the Lake Minnewanka shoreline for 7.8 km, then uphill to a pass with wide wildflower meadows and views of the Palliser Range. Parks Canada sets a group rule here from July 10 to September 15 each year: see its page.
Parks Canada: 1.2 km one way, about 100 m of climbing, about 45 min return (their estimate). A short, steep climb from the Lake Louise boathouse to a view over the lake and the Chateau.

Parks Canada: up to 5.7 km one way, about 25 m of climbing, about 2 h return (their estimate). Walk or bike along the Bow River at Lake Louise. Parks Canada lists a seasonal wildlife closure on part of the west side: see its page.
Parks Canada: 3.7 km one way, about 520 m of climbing, 3 to 4 h return (their estimate), from the Bow Valley Parkway. Up to the site of a former fire tower, with wide views of the middle Bow Valley.

Parks Canada: 6.3 km one way, about 585 m of climbing, 4 to 5 h return (their estimate). A steady climb through thick forest into subalpine meadows and a glacial lake. Parks Canada notes snow stays on this trail early in the season and suggests it from July on.

Parks Canada: 3.9 km one way from the Lake Louise lakeshore, about 495 m of climbing, 2 h 30 to 3 h return (their estimate), to a lake below tall peaks with a seasonal tea house. Side trips from the lake: the Big Beehive (1.5 km one way, about 150 m up) and the Little Beehive (0.9 km one way), site of an old fire lookout.

Parks Canada: 5.9 km one way from the Lake Louise lakeshore, about 595 m of climbing, about 4 h return (their estimate), past the end of the lake toward the peaks and glaciers, with a seasonal tea house. With Lake Agnes and the Highline Trail it makes a 14.3 km loop.

n: Paradise Valley and Giant Steps Trail
hikes.text: Parks Canada's Paradise Valley and Giant Steps Trail: 9.8 km one way, about 595 m of climbing, 7 to 8 h return (their estimate), with views of Mount Temple, midsummer wildflowers and the Giant Steps waterfall.
Parks Canada: 5 km one way from the Lake Louise lakeshore, about 990 m of climbing, 5 to 6 h return (their estimate). A steep hike up a well-known peak.

Parks Canada's Larch Valley / Minnestimma Lakes Trail: 4.5 km one way from Moraine Lake, about 570 m of climbing, 3 h 30 to 4 h return (their estimate), into a larch forest above the lake with views of the Ten Peaks.

n: Sentinel Pass via Larch Valley Trail
hikes.text: Parks Canada: 5.6 km one way from Moraine Lake through Larch Valley, about 750 m of climbing, 4 h 30 to 5 h 30 return (their estimate). Steep switchbacks to a high pass between Larch Valley and Paradise Valley.

Parks Canada: 5.7 km one way from Moraine Lake, about 560 m of climbing, 4 to 5 h return (their estimate). It leaves the Larch Valley trail and runs high along the valley side above Eiffel Lake and the Valley of the Ten Peaks.

Parks Canada: 11.5 km one way from the Fish Creek parking area, about 835 m of climbing, 8 to 9 h return (their estimate). The first 4 km are on a wide access road, then past Boulder Pass and Ptarmigan Lake to alpine meadows and lakes. It leads on to the Skoki backcountry.

Parks Canada: 3.8 km one way, about 95 m of climbing, about 3 h return (their estimate). Along the Bow Lake shore, then up into the basin below Bow Glacier Falls, where meltwater from the Wapta Icefield starts the Bow River.
Parks Canada: 5.9 km one way, about 530 m of climbing, 4 to 5 h return (their estimate), to an alpine lake in a valley with wide views. Dolomite Pass is beyond it (8.9 km one way).

Parks Canada: 2.2 km one way, about 80 m of climbing, about 1 h 30 return (their estimate), to the widest waterfall on the Kicking Horse River. Roots along the way; Parks Canada notes there is no maintained trail to the base of the falls. It lists the 2 km Wapta Falls Road as closed from late October to late May.

Parks Canada's Kicking Horse Fire Road: 6.9 km one way from the Natural Bridge parking area, about 60 m of climbing, about 4 h return on foot or 2 h by bike (their estimate). An old forest road to a picnic site at 1.8 km and an old bridge over the Otterhead River at the end.
Parks Canada: a 5.2 km loop around Emerald Lake, about 2 h (their estimate), on gravel with mountain and glacier views. Parks Canada says the east side can be muddy and rooty.

Parks Canada: 1 km one way, about 55 m of climbing, about 45 min return (their estimate). A narrow shaded path along the Kicking Horse River, across from the Monarch campground, known for wildflowers.

Parks Canada: up to 6.4 km one way along the Yoho River from Takakkaw Falls, about 270 m of climbing, about 4 h (their estimate). Easy packed gravel at first, with side trips to Point Lace Falls, the Angel's Staircase Falls viewpoint and Duchesnay Lake; moderate beyond, to Laughing Falls (4.5 km) and Twin Falls. Parks Canada lists the Yoho Valley Road season as mid-June to mid-October.

Parks Canada: 2.9 km one way from the Lake O'Hara parking lot, about 140 m of climbing, about 2 h return (their estimate). Along the Great Divide trail for 2 km, then a forest trail to a lake below the cliffs of Narao Peak.
Parks Canada: 4.8 km one way, about 305 m of climbing, about 3 h 30 return (their estimate). Along the Emerald Lake shore, then through old hemlock and cedar to a natural amphitheatre.

Parks Canada's Yoho Glacier Moraine: 8.6 km one way from Takakkaw Falls, about 425 m of climbing, about 7 h return or 2 days (their estimate), from forest in the Yoho Valley to the bare rock left by a shrinking glacier.
Parks Canada: 9.8 km one way from Takakkaw Falls past Laughing Falls, about 690 m of climbing, about 7 h return or 2 days (their estimate). Moderate to steep forest climbing into a hanging valley.

Parks Canada: 3.2 km one way, about 400 m of climbing, about 2 h 30 return (their estimate). 1.2 km on the old Hoodoo Creek campground road, then a steep, open trail (2 km) to hoodoos: pillars of glacial debris capped by rock.

Parks Canada: 3.5 km one way to the lower fire lookout (moderate, about 495 m of climbing, about 3 h return) and 5.7 km to the upper lookout (difficult, about 940 m, about 5 h 30). A steep climb through open forest, with views of the Kicking Horse and Beaverfoot valleys at the top. The trailhead is across the highway from the Wapta Falls day-use area.

Parks Canada: 5.1 km one way from Emerald Lake, about 915 m of climbing, about 5 h return (their estimate). A steep, steady climb to a small alpine lake ringed by cliffs, passing Hamilton Falls at 0.8 km.

Parks Canada: a loop from Takakkaw Falls along the Iceline to a high bench with glacier views. Back through the Little Yoho Valley and Laughing Falls it is 20.3 km and about 1,090 m of climbing (about 8 h or 2 days); back past Celeste Lake it is 17.4 km and about 970 m (about 7 h or 2 days). Their estimates.

Parks Canada: a 20.5 km loop from Takakkaw Falls, about 1,110 m of climbing, about 7 h 30 or 2 days (their estimate), through the Yoho Valley with views of Twin Falls from below and above. It uses a seasonal suspension bridge: see Parks Canada's trail report.

Parks Canada: 2.3 km one way, about 200 m of climbing, about 1 h 30 return (their estimate). A quiet forest path off Highway 93 South near Radium Hot Springs; Parks Canada suggests it early in the season and when the leaves turn in fall.

Parks Canada's Sinclair Canyon trail (Juniper): 2.8 km one way, about 350 m of climbing, about 2 h return (their estimate). Along the rim of Sinclair Canyon and down into it, with a short detour to red chairs above the Radium Hot Springs pools.

Parks Canada: the first 1.6 km is an easy interpretive trail (about 30 m of climbing, 1 h return) about lightning, wildfire and regrowth. It goes on for 7.2 km more to the park boundary (moderate) and into Mount Assiniboine Provincial Park.

Parks Canada: 0.9 km one way, about 65 m of climbing, about 30 min return (their estimate). Along the rim of a narrow canyon with many bridges to look down from, interpretive signs and red chairs at the end.

Parks Canada: 4.6 km one way, about 455 m of climbing, about 3 h return (their estimate). A cool forest trail near Radium Hot Springs; the trailhead is 100 m along the highway from the parking pullout.
Parks Canada: 2.7 km one way, about 155 m of climbing, about 2 h return (their estimate). Down to Swede Creek, then along it to a quiet lake in the forest.

Parks Canada: a 7 km loop, about 195 m of climbing, about 2 h 30 (their estimate), over two bridges on the Kootenay River and through old forest; or 2.6 km one way to the lake and back. Check Parks Canada's page for current closures here.

Parks Canada: 4.9 km one way, about 405 m of climbing, about 3 h return (their estimate). A very busy trail up to an alpine basin where glacier meltwater pours down tall rock walls. Parks Canada also runs guided Burgess Shale fossil hikes here.

Parks Canada: 10 km one way, about 1,250 m of climbing, about 8 h (their estimate). Through forest and avalanche paths to wide views between Kindersley Pass and the Kindersley-Sinclair Col; it can link with the Sinclair Creek trail. Parks Canada requires groups of at least four here because of grizzly bears: see its page.

Parks Canada: 6.2 km one way, about 1,005 m of climbing, about 6 h (their estimate). Along Sinclair Creek through alpine meadows to views around the Kindersley-Sinclair Col; it can link with the Kindersley Pass trail. Parks Canada requires groups of at least four here because of grizzly bears: see its page.

Parks Canada: 10.2 km one way from the Paint Pots day-use area, about 700 m of climbing, about 6 h return or 2 days (their estimate). Beside fast water to Tumbling Falls and a backcountry campground; one of the ways onto the Rockwall Trail.

Parks Canada: 54.1 km one way, about 3,405 m of climbing, 3 to 5 days (their estimate). Over three alpine passes through meadows and below hanging glaciers, along a limestone cliff up to 900 m high. Several access trails from Highway 93 South; backcountry campgrounds need permits.
Parks Canada: 31 km return, about 65 m of elevation, 10 to 12 h (their estimate). Trail 10, along the Athabasca River side of the valley; open to bikes, dogs and horses.
Parks Canada: 4.4 km return, about 100 m of elevation, 2 to 4 h (their estimate), trails 7 and 7g along the canyon. Check Parks Canada's page for current closures here.

n: Hike to Toe of Athabasca Glacier
hikes.text: Parks Canada: 1.8 km return, about 60 m of elevation, about 1 h (their estimate), trail 52 from the Icefields Parkway toward the toe of the Athabasca Glacier.
Parks Canada: 8 km return to the pass, 2 to 3 h, or 2.4 km return to the first viewpoint, about 1 h; about 390 m of elevation (their estimates). Trail 50, near the Columbia Icefield.
Parks Canada: an 8.2 km loop, about 460 m of elevation, 4 to 6 h (their estimate), trail 22 at Maligne Lake.
Parks Canada: 10.4 km return, about 500 m of elevation, 4 to 6 h (their estimate), trail 23 from Maligne Lake.
Parks Canada's Moose Lake Loop: 2.7 km, about 59 m of elevation, 1 to 2 h (their estimate), trail 20 at Maligne Lake.
Parks Canada: 8 km return, about 700 m of elevation, 4 to 6 h (their estimate), trail 30 from Miette Hot Springs.
Parks Canada: 1.4 km return, about 70 m of elevation, about 1 h (their estimate), trail 41 below Mount Edith Cavell.
Parks Canada: 7 km return, about 500 m of elevation, 3 to 5 h (their estimate), trail 42 at Mount Edith Cavell.
Parks Canada: loops from 1.8 km to 8.9 km return, half an hour to half a day (their estimate): Wetland Way, Emerald Loop and Valley Loop, south of the town of Jasper.
Parks Canada's Virl, Dorothy and Christine Lakes: 8.6 km return, about 250 m of elevation, 4 to 6 h (their estimate), trails 60 and 60a west of Jasper.
Parks Canada: 13.6 km return, about 1,200 m of elevation, 5 to 8 h (their estimate), trail 5 up The Whistlers.
Parks Canada: 2.2 km return, about 150 m of elevation, 1 to 2 h (their estimate), trail 5a to the summit of The Whistlers.

Parks Canada: 10.4 km return to Bertha Lake (5.2 km return to Lower Bertha Falls), about 460 m of climbing, about 4 h 30 (their estimate). From the townsite up to a viewpoint over Upper Waterton Lake, then along the creek to the falls and the lake. Parks Canada notes the trailhead is in an avalanche path and posts an advisory for it.

Parks Canada: 17.2 km return, about 675 m of climbing, about 6 h (their estimate). Reached by a 15-minute boat ride across Upper Waterton Lake (or 14 km on the Wishbone trail). Waterfalls, steep slopes, and a tight tunnel onto a narrow ledge above a cliff; a side trip looks at Hell Roaring Falls.
Parks Canada: 3 km, about 123 m of climbing, about 1 h (their estimate). A wide trail with steep parts to the BC border and Akamina-Kishinena Provincial Park, with Wall and Forum lakes beyond.
Parks Canada: 9 km return, about 350 m of climbing, about 3 h (their estimate). A steady climb to a viewpoint below a 250 m waterfall, with views of Mount Lineham and Mount Blakiston.

Parks Canada: 16.4 km return, about 150 m of climbing, about 5 h (their estimate), on a former fire road from Red Rock Canyon, also used by bikes and horses. It leads to Goat Lake, Avion Ridge and the Snowshoe campground. Parks Canada notes bridge work on this trail: see its page.

Parks Canada's Wishbone/Vimy: 26.2 km return, little elevation, about 8 h (their estimate). A wide trail through aspen and birch and over open prairie to Wishbone Landing on Middle Waterton Lake, with a steep branch to Vimy. Parks Canada sets seasonal group and bear spray rules here: see its page.
Parks Canada: 7.4 km return, little elevation, about 2 h 30 (their estimate). A prairie walk below Bellevue Hill, known for spring and summer wildflowers.
Parks Canada: 2.8 km return, about 225 m of climbing, about 1 h (their estimate). Short and very steep, to a bluff on Mount Crandell with views of the townsite, the lakes and the prairie.

Parks Canada: from the Akamina Parkway, 3.6 km return (about 75 m of climbing, 1 h); from the Red Rock Parkway, 4 km return on an old cart track (about 125 m, 1 h 15); both easy. From the townsite, 12.4 km return (moderate, about 270 m, 4 h), shared with bikes.
Parks Canada's Cameron Lakeshore: 3 km return, little elevation, about 1 h (their estimate), along a subalpine lake with views south into Glacier National Park (U.S.).
Parks Canada: 1 km return, about 30 min (their estimate), from the Cameron Lake parking lot to a sheltered subalpine lake.
Parks Canada: 2 km return, little elevation, about 45 min (their estimate), from the Red Rock Canyon lower parking lot to a waterfall with viewpoints.

Parks Canada: 8.4 km return from the Illecillewaet Valley parking lot (2 km less from the campground), about 320 m of elevation change, about 2 h 30 (their estimate). Natural trail and rock toward the Illecillewaet Glacier, stopping well short of the ice, with a view of Mount Sir Donald and the Vaux Glacier.

Parks Canada's Lower Beaver Valley: 10.2 km return, about 320 m of elevation change, about 3 h 30 (their estimate). A valley-bottom trail through old-growth forest, open to bikes; the maintained trail ends near the Grizzly Creek bridge.

Parks Canada: 12.8 km return from the Rogers Pass Discovery Centre, about 780 m of elevation change, about 4 h (their estimate), through avalanche paths into alpine meadows, steepest near the pass. Parks Canada does not allow dogs here and sets a group rule for July 15 to September 30: see its page.

Parks Canada: 15.6 km return, about 740 m of elevation change, about 7 h (their estimate). From interior rainforest into subalpine forest, to a pass where limestone and shale cover the older bedrock, with gentle alpine ridges beyond.

Parks Canada: 10.2 km return from the Illecillewaet Valley parking lot, about 795 m of elevation change, about 5 h (their estimate). Steep, to an open alpine basin between Avalanche Crest and a ridge of Eagle Peak.

Parks Canada: 15.6 km return from the Illecillewaet Valley parking lot, about 1,030 m of elevation change, about 6 h 30 (their estimate). Very steep, past Marion Lake (6.4 km return) into alpine tundra, ending on a narrow ridge.

Parks Canada: 15.8 km return from the Illecillewaet Valley parking lot, about 870 m of elevation change, about 6 h (their estimate). A valley walk with waterfalls, then a steep moraine after 4 km, ending above the lower Illecillewaet Glacier near the Asulkan Cabin (Alpine Club of Canada, by reservation). Parks Canada removes seasonal bridges from late September.

Parks Canada: 13.4 km return from the Illecillewaet Valley parking lot, about 960 m of elevation change, about 6 h (their estimate). Very steep and rocky, up the ridge between the Illecillewaet and Asulkan valleys.

Parks Canada: 12.8 km return from the Illecillewaet Valley parking lot, about 1,145 m of elevation change, about 6 h (their estimate). Very steep switchbacks and boulder fields to a high viewpoint over the Illecillewaet Icefield; Parks Canada notes a steep snow slope near the top.

Parks Canada: 12.2 km return from the Illecillewaet Valley parking lot, about 1,010 m of elevation change, about 5 h (their estimate). Very steep, from the valley to the Sir Donald backcountry campsite (permit needed); Parks Canada says route-finding skills are needed past the Perley Rock turn-off.

Parks Canada: 6.4 km return, about 820 m of elevation change, about 4 h (their estimate). Very steep: switchbacks, rock stairs and a rope-assisted scramble to an alpine meadow and the Hermit backcountry campground (permit needed).

Parks Canada: a 1.7 km loop, little elevation change, about 40 min (their estimate). An interpretive walk among the stone pillars that once carried the railway across the valley, part of Rogers Pass National Historic Site.
Parks Canada: a 350 m loop, about 15 min (their estimate). A ramped, barrier-free boardwalk through rainforest with cedar, hemlock and devil's club; the paving up to it is uneven.
Parks Canada: a 430 m loop, about 30 min (their estimate), through mossy boulders and forest, with rock stairs, uneven stones to step on and steep parts.

Parks Canada: 1 km return, about 95 m of elevation change, about 1 h (their estimate). Steeply down to a waterfall, and back up. Parks Canada notes there is no left turn into the parking lot from the east.

Parks Canada: a 2.5 km loop, about 133 m of elevation change, about 1 h (their estimate), through cedar-hemlock rainforest 1.9 km up the Meadows in the Sky Parkway. Low, so Parks Canada says it is popular early (April to May) and late (October to November).
Parks Canada: a 5 km loop, about 63 m of elevation change, about 1 h 30 (their estimate), from the Nels Nelsen Historic Area. Used year-round for hiking, biking, running and snowshoeing.
Parks Canada: a 2 km loop, about 21 m of elevation change, about 30 min (their estimate), from the Nels Nelsen Historic Area. Used year-round for hiking, biking, running and snowshoeing.

Parks Canada: 2 km return, about 40 m of elevation change, about 40 min (their estimate), 11.5 km up the Meadows in the Sky Parkway. A short forest walk with valley views, ending at an old twisted wooden bridge that Parks Canada says not to cross.

Parks Canada: 4.4 km return, about 116 m of elevation change, about 1 h 30 (their estimate). Links the Columbia Park area of Revelstoke, off Highway 23 North, to the park near the Welcome Kiosk; mostly used by bikes.

Parks Canada: 20 km return, about 1,353 m of elevation change, 6 to 8 h (their estimate), from the base of Mount Revelstoke (1.9 km up the parkway) to the summit, through rainforest and subalpine forest to alpine meadows. It crosses the Meadows in the Sky Parkway six times.
Parks Canada: 15 km return, about 982 m of elevation change, 5 to 7 h (their estimate), from the Monashee picnic area to the summit area, without crossing the parkway.

Parks Canada: 1 km return, about 27 m of elevation change, about 30 min (their estimate), from the Balsam Lake parking area to a forested knoll over the Columbia Valley. No dogs above Columbia Viewpoint (Parks Canada).

Parks Canada: 2 km return, about 91 m of elevation change, about 40 min (their estimate), through subalpine forest from Balsam Lake to the trails on the upper summit. No dogs above Columbia Viewpoint (Parks Canada).

Parks Canada: a 1 km loop, about 28 m of elevation change, about 20 min (their estimate), with views of the Columbia River and signs on David Thompson's travels. No dogs above Columbia Viewpoint (Parks Canada).

Parks Canada: a 750 m loop, about 24 m of elevation change, about 20 min (their estimate), through subalpine meadows with art and stories of the Secwepemc, Ktunaxa and Syilx / Okanagan peoples, past the Icebox, a rock cleft that holds snow all year. No dogs above Columbia Viewpoint (Parks Canada).

Parks Canada: 11.6 km return from the Upper Summit shuttle stop, about 405 m of elevation change, 4 to 6 h (their estimate), on the Eva Lake trail then 400 m to the lake. Parks Canada says deep snow usually limits these summit trails to mid-July through September. No dogs above Columbia Viewpoint.

Parks Canada: 14.2 km return from the Upper Summit shuttle stop, about 465 m of elevation change, 5 to 7 h (their estimate), through meadows, a boulder valley and subalpine forest to a lake with a 1920s warden cabin and a backcountry campground (permit needed). ncc-mm.Technical: The club's technical trails are mostly hand-built, with natural or built obstacles such as rocks, roots, logs, drops and jumps.
ncc-mm.Freeride: The club's freeride trails add jumps, ride-on features, gaps, narrow surfaces, wallrides and berms.

ncc-st.Technical: The club's technical trails are mostly hand-built, with natural or built obstacles such as rocks, roots, logs, drops and jumps.

kam-kbrmap.Flow: On the Kamloops Bike Ranch map, flow trails are machine-cut with built features (dirt jumps, berms, gaps, wall rides, narrow surfaces) and need jumping skills.
kam-kbrmap.Technical: On the Kamloops Bike Ranch map, technical trails are mostly hand-built on natural terrain, with rocks, roots, logs, drops and jumps; jumping skills may still be needed.

rev.Freeride: Revelstoke's freeride trails are machine-built and need jumping skills: wider, smoother tread with berms, rollers, jumps and wallrides that get bigger with the grade.
rev.Technical: Revelstoke's technical trails are rougher singletrack with roots, rocks and tighter corners; harder grades add steeps and drops.

sepaq-msa.Cross-country: The Sépaq map lists it in the Parc du Mont-Sainte-Anne XC network, which needs an XC ticket or pass bought at the park.
sepaq-msa.Narrow cross-country: The Sépaq map lists it in the Parc du Mont-Sainte-Anne XC network (XC ticket or pass from the park) and draws it as a narrow trail.
sepaq-msa.Downhill: The Sépaq map lists it in the Station Mont-Sainte-Anne downhill network, which needs a DH ticket or pass bought at the resort.

mh-basler.Two-way: The map says every trail in the network is two-way, so riders may meet others coming the other way.

trca-ah.Single-track: On TRCA's Albion Hills map, single-track trails are for mountain biking only; the wider park trails are shared with hikers. TRCA calls its difficulty ratings a guideline only: trail conditions can change at any time.
